catalogTitle: צד ב: לימודים משיחתן של עבדי אבות

oneLiner.en: Through Eliezer, Rivka and Lavan, the Rav shows that a tzaddik is absorbed in serving Hashem while a rasha is absorbed in this world, and that only an honest Jew is drawn to a tzaddik.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Eliezer, who saw Hashem's help at every step and thanked Him, and teaches that everything is guided by hashgacha pratis, illustrated by the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a worm saved by a wind. He explains why the Torah dwells on the talk of the Avos' servant: Eliezer's level can be understood and learned from. An honest Jew enjoys seeing a tzaddik, while one who is not mocks him, as with Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, the Chasam Sofer and Dovid HaMelech. Rivka, seeing a true tzaddik for the first time, ran home so excited that, against the nature on which the halachos of jewelry on Shabbos rest, she never took off her new bracelets, which Rashi links to the Luchos. Lavan, who sensed no holiness, ran out hoping to swindle a man indifferent to this world. The Rav adds the power of a tzaddik's word, from Avraham's hesped for Sarah to Moshiach.

en: Eliezer recognized that Hashem was guiding every step of his mission and thanked Him for each success; the Rav teaches that every event in the world is controlled by Hashem's hashgacha pratis.
An honest Jew is drawn to a tzaddik and enjoys his ways, while one who is not honest cannot bear him and looks for faults and mocks him.
Rivka, seeing a true tzaddik for the first time, was so taken by Eliezer's prayer and thanks that she did not even take off her new jewelry to show her mother.
The theme of the parsha is that a rasha is absorbed in this world while a tzaddik is absorbed in serving Hashem.
A tzaddik's word has power to enter people's hearts; Avraham's hesped moved the people of Ches to give him the grave, and Moshiach will win the world with his word.
Avraham paid four hundred shekels for the grave because money meant nothing to him beside a mitzvah, and so it is with honest Jews who spend freely on mitzvos.

candidateTopics: the bracelets and the Ten Commandments

title.en: Eliezer sees Hashem's hand in everything

summary.en: The Rav opens with Eliezer's prayer and his bowing in thanks at each success, and teaches that every event is guided by Hashem. He tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a worm saved by a sudden wind and brings Dovid HaMelech's words in Tehillim 73.

title.en: Why the Torah dwells on Eliezer's words

summary.en: The Rav brings that the talk of the Avos' servants is finer than the Torah of the sons, and explains that the Avos are beyond our grasp while Eliezer can be understood and learned from. He then reads Rivka's report to her mother and Lavan's reaction, and explains that an honest Jew enjoys seeing a tzaddik while one who is not looks for faults.

title.en: Tzaddikim are mocked; Rivka sees a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav recalls how in his day not everyone appreciated Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, and notes that even the Chasam Sofer suffered from scoffers. Rivka, raised among reshaim, saw a true tzaddik for the first time when she watched Eliezer daven; and Dovid HaMelech too was mocked by drinkers because he always davened.

title.en: Rivka's report and the jewelry halachah

summary.en: Rivka saw Eliezer bow and thank Hashem and ran home to tell her mother how he davened. The Rav explains that the Torah gives insight into the world, as the halachah that a woman may not go out with jewelry on Shabbos rests on her nature to take it off and show it; then Lavan saw the jewelry and heard her account.

title.en: Rivka keeps her bracelets; Lavan's greed

summary.en: Against that nature, Rivka was so absorbed in the tzaddik that she left the jewelry on her hands. Lavan understood from her that here was a man uninterested in this world and ran out to swindle him; the Rav reads 'standing over the camels' as Eliezer standing over his eye, and says a tzaddik desires only closeness to Hashem.

title.en: The power of a tzaddik's word

summary.en: The Rav asks why Avraham eulogized Sarah before buying a grave, and answers that his words had to make the people want to do a tzaddik's will. He compares Moshiach, who per the Rambam will be known by gathering Israel and building the Beis HaMikdash, and will win people with a word. Avraham paid four hundred shekels gladly, as honest Jews spend freely on mitzvos.

title.en: Holy bracelets and the parsha's message

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rivka kept the bracelets on because, as Rashi says, they corresponded to the Luchos and the Ten Commandments, just as one who davens well does not want to take off his tefillin; the full spelling of 'tzemidim' for Rivka and the short spelling for Lavan show who sensed the holiness. He closes that a rasha is absorbed in this world and a tzaddik in serving Hashem.

catalogTitle: “ויצא יצחק לשוח בשדה” - לבטל הקטרוגים הגדולים על זיווגו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak's going out 'lasuach basadeh' was a Mincha prayer at Har HaMoriah that broke through the great accusations of Lavan-Bilam against his match with Rivkah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Eliezer, Avraham's devoted disciple, who had a personal interest in marrying his own daughter to Yitzchak yet carried out the mission faithfully and even prayed against his own interest. Avraham rejected him as a mechutan because of lineage, and Lavan's words 'come in, blessed of Hashem' show that Eliezer had become blessed. The great novelty is that Lavan, identified with Bilam, the head of the forces of impurity, consented to that blessing. Lavan and Besuel schemed to kill Eliezer and keep Yitzchak from ever marrying; Besuel died of his own poison, and Rivkah's courageous 'I will go' broke Lavan's sorcery, like the Exodus from Egypt. To overcome these accusations Yitzchak prayed Mincha at Har HaMoriah, the source of all matches, hidden in ordinary conversation as the Ramban and Kedushas Levi explain. The Rav closes with Avraham finding Me'aras HaMachpelah through his self-sacrificing hospitality, and urges yeshiva students to give time to bring others close.

en: Eliezer had a personal interest against the match, yet he fulfilled Avraham's mission completely and even prayed for its success against his own interest.
The novelty of 'come in, blessed of Hashem' is that Lavan, who is Bilam, the head of the forces of impurity, himself consented to Eliezer's blessing, as the bad angel answers amen on Erev Shabbos.
Rivkah's courageous 'I will go', said against her powerful brother, broke Lavan's sorcery, and in that merit the Jews left Egypt.
Yitzchak's 'lasuach basadeh' was his Mincha prayer at Har HaMoriah, the place from which all matches come, needed to break the accusations against his match.
The greatness of Mincha is that a person stops in the middle of his work and occupations to speak to Hashem.
Avraham was shown Me'aras HaMachpelah only after he disregarded his own comfort for his guests, which meant Adam and Chava too had to set aside their comfort for him.
Just as Avraham, out of gratitude for being brought close to Hashem, brought others close, every yeshiva student should give some of his time to bring others close.

title.en: Eliezer's interest and the plot of Besuel and Lavan

summary.en: The Rav describes Eliezer as Avraham's disciple who wanted his own daughter for Yitzchak and only noticed his interest on retelling the events. He then tells the Midrash that Besuel tried to poison Eliezer to block Yitzchak's marriage, and identifies Lavan with Bilam.

title.en: Why Avraham refused Eliezer as mechutan

summary.en: Bringing the Tzidkas Hatzaddik, the Rav explains that in a shidduch one avoids a family descended from a non-Jew without conversion, so Avraham refused Eliezer, who was of Canaan. Lavan's 'come in, blessed of Hashem' shows Eliezer became blessed by overcoming his personal interests.

title.en: Eliezer's prayer against his own interest

summary.en: The Rav stresses that Eliezer prayed wholeheartedly for the success of a mission against his own interest, something extraordinary since prayer can only come from the heart. He explains why Eliezer chose chesed as the sign: middos are inherited, and chesed was Avraham's essence.

title.en: The head of impurity agrees to the blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains that usually something must be given to the 'other side', but here Lavan-Bilam, the head of the chariot of impurity, himself said 'blessed of Hashem'. He compares this to the Gemara's two angels on Erev Shabbos, where even the bad angel answers amen.

title.en: 'Let the girl stay with us' and Besuel's death

summary.en: The Rav reads the request that Rivkah stay 'days or ten' as the Midrash's seven days of mourning or twelve months, since Besuel had just died of his own poison, and asks what kind of answer 'do not delay me' is. He explains that Lavan, being Bilam, held Yaakov for twenty years with sorcery and wanted to hold Eliezer the same way.

title.en: Lavan's diplomacy and Rivkah's 'I will go'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that in the merit of Rivkah's 'I will go' the Jews left Egypt. He explains Lavan's request as diplomatic speech hiding Besuel's death, Eliezer's veiled reply showing he knew, and Rivkah standing up against her brother's sorcery.

title.en: A new creation, and leaving like Egypt

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham was a new creation with no ties to Terach, and Rivkah likewise owed her father nothing, so she could refuse to stay. He compares her last-minute departure with self-sacrifice to the haste of the Exodus, breaking a sorcery that kept anyone from leaving.

title.en: 'From Hashem' means from Har HaMoriah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'the matter came from Hashem' as coming from Har HaMoriah, where Rivkah's birth was announced, and brings Tosafos that Yitzchak's 'sadeh' was Har HaMoriah. In the frightening twenty-four hours when Lavan-Bilam sought to swallow Klal Yisroel, Yitzchak prayed there, at the place where all matches originate.

title.en: Prayer hidden in conversation

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Ramban explains 'lasuach' as Yitzchak strolling with friends, and answers with the Kedushas Levi that tzaddikim clothe prayer in ordinary talk so it can pass the accusing angels. He tells of the Kedushas Levi talking in the kitchen at Mezritch and of a tzaddik's complaint about milk.

title.en: The greatness of Mincha

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Ramban hints at how great the accusation was, and that Yitzchak's talk with his friends was his Mincha. Mincha's greatness is stopping in the middle of work to speak to Hashem, at a time of strict judgment, and this prayer broke the kitrug; he then urges preparing for the blessing of Shabbos.

title.en: How Avraham found Me'aras HaMachpelah

summary.en: The Rav brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Avraham found Me'aras HaMachpelah while chasing the calf for his guests, and asks why it was revealed then, decades before he needed it. He brings a Midrash that Adam and Chava did not want Avraham there, and the halacha that one may not make a neighbor uncomfortable.

title.en: Hospitality beyond one's own comfort

summary.en: The Rav describes Avraham, ninety-nine years old on the third day after his milah on a hot day, running after guests with no thought for his comfort, so Adam and Chava had to yield their comfort for him. He explains that Avraham's hospitality brought people under the wings of the Shechinah, out of gratitude that Hashem had brought him close.

title.en: Giving time to bring others close

summary.en: The Rav notes the many children in yeshivos and the far greater number without Torah education, and says every yeshiva student should feel Avraham's gratitude and give at least a half hour a week to learn with others. He explains that giving time, like giving tzedakah, causes no loss but brings more.

catalogTitle: Explaining יצחק's Fondness of עשו and the meaning of ויגדלו הנערים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak loved Esav because the food Esav brought him was really prepared by Yaakov with kedushah, so Yitzchak took Esav for a hidden tzaddik.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the many blessings of Parshas Toldos, the sixth sedra, and links the number six and the root of the word bracha to doubling. He then asks how Yitzchak could prefer Esav because of his hunting, or be fooled by him. Through Rashi's statement that the twins 'grew up' at thirteen, though the arithmetic makes them fifteen, he explains that on the day a tzaddik passes away all his days come down to escort him, as with Eliyahu and Elisha. Since every tzaddik has an opposing rasha, Nimrod died the day Avraham did: Yaakov absorbed the kedushah at Avraham's bedside, while Esav absorbed the tumah of the slain Nimrod. That day Esav became a heretic, so his own shechitah could not be eaten. Yaakov therefore prepared the food that Esav brought; Yitzchak sensed its kedushah and thought Esav a hidden tzaddik, until the day of the brachos.

en: Toldos, the sixth sedra, is full of blessing; the number six and the letters of the root of bracha express doubling, and the vessel that holds blessing is shalom.
On the day of a tzaddik's passing all his days come down to escort him, so he is greater that day than ever, which is why Eliyahu could give Elisha a double portion only then.
Every tzaddik has an opposing rasha of his measure, so Nimrod died the day Avraham died and Esav died the day Yaakov was buried.
On the day of Avraham's passing Yaakov absorbed great kedushah at his bedside and Esav absorbed great tumah from the slain Nimrod; this is how 'the boys grew up' at fifteen.
A real tzaddik measures food by its kedushah, not its taste, and kedushah enters food through the intention with which it is prepared.
Yaakov prepared the food that Esav brought Yitzchak, so Yitzchak sensed kedushah in it and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik.

candidateTopics: the day of a tzaddik's passing

title.en: Toldos, the sedra of blessing

summary.en: The Rav shows that every aliyah of Toldos contains a blessing, ties the sixth sedra, the sixth aliyah and the sixth hakafah to blessing, and explains the root of bracha as doubling. He ends with the Mishnah that only shalom is a vessel for blessing.

title.en: Why did Yitzchak love Esav?

summary.en: Setting aside the topic of emunah for later sedros, the Rav brings the passuk that Yitzchak loved Esav for his hunting, with Rashi (Esav trapped his father) and Onkelos (Yitzchak ate from his hunting). He asks how Yitzchak could prefer Esav for good food or be fooled by him, and notes the same pattern at the brachos.

title.en: The day the bechorah was sold

summary.en: Following Rashi, the Rav describes the day Avraham passed away: Yaakov cooked round lentils as a mourner's meal, and Esav came home after five sins, among them killing Nimrod for Adam's garment and denying techiyas hameisim. This made Esav an apikores, and the Rav asks how Yitzchak could then eat meat Esav brought.

title.en: Vayigdelu hanearim: thirteen or fifteen?

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that 'the boys grew up' means they turned thirteen, and shows by the ages in the pesukim that on the day Avraham died they were fifteen. He rejects calling it a misprint, since one becomes grown at thirteen, not fifteen.

title.en: All one's days come on the last day

summary.en: The Rav asks how Eliyahu could give Elisha double his own spirit, and answers with the Agra deKallah, the Bnei Yissaschar and the Zohar that time is a creation, each day ascends with what was done in it, and on a tzaddik's last day all his days return to escort him. So Moshe said 'today I am 120', and the Chasam Sofer grieved that he was not at his rebbe's bedside.

title.en: Every tzaddik has his opposing rasha

summary.en: From the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya on his deathbed, the Rav explains that each tzaddik has a rasha of his measure who keeps the scale balanced. Nimrod, whose name means rebellion, was Avraham's opponent, and he was killed the very day Avraham passed away.

title.en: Kedushah at one bedside, tumah at the other

summary.en: The Rav shows that Esav was Yaakov's opponent and died the day Yaakov was buried, as the Gemara in Sotah relates. Then he explains the day Avraham died: Yaakov at the bedside absorbed the kedushah of Avraham's 175 years, while Esav absorbed the tumah around the slain Nimrod, so both 'grew up' that day.

title.en: Michrah kayom: two philosophies

summary.en: The Rav reads 'sell me as this day' as Yaakov telling Esav that the nature of this day decides who needs the bechorah. He contrasts the tzaddik's 'today to do them, tomorrow the reward' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die', and Esav agrees that by his view he has no use for it.

title.en: A tzaddik tastes kedushah, not flavor

summary.en: The Rav explains that a real tzaddik enjoys life through Torah and mitzvos but measures food by its kedushah, telling of the Yismach Moshe who ate soapy water unaware. Kedushah enters food through kavanah, as with a wife cooking for Shabbos, matzah baked lishmah and the korban Pesach; then he begins his answer: Yaakov prepared Yitzchak's food so that Yitzchak would not sense Esav's treif shechitah.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe and the borrowed plates

summary.en: To show that tzaddikim sense what they may not eat, the Rav tells a story he heard from an eyewitness: the Slonimer Rebbe, visiting Yerushalayim, would not eat from plates borrowed from a bearded man who had not immersed them, and contrasted him with the beardless host.

title.en: Yitzchak's mistake and the day of the brachos

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Yitzchak sensed kedushah in the food Esav brought, which Yaakov had made, and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik; this reconciles Onkelos and Rashi. On Pesach night Rivka's prophecy forced Yaakov to bring the food himself, and the truth came out. He closes with a story of a tzaddik whose chulent tasted of his own handful of beans.

catalogTitle: זיווגים - משל לענינים גבוהים עד מאד

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the bond between husband and wife, rooted in the place of the mizbe'ach, is a mashal for the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael and between every Jew and Eretz Yisrael, and draws from Parshas Chayei Sarah how a shidduch should be pursued.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that the match of Yitzchak and Rivkah 'came from Hashem' from Har HaMoriah. He gathers three puzzles: Miriam bas Bilgah kicking the mizbe'ach, Maseches Gittin opening with a get from overseas, and the mizbe'ach shedding tears over a divorce. Through the Avnei Nezer he explains that a wife senses her bond to her husband as Klal Yisrael senses its bond to Hashem, a sensitivity special to Shevet Levi. The bond comes from Adam and Chava being one, formed from the earth of the mizbe'ach, which spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael; exile is like a get. He interprets the mizbe'ach's measurements in the three Batei Mikdash, returns to Miriam bas Bilgah and the Greeks, and explains why Rivkah was born at the akeidah. The second half turns to the parsha as the parsha of zivugim: a zivug is decreed, yet a person can spoil it, so he needs tefillah, careful hishtadlus and unlowered standards, as Avraham, Eliezer and the daughters of Tzelafchad show.

en: The bond between husband and wife is a mashal for the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and a wife instinctively senses whether that bond is intact.
Adam and Chava, and with them every future husband and wife, were once one, formed from the earth of the place of the mizbe'ach, so the mizbe'ach bears witness to every zivug.
Every Jew's root is in Eretz Yisrael, which is an extension of the mizbe'ach, so exile from the land is like a get, and this is why Maseches Gittin opens with a get from 'medinas hayam'.
Rivkah was born at the time of the akeidah because the akeidah took place on the mekom hamizbe'ach, the place from which zivugim come.
A zivug is decreed from Heaven, yet a person with free choice can spoil it, so he must daven and make careful hishtadlus according to his level.
In a shidduch one must not lower one's standards of yiras shamayim, even if it means waiting, as the daughters of Tzelafchad waited until forty for a fitting match.

candidateTopics: the mizbe'ach and the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael
the akeidah and the birth of Rivkah

title.en: Learning the parsha of the Avos; 'from Hashem came the matter'

summary.en: The Rav says the parshiyos of Bereishis must be learned in depth because they hold the foundations of emunah and show how great the Avos were. He then brings the passuk 'from Hashem came the matter' and the Midrash that the match of Yitzchak and Rivkah came from Har HaMoriah, and says he will explain it.

title.en: Three puzzles: Miriam bas Bilgah, Gittin and the weeping mizbe'ach

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara at the end of Sukkah about Miriam bas Bilgah, who married a Greek officer and kicked the mizbe'ach. He asks why Maseches Gittin opens with a get brought from overseas and why, at its end, specifically the mizbe'ach sheds tears over a divorce, and brings the Avnei Nezer's question why a bas Levi who remarried on one witness loses her right to maaser.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer: the sensitivity of Shevet Levi

summary.en: Following the Avnei Nezer, the Rav explains that the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael is like that of chassan and kallah, and a wife senses her bond to her husband. Shevet Levi is especially sensitive to this bond, which is why they did not serve the eigel; a bas Levi who believed one witness that her husband died showed she lacks Levi's sensitivity, so she loses maaser.

title.en: Adam and Chava from the earth of the mizbe'ach

summary.en: The Rav explains that the bond of husband and wife comes from Adam and Chava having been one body, and that they were formed from the earth of the place of the mizbe'ach, the place of peace between Hashem and Klal Yisrael. Explaining zivug rishon as the match set at creation, he answers why the mizbe'ach weeps over one who divorces his first wife: it knows they were once together beneath it.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, exile and the get from overseas

summary.en: The Rav explains that all of Eretz Yisrael is an extension of the mizbe'ach and every Jew has his root there, so exile is called gerushin. 'Medinas hayam' alludes to the far edge of the world and of history shown to Moshe, where Jews drown in heresy and doubt; this is why Gittin opens with a get from medinas hayam, and he adds the Pri Tzaddik that the churban is like a get.

title.en: The mizbe'ach of Shlomo: twenty-eight amos

summary.en: The Rav brings the measurements of the mizbe'ach and the Gemara in Zevachim that Shlomo's mizbe'ach was smaller because he did not know its exact place, while the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah learned it could be sixty amos. He explains Shlomo's twenty-eight amos as 'koach' of 'the power of His deeds He told His people', alluding to the first passuk of Bereishis, which Rashi says speaks of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Lamed-bais of the second Mikdash and sixty for the third

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the second Beis HaMikdash most of Klal Yisrael lived abroad but were in Eretz Yisrael with their hearts, so its mizbe'ach was thirty-two, 'lev', the last lamed and first beis of the Torah. The third will have sixty amos, like the letters of Birkas Kohanim ending in shalom, the first two Batei Mikdash together making up that sixty.

title.en: Why Miriam bas Bilgah kicked the mizbe'ach

summary.en: Returning to the end of Sukkah, the Rav explains that Sukkos expresses the bond of Hashem and Klal Yisrael that the mizbe'ach represents. Miriam bas Bilgah betrayed not only her husband but the nimshal, Hashem Himself, and since the mizbe'ach testified to her true zivug, her guilty conscience could not bear it and she kicked it; the Greeks' decrees aimed to break this bond, and the miracle came through Shevet Levi.

title.en: Rivkah born at the akeidah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that after the akeidah Avraham regretted not having married off Yitzchak, and was told Rivkah had just been born. With the Arizal's words on Yitzchak at the akeidah and the Gemara that the place of the mizbe'ach is where Yitzchak was bound, he explains that the akeidah's place, the source of zivugim, overcame the accusations against Yitzchak having children, and this is 'the matter came from Har HaMoriah'.

title.en: The parsha of zivugim: decree and tefillah

summary.en: The Rav calls Chayei Sarah the parsha of zivugim and brings the Gemara in Moed Katan that one may arrange a match on Chol HaMoed lest another precede him through tefillah, though a heavenly voice declares each match. He brings the Sefer Chassidim that a zivug taken through tefillah does not last, the Chasam Sofer on a word spoken in a shidduch, and the Midrash that matching couples is as hard as splitting the sea.

title.en: Why the Torah tells the shidduch of Yitzchak

summary.en: The Rav explains that Me'aras HaMachpelah belonged to Avraham and Sarah as a zivug, and that the Torah relates the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivkah at length to teach parents how to make a shidduch. He says a true zivug is a person's greatest success, shows Yitzchak and Rivkah in the acrostic of Nishmas, and says every Yitzchak's success depends on his Rivkah.

title.en: Free choice and hishtadlus; Avraham's oath to Eliezer

summary.en: The Rav says that though a zivug is decreed, a person with free choice can spoil it, so each must make hishtadlus according to his level and, if unsure, consult a chacham or tzaddik. Avraham, who trusted Eliezer with all his wealth, still made him swear when it came to Yitzchak's shidduch, showing how seriously it must be taken.

title.en: Tefillah and not lowering standards

summary.en: The Rav points out that Avraham and Eliezer both davened, and says one must daven for a shidduch since one does not know what is good. He says one must be stubborn and not lower one's standard of yiras shamayim, and that Eliezer spoke openly of Hashem to Lavan and Besuel, presenting Avraham as he truly was.

title.en: The daughters of Tzelafchad waited

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Bava Basra praising the daughters of Tzelafchad, who married only at forty because they waited for a match fitting for them. Orphans of a father executed as the mekoshesh, they did not lower their standards and trusted Hashem would give them their zivug; he adds that tzaddikim like Yitzchak and Yaakov also married late.

title.en: Waiting, true wealth, and learning the parsha

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Adam searched among all the animals before Chava was brought to him, showing that one must wait until the time comes. He says one should present oneself truthfully and seek a home that is a dwelling for the Shechinah, explains Eliezer's gift of a beka as wealth meaning Torah, says no one can spoil what is decreed, and closes that the parsha must be learned for its lessons, not as history.

catalogTitle: יש סודות עמוקים בזיווגים' אליעזר שדכן ראשון שבתורה...

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Eliezer, the first shadchan in the Torah, is never named in the parsha: Hashem Himself made the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka without the lie every other shidduch needs, and he goes on to show how Rivka and Lavan each saw Eliezer's avodas Hashem through their own eyes.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Eliezer's name never appears in the parsha, though a name expresses a person's mission and Eliezer's mission was this shidduch. After the Midrash of the matron who tried to match a thousand couples, he explains that shidduchim come straight from Hashem, and cites a sefer that no shidduch can be closed without a lie; this is why the shadchan is paid, and R' Yaakov Emden's reading of the word shadchan says the same. The shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka needed no lie, 'in the way of truth', so the helper's name is left out. He then describes Eliezer's prayers as a picture of an oved Hashem, and shows how Rivka, seeing a tzaddik for the first time, repeated every word and gesture, while Lavan saw only money. He ends with Avraham's hesped for Sarah, the Midrash of Esther's 127 provinces, and how Sarah made up her first three years at night.

en: A person's name holds his mission in the world, and a change of name can bring a new mission; Eliezer's name, 'my G-d is help', fits his mission of bringing Yitzchak his 'helpmate'.
Shidduchim are Hashem's own domain, and every couple has a story of how Hashem brought them together.

Because a shidduch is so holy, it can only come down into this world wrapped in a lie, and that is why the shadchan must be paid; the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka needed no lie, so Eliezer is not named.
A person with a pure heart enjoys seeing a tzaddik's avodah, while one cut off from it finds no grace in it and only criticizes, as Dovid HaMelech describes his mockers.
Rivka was so taken by Eliezer's avodas Hashem that she did not even show her mother the new bracelets, while Lavan saw only the wealth.
Esther merited 127 provinces for Sarah's 127 equally good years, because Sarah made up her first three years by serving Hashem at night.

title.en: Why Eliezer's name is never mentioned

summary.en: The Rav notes that Eliezer, the shadchan for Yitzchak, is called only 'the man' and 'the servant' in the whole parsha. He explains that a name holds a person's mission, brings Rashi on the angel's words to Yaakov and the custom of changing a sick person's name, and asks why Eliezer's name, which fits his mission of bringing the 'ezer', is left out.

title.en: The matron's thousand matches

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash of the matron who claimed she too could make matches, paired a thousand servants in one night and found them battered by morning. He contrasts people who go through life without seeing Hashem with those who see His hashgachah daily, and says every couple can tell how Hashem brought about their shidduch.

title.en: The shadchan's lie and his pay

summary.en: The Rav cites a sefer that no shidduch can be closed without a lie, because something so holy can only come into the world through something lower. This answers why the shadchan must be paid, as in R' Yaakov Emden's reading of the word shadchan. The shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka needed no lie, 'in the way of truth', so the name Eliezer, the helper, is left out.

title.en: Eliezer's prayers: a picture of avodah

summary.en: The Rav describes Eliezer's prayer at the well and his thanks to Hashem as a picture of an oved Hashem that should bring a learner to tears. He brings Rashi that the talk of the servants of the Avos is dearer than the Torah of the sons, since the Avos' avodah was hidden and the servant's is open, and asks what Rivka's report 'like these words' and Lavan's 'so the man spoke to me' mean.

title.en: Finding grace in a tzaddik's avodah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew with a pure heart enjoys mitzvos and finds grace in a tzaddik's avodah, while someone cut off from it is bored by Shabbos and only criticizes. He brings Dovid HaMelech's words in Tehillim about those who sat and mocked him over drink, while he continued to pray to Hashem.

title.en: Rivka sees a tzaddik for the first time

summary.en: Rivka grew up in the house of Besuel and Lavan and had never seen a true tzaddik; Eliezer, a talmid chacham who taught his master's Torah, bowed and prayed before her, and she ran and repeated every word and gesture. The Rav then turns to the halachic background of women's jewelry on Shabbos, from the perek in Maseches Shabbos, to set up his next question.

title.en: The bracelets still on her hands

summary.en: The Rav asks why Lavan saw the bracelets still on Rivka's hands, when a girl with new jewelry would take it off to show it. He answers that she was so excited by Eliezer's avodah that she spoke only of that, while Lavan concluded that a pious man who does not know what money is could be exploited and ran out to him; in the end Lavan received only delicacies.

title.en: Avraham's hesped and Eliezer's gifts

summary.en: The Rav asks why Avraham eulogized Sarah before buying a grave, the reverse of the usual order, and explains that his words of mussar broke the Bnei Ches' greed so they would sell the Me'aras HaMachpelah at a fair price. He contrasts tzaddikim, for whom this world is passing, with others, then shows from Rashi and the Bnei Yissaschar that Eliezer's gifts carried meaning, the luchos and the Ten Commandments, which Lavan could not see.

title.en: Esther's 127 provinces and Sarah's nights

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains the Midrash in which Rabbi Akiva woke his sleeping audience by saying that Esther ruled 127 provinces because she descended from Sarah, who lived 127 years. He asks why Esther got all 127 when Sarah did not serve Hashem in her first three years, and answers that she made them up by rising at night, which Avraham praised in his Eishes Chayil hesped; this is what Rabbi Akiva hinted to the sleepers.

catalogTitle: דרוש על "כי ציד בפיו"; וחילוק בין שיטת יעקב לשיטת עשו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Yitzchak needed tasty food to bless, why he loved Esav "ki tzayid befiv", and how the way of Yaakov, closing oneself to the pleasures of this world, differs from the way of Esav.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with stories of tzaddikim who did not notice what they ate, and asks why Yitzchak needed tasty food before blessing. He explains that a person needs new heavenly influence at every moment, and food carries sparks of holiness; a tzaddik senses that holiness, as stories of the Slonimer's disciple and the Belzer Rav show. Rivka never told Yitzchak who Esav was; Yitzchak took Esav for a hidden tzaddik, because the food Esav brought was really prepared and slaughtered by Yaakov. This explains "ki tzayid befiv" and the extra hei in "tzeidah". The blessing, measure for measure, was food that brings Torah, and above all G-dliness. The Rav then contrasts Yaakov's way, closing the door to worldly pleasure to taste the World to Come, with Esav's "eat and drink, for tomorrow we die". He ends with stability, serving Hashem when the heart is closed, and the Yismach Moshe on Yaakov receiving the blessing in Esav's clothes.

en: A person needs a constant renewal of heavenly influence, and food carries sparks of G-dliness that the one who eats takes into himself.
Yitzchak wanted tasty food in order to absorb more holiness before blessing, since a tzaddik senses the holiness or its absence in food.
Yitzchak loved Esav because he took him for a hidden tzaddik; the holiness he felt in the food came from Yaakov, who secretly prepared it.
Yaakov's portion is G-dliness and the World to Come; Esav's is the pleasures of this world, and the two cannot rise together.
Only one who closes himself to the pull of this world's pleasures can taste the sweetness of serving Hashem.
A person's true level is measured in times of difficulty and closed-heartedness, by his deeds, not by moments of inspiration.

candidateTopics: Yaakov and Esav: this world and the World to Come

title.en: Tzaddikim who did not notice their food

summary.en: Starting from Rivka's plan to prepare tasty food for Yitzchak, the Rav tells how the Yismach Moshe once ate a pot of dishwater without noticing, and how a tzaddik in Tzfas, deep in learning, drank glasses of brandy thinking it was water. He concludes that such things meant nothing to tzaddikim.

title.en: Why Yitzchak needed tasty food

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yitzchak needed tasty food before blessing, and why a blessing the Midrash reads as Torah is phrased as plenty of grain and wine. He then asks about "ki tzayid befiv": Onkelos reads it as eating from Esav's hunt, which does not fit the words, and Rashi reads it as Esav deceiving his father; he also notes the extra hei in "tzeidah".

title.en: Eating to absorb new holiness

summary.en: The Rav explains that every moment brings a new heavenly influence, and a person renews himself through tefillah and through eating, since food holds sparks of G-dliness. He brings the Leviasan feast, matzah as the vessel of freedom, and Shabbos food, and stresses preparing and eating food with holiness.

title.en: Tzaddikim sense holiness in food

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak wanted tasty food to absorb holiness before blessing, since tzaddikim sense the holiness in food. He tells of a disciple of the Slonimer who could not taste meat slaughtered by a shochet who had not gone to the mikveh, and of the Belzer Rav who sensed that his dentist had not gone to the mikveh.

title.en: Esav as a hidden tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yitzchak could enjoy food brought by Esav. Rivka never told Yitzchak who Esav was; Yitzchak thought him a hidden tzaddik, like Reb Shmuel of Karov, because the food was really prepared by Yaakov. This explains "ki tzayid befiv" on both its readings.

title.en: The hidden hei and the night of the blessings

summary.en: The Rav explains the extra hei in "tzeidah" as a hint to the five laws of shechitah, showing that Yaakov did the slaughtering, written but not read so that Yitzchak would not hear. On the night of the blessings Esav brought dogs and Yitzchak sensed Gehinnom, and Yaakov's holy food earned a blessing measure for measure: food that brings Torah.

title.en: The blessing of G-dliness

summary.en: Bringing the Midrash that "veyiten lecha haElokim" means G-dliness itself, the Rav explains that food eaten with holiness shows in one's learning and davening, that oneg Shabbos is Yaakov's portion, and that the heart of the blessing is that Hashem gives G-dliness to whoever opens himself to it. He brings the words to Chana, a passuk in Tehillim, and the Lechovitcher's story of the simple Jew's beard.

title.en: Close one door to open the other

summary.en: The Rav teaches that one must close the door to this world's pleasures to open it to holiness, each according to his level. He explains the two forces of Yaakov and Esav through Rashi's "when one rises the other falls" and the Tzvi LaTzaddik on Yerushalayim and Tzor, and says that only to the extent one shuts out worldly pleasure does one taste Shabbos, learning and davening.

title.en: Two outlooks: today and tomorrow

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Yaakov's outlook, "today to do them, tomorrow to receive their reward", with Esav's "eat and drink, for tomorrow we die", and shows how Esav's outlook led him to sell the birthright. A tzaddik's share of this world is only a means, like the money one needs for mitzvos, as Reb Meir of Premishlan taught.

title.en: Why Yitzchak left Rechovos

summary.en: The Rav notes that tzaddikim are troubled when things suddenly go too well. Yitzchak dug the wells Esek and Sitnah amid strife, and at Rechovos finally had peace, yet he left for Be'er Sheva, because he knew a person does not come to this world for comfort but to serve Hashem.

title.en: Stability and the test of a closed heart

summary.en: From Rivka's anguish over a child who seemed drawn both to the beis medrash and to idolatry, the Rav speaks of people who are good only in a good environment, and teaches that true fear of Heaven does not change with place or time. A person is measured in his low times, not his inspired ones; he brings the Yaaros Devash on "simeini kachosam al libecha": the heart is sometimes open and sometimes closed, but the hands, the deeds, are always visible.

title.en: The blessing in Esav's clothes

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe's dream: Yaakov and Esav were born together so that each would have free choice by rubbing against the other, and Yaakov had to receive the blessing dressed in Esav's clothes, showing that even in such a state a Jew is fit for blessing. He closes with Rabbi Meir's view that Jews are always called Hashem's children, and that every Jew should rejoice that he is a part of Yaakov.

catalogTitle: The פרשה of ברכה Ushers in כסלו the Month of ברכה The Opposing Philosophies of the צדיק and the רשע (Explanation of the meaning of ויגדלו הנערים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Parshas Toldos, the first sedra of Kislev, is full of bracha, and explains 'vayigdelu hane'arim' through the opposing philosophies of the tzaddik and the rasha and the power of a tzaddik's last day.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Kislev, the month of bracha: Chanukah's candles are added night by night, and the letters of the word bracha each mean addition, one becoming two. Six is the number of bracha, so Toldos, the sixth sedra and the first Shabbos of Kislev, has every aliyah end in bracha and uses the word 32 times. He then explains Yaakov's 'michra kayom': the tzaddik sees today as the time to do mitzvos and the rasha sees it as the time to enjoy. Rashi says the boys grew up at thirteen, but by count they were fifteen, on the day Avraham died. Using Eliyahu's double portion to Elisha, he explains that on a person's last day all his days gather, and that every tzaddik has a matched opponent. Yaakov absorbed Avraham's kedusha while Esav absorbed Nimrod's tumah. Finally he explains Yitzchak's love of matamim and of Esav through the kedusha placed in food.

en: Kislev is the month of bracha, and the word bracha itself means addition: in units, tens and hundreds its letters each turn one into two.
Toldos, the sixth sedra, is the sedra of bracha: every aliyah ends with a bracha and the word appears 32 times.
The tzaddik and the rasha hold opposing philosophies of 'today': for one it is the time to do mitzvos, for the other the time to enjoy before death.
On the day a person leaves the world all his days gather to him, so one present at a tzaddik's passing can receive far more than usual.
'Vayigdelu hane'arim' means that at fifteen, on the day Avraham died and Nimrod was killed, Yaakov grew in kedusha and Esav grew in tumah.
Tzaddikim do not enjoy the physical taste of food, but they feel and enjoy the kedusha put into it by the one who prepares it.

title.en: Kislev, Chanukah and the word bracha

summary.en: The Rav opens with Kislev as a month whose whole character is Chanukah, a Yom Tov of bracha since its candles are added night by night. He explains that each letter of the word bracha means addition, one becoming two in units, tens and hundreds.

title.en: Six is bracha: the sixth sedra

summary.en: The Rav explains that six is the number of bracha: the vav means 'and', Yosef is the sixth of the Ushpizin, and Toldos is the sixth sedra. He shows that every aliyah of Toldos ends with a bracha, that shishi carries a double bracha, and that the word appears 32 times in the sedra.

title.en: Being a vessel, and the tzaddik's 'today'

summary.en: The Rav says that Shabbos is the source of bracha and a person must make himself a whole vessel to hold it. Turning to Yaakov's words 'michra kayom', he introduces two opposing philosophies and describes the tzaddik's: life passes fast, its purpose is Olam Haba, and today is for doing mitzvos.

title.en: The rasha's philosophy and the sale

summary.en: The Rav describes the rasha's philosophy, to eat and drink today because tomorrow one dies, and explains the sale of the bechorah through it: to Esav it was worth nothing, to Yaakov everything. He then brings 'vayigdelu hane'arim' with Rashi's thirteen years, and Rashi that on that day Avraham died and Yaakov prepared the mourner's meal.

title.en: Why fifteen, and Elisha's double portion

summary.en: By a calculation of the years the Rav shows that on that day the twins turned fifteen, as Rabbeinu Bachya insists, and asks why the pasuk calls them grown at fifteen and not at thirteen. To answer he brings Eliyahu's ascent, Elisha's request for a double share of his spirit, and the Gemara showing Elisha did everything twice.

title.en: All one's days gather on the last day

summary.en: The Rav asks how Eliyahu could give double what he had, and answers that each day a person is only what he accomplished that day, but on his last day all his days come to accompany him, as the mefarshim explain Moshe's 'I am 120 years today'. He adds the Chasam Sofer's lament that he was not at his rebbe Rav Nosson Adler's bedside.

title.en: Every tzaddik has his matched opponent

summary.en: The Rav explains that every person comes down with an opposing force: Avraham had Nimrod, Yitzchak Yishmael, Yaakov Lavan and Esav. From Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's answer to his talmidim he shows that the opponent is matched to the tzaddik and leaves with him: Nimrod died the day Avraham died, and Esav was killed at Yaakov's burial.

title.en: Vayigdelu: kedusha and tumah absorbed

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov stood at Avraham's bedside and absorbed the kedusha of his whole life, while that same day Esav killed Nimrod and absorbed all the tumah of Nimrod's life. This is 'vayigdelu hane'arim': both grew great at fifteen, one in kedusha and one in tumah. He then turns to Yitzchak's request for matamim before the brachos.

title.en: Tzaddikim who do not taste their food

summary.en: Recalling that a tzaddik has no interest in what Olam Hazeh offers, the Rav tells how the Yismach Moshe ate dishwater as soup, and how the Levushei Serad drank glass after glass of whiskey thinking it was water. He mentions a Yid who for forty years did not know how food tastes, and asks why then Yitzchak wanted matamim.

title.en: The cholent's secret ingredient

summary.en: The Rav tells of a rav who could not reproduce a rebbe's cholent at home until the rebbetzin revealed that the rebbe dropped in beans saying 'lekavod Shabbos kodesh'. From this he explains that food holds ruchniyus, that kedusha enters food prepared for learning, davening and Shabbos, and that tzaddikim enjoy that kedusha, a taste of Olam Haba, not the physical taste.

title.en: Rivka's food, Yitzchak's love, and the application

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yitzchak could eat meat Esav, an apikores, had slaughtered, and answers that Rivka prepared it herself with kedusha, so Yitzchak felt kedusha and thought Esav a hidden tzaddik. When Esav finally brought his own meat Yitzchak felt Gehinom enter. He concludes that whoever makes something puts his neshama into it, applying this to food, restaurants and tefillin, and wishes a good Shabbos.

catalogTitle: ביאור על "פני כל אחיו נפל'" וסמך לי' "אלה תולדות יצחק"

oneLiner.en: Building on the Ba'al HaTurim that Yishmael's fall at the end of Chayei Sarah is followed by 'Eleh toldos Yitzchak', the Rav explains why Yishmael rose so high in our time as a sign of the coming geulah, and that Torah study, especially teaching others, and tzedakah are what bring it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Bnei Yissaschar: the Torah reading of Yishmael's success on Rosh Hashanah arouses mercy, since if Avraham's son Yishmael is so blessed, Yaakov's children surely are. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that Yishmael's fall precedes 'Eleh toldos Yitzchak', the sprouting of Moshiach, and explains the sedra's name: Yaakov receives the blessings while dressed in Esav's garments. Through Rabbeinu Bachya and the Zohar he shows that the galus of Yishmael is the deepest spiritually, a maidservant inheriting her mistress, and that Yishmael holds Eretz Yisrael through an empty bris. He explains that a time of the ketz brings accusation and upheaval, that the world's degeneration is demolition before rebuilding, and that Yishmael was made great only to fall. From Rashi on Yishmael's years he derives that Yaakov's toil in Torah brought Yishmael's death, and he urges Torah of chesed, teaching others, tzedakah, drawing in those without yichus, and kindling new light in Kislev.

en: Following the Ba'al HaTurim, the fall of Yishmael ('al pnei chol echav nafal') is the signal for the rise of Yitzchak's line and the coming of Moshiach ben Dovid.
Yishmael's great success comes only because he is a child of Avraham, so Avraham's true children, Yitzchak's seed, will surely receive blessing even when they seem clothed in Esav's garments.
The galus of Yishmael, though physically lighter than the galus of Edom, is spiritually the lowest, because it is a maidservant taking over from her mistress.
Yishmael was made so great in our time so that his fall should be great, and the greater the fall, the greater the rise of Yitzchak's line, the sprouting of ben Dovid.
Yishmael died when Yaakov began toiling in Torah at the house of Shem and Ever, which shows that Yaakov's Torah brings Yishmael's fall and the geulah.
Israel is redeemed through Torah and tzedakah, and Torah taught to others is 'Toras chesed', a form of tzedakah that even bachurim without money can give.
In tefillah b'tzibur the merits of everyone combine, so choosing a tzaddik ben rasha as shaliach tzibur loses nothing and adds the merit of drawing near the distant.

title.en: Yishmael's fall and the toldos of Yitzchak

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar on why Yishmael's blessings are read on Rosh Hashanah, then the Ba'al HaTurim linking 'al pnei chol echav nafal' to 'Eleh toldos Yitzchak'. He explains the name Toldos through Yaakov receiving the blessings in Esav's garments.

title.en: Bread and water for the enemy; the galus of Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbeinu Bachya that Avraham foresaw Yishmael's great hatred of Israel and therefore gave him bread and water, as the passuk in Mishlei advises with an enemy. He explains that the galus of Yishmael, though physically easier than Edom, is spiritually the lowest: a maidservant inheriting her mistress.

title.en: An empty bris for an empty land

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Bnei Yishmael were given Eretz Yisrael, empty, in the merit of their empty milah. He contrasts it with a Jew's bris, a lifelong task of guarding the eyes, the tongue and the bris itself.

title.en: 'Drive out the maidservant' and the accusation at the ketz

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Sarah's demand to drive out Yishmael with today's nations who want to drive Jews out of Eretz Yisrael, and asks why it happens now. He explains the two kinds of geulah time, and that when a ketz arrives the Satan accuses, so that a missed ketz brings harsh decrees, as in the years of Tach and in the 1940s.

title.en: A ketz in the air and the Chofetz Chaim's Mississippi

summary.en: The Rav brings a ketz from the Ta'amei HaMitzvos of Rabbi Chaim Vital and asks whether we are ready to greet Moshiach. He notes that even the world's experts call the situation a powder keg, and tells how the Chofetz Chaim in Radin spoke of the Mississippi flood as a call to teshuvah.

title.en: Demolition before building; Yishmael made great to fall

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara's picture of a degenerate world before Moshiach as demolishing the old to build the new, brings Rabbeinu Bachya that the nations will agree to Yaakov's blessings and Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi's poem of the maidservant, and concludes that Yishmael was made great so that his fall would be great.

title.en: Torah and tzedakah; Yaakov's learning and Yishmael's death

summary.en: The Rav says that Moshiach is brought by Torah and tzedakah, not by rallies, citing the passuk of Tziyon redeemed through tzedakah and the Or HaChaim. He then brings Rashi that Yishmael's years are counted to reveal Yaakov's fourteen years at Shem and Ever, and derives that Yaakov's toil in Torah caused Yishmael's death.

title.en: Toras chesed: learning with others

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that Torah taught to others is 'Toras chesed', and the passuk of the rich and poor meeting, where Hashem made both. He calls for renewing the program in which older bachurim give half an hour to learn with weaker younger ones, since bachurim can give tzedakah with their Torah and time.

title.en: The chassid who gives of himself

summary.en: The Rav brings a saying comparing the chassid to sugar that dissolves into the tea, and a saying in the name of the Ba'al HaTanya on burning nail clippings even at a cost to oneself. He adds that giving time to another does not make one poorer, citing the Gemara on tzedakah and the early chassidim who spent hours on tefillah.

title.en: Tzaddik ben rasha as shaliach tzibur

summary.en: The Rav asks how Rashi's 'the prayer of a tzaddik ben tzaddik is not like that of a tzaddik ben rasha' fits with the halachah preferring a shaliach tzibur without yichus. He answers that in tefillah b'tzibur all merits combine, so nothing is lost and the merit of drawing near the distant is added, and he urges drawing in bachurim without family advantages.

title.en: Avraham born in hiding from the Satan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that Avraham's holy soul came into a lowly family because the Satan blocked it, as he blocks Moshiach, and that Yaakov's blessings likewise came only through a ruse. Avraham had to break through the coarseness of his upbringing, and the Rav brings a similar saying from a great tzaddik about his own father.

title.en: Breaking through the darkness; new light in Kislev

summary.en: The Rav describes the darkness of the present generation, flooded with foreign culture and ideas, as the demolition before the building, to be broken through with Torah and tzedakah. He closes with Chanukah and Kislev: each night a new light, and lighting another's candle does not diminish one's own.

catalogTitle: שהיו ליצני הדור אומרים. . . הגריעותא של ליצנות

oneLiner.en: Starting from Rashi's 'the scoffers of the generation', the Rav explains leitzanus as the root of tumah and the opposite of emunah, and traces it through Pharaoh, the nachash and Esav, against the truth of Avraham, Yaakov and Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Rashi speaks of 'the scoffers of the generation' rather than its tzaddikim, and answers from the sefarim that emunah opens kedusha while leitzanus opens tumah. A joke, he explains, is laughter at what is absurd and untrue; leitzanus lets a person deny reality, which is how Pharaoh withstood plague after plague. Emunah is the opposite: the spark of kedusha in a person draws him to greater kedusha, as Elisha was drawn after Eliyahu, as a magnet draws iron. From the Rambam's ruling that Moshiach need not show signs, the Rav explains that Moshiach, like Avraham and unlike Eliyahu at Carmel, will draw the world by the truth of his words alone. Esav, born sixty years after Yitzchak, is the root of leitzanus. The Rav then explains Yaakov's 'mirmah' as a se'ir la'azazel directed by prophecy, and ends with the brachos of the parsha.

en: Just as emunah is the entrance to kedusha, leitzanus is the entrance and root of tumah.
Laughter is aroused by what is absurd and departs from truth; leitzanus is the power to deny reality and the conclusions of one's own mind.
Emunah comes from the spark of kedusha in every person, which draws him to greater kedusha, as Elisha was drawn to Eliyahu and as a magnet draws iron.
The Rambam's Moshiach needs no signs because he will draw the whole world to emunah by the truth of his word, like Avraham Avinu and greater than Eliyahu's miracle at Carmel.
Esav, the root of leitzanus, truly believed, but mocked away what he knew; his birth is why Rashi speaks of the scoffers of the generation.
The Torah measures exactly what portion the sitra achra must be given, as with the se'ir la'azazel; Yaakov's 'mirmah' was such a portion, done only by prophecy.

Adar and the defeat of Amalek

title.en: Why 'the scoffers of the generation'

summary.en: The Rav opens with Rashi that the scoffers of the generation said Sarah conceived from Avimelech, and asks why Chazal speak of scoffers rather than tzaddikim of the generation. He brings from the sefarim that emunah begins kedusha and leitzanus begins tumah, and that leitzanus is the opposite of truth.

title.en: What makes people laugh

summary.en: The Rav explains that a joke is funny because it is absurd and far from reality, and that a person has a power that takes pleasure in the opposite of truth. This is also why people laugh at a madman, who lives in a world of fantasy away from reality.

title.en: Pharaoh the scoffer and the plagues

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Hashem 'mocked' Mitzrayim and the Chasam Sofer that Egypt's whole success through Yosef and his family was a joke played on it, measure for measure for Pharaoh's leitzanus. He asks where Chazal saw that Pharaoh was a scoffer, and answers that only leitzanus, which escapes reality with a joke, let him hold out against plague after plague.

title.en: Leitzanus, the opposite of emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that leitzanus denies what the mind itself sees while emunah believes beyond what is seen, so leitzanus is the root of tumah. Hashem answers scoffers with mockery; one jest pushes away much rebuke; leitzanus is the opposite of Yaakov's truth. The nachash, the first scoffer, answered Chava's reasoning with mockery.

title.en: The spark of kedusha and the magnet

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah comes from the spark of kedusha that gives every creation its existence, which is drawn to greater kedusha. Scoffers mock when a tzaddik passes; Elisha ran after Eliyahu as iron to a magnet, and a strong enough magnet draws even weaker metal. Ehrliche Yidden are drawn to tzaddikim of every kind, those one understands and those one does not.

title.en: The Rambam: Moshiach needs no signs

summary.en: The Rav reads the Rambam in Hilchos Melachim that Moshiach need not perform signs and wonders, since Rabbi Akiva served Ben Koziva as Moshiach, and the Raavad's gloss. He contrasts this with the grand picture of Moshiach Yidden carried through galus at the Shabbos table, and says the Rambam's plain description can seem a disappointment.

title.en: Eliyahu's miracle and Avraham's word

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Rambam's view of Moshiach is in fact very great. Eliyahu needed fire from heaven to bring the people to say Hashem is G-d, while Avraham Avinu made Hashem known on earth without miracles, through the truth and power of his person; true words enter the heart. He adds a story of a man whose doubts in emunah dissolved through words of truth.

title.en: Moshiach's greatest miracle

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Rambam rules only that Moshiach need not show signs: his word will slay the kefirah in people's hearts, and his miracle will be turning all nations to call in Hashem's name and bringing all Yidden to Eretz Yisrael by his word alone. Eliyahu, who needed a miracle, will be Moshiach's armor-bearer, as Rabbi Akiva was Ben Koziva's; emunah is the power to follow beyond the mind, and leitzanus its opposite.

title.en: Esav the scoffer and the bechorah

summary.en: The Rav brings that Esav is called 'shav', the opposite of Yaakov's truth, and is the nachash itself. Among Esav's sins was despising the bechorah, yet he later wept over the brachos; the Rav answers that Esav truly believed, having grown up in Yitzchak's holy home, but mocked his belief away. This is why Adar, whose sense is laughter, is the month that defeats Esav and Amalek.

title.en: Esav's birth and the scoffers' answer

summary.en: The Rav returns to Rashi: when Esav, root of leitzanus and of the kelipah of Amalek, was about to be born, the scoffers of the generation had to be answered, so Hashem made Yitzchak's face like Avraham's. Esav was punished by mockery, as Pharaoh was: he planned with Yitzchak that whoever came with Yaakov's voice would be Esav, so when Yaakov came with his own voice the plan turned against Esav.

title.en: 'Bemirmah' and the portion of the sitra achra

summary.en: On 'your brother came bemirmah', the Rav brings the Targum 'with wisdom' and the Midrash 'with the wisdom of his Torah'. He explains that tumah must exist until it is removed from the earth, so the Torah directs giving it a measured portion, as with the seudah at a siyum and the se'ir la'azazel, which the Ramban explains is sent to the sitra achra and would be idolatry without the Torah's command.

title.en: Shadchan money, Rivka's prophecy and Yaakov

summary.en: From the Zohar that every year Yaakov receives the brachos on Rosh Hashanah and a gift is sent to Esav on Yom Kippur, the Rav explains Rabbi Yaakov Emden on shadchan money: since Hashem makes the match, the shadchan's fee is the portion thrown to the other side. Yitzchak and Rivka's holy shidduch needed none, but Yaakov's brachos did; Yaakov, who would never lie, did so only because Rivka told him it came by prophecy, so Yitzchak found no opposition.

title.en: Esav's material brachos and Yaakov's bracha

summary.en: The Rav explains that the 'mirmah' nullified the accusation, and that the wisdom of the Torah measures when it is allowed. Esav's brachos were only material, and he was given Italia shel Yavan, which did not yet exist, while Yaakov's bracha 'v'yiten lecha haElokim' was Torah and Hashem Himself. He closes that this parsha of the brachos gives strength to go with Elokus and that the main bracha is to feel Hashem and Moshiach.

catalogTitle: "ועשה לי מטעמים כאשר אהבתי" - איזה מין מאכלים אהב הצדיק יצחק אבינו?

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the 'delicacies Yitzchak loved' were foods carrying kedushah and an influx of Torah and fear of Heaven, prepared in truth by Rivkah, and from there turns to how a Jew's eating and his learning bring the redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer's answer to why Yaakov feared being discovered, and asks how a tzaddik like Yitzchak could ask for 'delicacies such as I love', illustrating with stories of tzaddikim who did not notice what they ate. He explains Rashi's two readings of 'for game was in his mouth' and the Midrash that Yitzchak's blessing meant Mikra, Mishnah, halachah and aggadah. Every food carries the word of Hashem that sustains creation, and a tzaddik senses its kedushah. Yitzchak felt great kedushah in the food Eisav served and took him for a hidden tzaddik, but in truth Rivkah cooked it; the Torah's spelling of 'tzayid' hints at the secret. Every Jewish meal can bring that blessing. The Rav then turns to the Baal HaTurim: when Yishmael falls, Yitzchak's era begins, and Yishmael falls through Yaakov's hidden learning. Torah learned with kedushah brings Moshiach.

en: The food Yitzchak loved was food in which he felt kedushah and an influx of Torah, tefillah and fear of Heaven.
Every moment brings new vitality from Above, and every food holds a 'word of Hashem' that a Jew takes in by eating.
Yitzchak thought Eisav was a hidden tzaddik because of the kedushah he felt in his food, but in truth Rivkah prepared it.
Yitzchak's blessing of dew, fat of the land, grain and wine is a blessing of Torah that comes through the food of Eretz Yisroel, and every Jew's meal can draw it down.
The fall of Yishmael that precedes Yitzchak's era is brought about by Yaakov's hidden learning in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever.
Torah brings Moshiach only when learned with its inner kedushah: seriously, with awareness that it is the Torah of Hashem.

title.en: Why Yaakov feared being discovered

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's question of what Yaakov had to lose, and his answer that Yaakov knew Eisav's shechitah was invalid, so Hashem would not let Yitzchak eat from it. He then reads the pesukim where Yitzchak asks for 'delicacies such as I love'.

title.en: Tzaddikim who did not notice their food

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Yismach Moshe ate soapy dishwater for supper without noticing, and how a tzaddik in Tzfas, absorbed in a difficult sugya, drank glass after glass of brandy thinking it was water.

title.en: 'I love pepper? I love the Creator!'

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yitzchak could speak of food 'as I love', and tells of Reb Boruch'l of Mezhibuzh and the Berditchever Rav sharing a room, where the Berditchever leapt up at the question whether he loves pepper, crying that he loves the Creator. He returns to the question: how can Yitzchak say 'as I love'?

title.en: Rashi's two readings and the blessing as Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'for game was in his mouth' with the Targum and Rashi's two readings, noting that Rashi brings a Midrash only when the plain meaning is difficult. He brings the Midrash that Yitzchak's blessing of dew, fat, grain and wine means Mikra, Mishnah, halachah and aggadah, and asks why the pesukim write 'tzayid' with a missing vav in one place and an extra heh in another.

title.en: Why man must eat: the word of Hashem in food

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem made people need food, and answers that creation is renewed every moment with fresh vitality that a person must take in, so learning cannot be put off to tomorrow. Eating and tefillah are bound together, and 'not by bread alone' teaches that within food lies the word of Hashem.

title.en: Kedushah in food and the tzaddik's sensitivity

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the special meal of the future, of Shabbos food and the fruits of Eretz Yisroel, and of how a kosher Jewish wife cooking with pure intent brings kedushah into the food. A tzaddik senses this inner taste, as shown by stories of the Chiddushei HaRim and of a chassid who could not eat meat from a shochet who had not gone to the mikveh.

title.en: Yitzchak took Eisav for a hidden tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yitzchak, far greater than these tzaddikim, could think highly of Eisav, who never mentioned Hashem's name. He answers that Yitzchak took Eisav for a hidden tzaddik, a very high level, and his proof was that after eating Eisav's food he learned and davened better.

title.en: In truth Rivkah cooked the food

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rivkah, knowing who Eisav was, cooked and prepared the food herself and let Eisav serve it, so Yitzchak felt its kedushah and believed Eisav was a hidden tzaddik deceiving everyone. Rashi's two readings together tell the true story, and the missing vav in 'tzayid' shows it was not really Eisav's game.

title.en: The blessing measure for measure

summary.en: The Rav explains the extra heh in 'tzayid' as a hint that the game was Rivkah's, and describes how on the night of the blessing Yaakov brought the food. Yitzchak blessed him measure for measure: as the food brought him Torah and closeness to Hashem, so the blessing of dew, grain and wine is the food of Eretz Yisroel that brings Mikra, Mishnah, halachah and aggadah, the deep meaning of the plain words.

title.en: Every Jewish meal as Yitzchak's delicacies

summary.en: The Rav describes how a Jew who washes, eats and bentches as he should receives the blessing of 'May G-d give you' at every meal: his bread is halachah and his drink aggadah, and bentching thanks Hashem for the fear of Heaven he ate. He contrasts the Shabbos meal with a gentile's festive dinner and explains 'satisfy us from Your goodness'.

title.en: When Yishmael falls, Yitzchak's era begins

summary.en: The Rav brings the Baal HaTurim at the end of Chayei Sarah, that when Yishmael falls Moshiach comes, and asks why specifically Yitzchak. He brings Rashi that Yishmael's years are given to calculate Yaakov's fourteen years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever, the Chasam Sofer's call in wartime to pray for Moshiach, and the Midrash that when kingdoms provoke each other one should await Moshiach.

title.en: Yishmael holds the fire that belongs to Yitzchak

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yishmael is the kelipah of chesed (water) and Eisav of gevurah (fire), yet today Yishmael holds the world's 'fire', and even stands on the Temple Mount, the place of the altar's eternal fire. When Yishmael falls, he will hand the fire over to Yitzchak, whose attribute is fire.

title.en: Yaakov's hidden learning makes Yishmael fall

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that Moshiach comes through the merit of Torah, and explains the juxtaposition: Yishmael falls through Yaakov's hidden learning in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever. The newspapers report the politics, but those who sit and learn make the real headlines; he adds Targum Yonasan and a Midrash on the fall of Persia.

title.en: Learning with the inner light of Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains, citing the Derech Hashem, that Hashem hid great lights in the words of Torah, and only learning with kedushah draws them out. He lists the conditions: teshuvah before learning, seriousness and refinement, remembering it is the Torah of Hashem, a brachah before each seder, and not interrupting, citing the Gemara on one who interrupts his learning.

title.en: The afikoman and the power of a kushya answered

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov came 'with wisdom of Torah' and showed Yitzchak the afikoman, explaining that the afikoman, the larger half, hints at the greater future redemption. He closes with Midrash Pinchas that answering a kushya in Torah can defeat an enemy of Israel, urges serious learning of the sedra, and prays to see Yishmael's fall and the redemption.

catalogTitle: The Power of An Atmosphere of קדושה and Vice Versa (Explanation of the meaning of ויגדלו הנערים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov and Esav 'grew up' on the day Avraham died, each absorbing the atmosphere of a passing, and teaches that atmosphere, of kedushah or its opposite, shapes a person, so a Jew must bring kedushah into the places of darkness, like the Chanukah lights.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi on 'Vayigdelu hane'arim': at thirteen Yaakov went to the beis medrash and Esav to avodah zarah, yet by the calculation Avraham died when they were fifteen. To explain what happens at fifteen he brings Elisha's request for a double portion at Eliyahu's passing and the Bnei Yissaschar: at a tzaddik's death all his mitzvos gather, and those present can gain greatly. Every tzaddik has a counterpart in tumah on his own level: Avraham and Nimrod, Yitzchak and Yishmael, Yaakov and Esav; when one leaves, the other must leave. On the day Avraham died Esav killed Nimrod, so Yaakov absorbed kedushah at Avraham's bedside while Esav absorbed Nimrod's evil. From here the Rav speaks about atmosphere: in the home, in today's polluted world, in Purim's limit to the fifteenth of the month, and in Chanukah, which carries light into the domain of darkness.

en: On the day a tzaddik passes away all the mitzvos and accomplishments of his life gather to accompany him, and a person who stands there can gain great levels.
Every tzaddik has an antagonist from the same level in tumah, and when the tzaddik leaves the world his counterpart must leave as well.
On the day Avraham died, Yaakov at his bedside grew in tzidkus while Esav, who killed Nimrod that day, absorbed Nimrod's evil; this is 'Vayigdelu hane'arim'.
Atmosphere is a great power: a home with mezuzah, sefarim and Shabbos has an atmosphere of kedushah, while bringing television and internet into it contaminates it.
The days after the fifteenth of the month, when the moon wanes, are the domain of the sitra achra, which is why Purim cannot go past the fifteenth.
Chanukah alone falls at the end of the month, at night and in the reshus harabim, because its lights carry kedushah into the domain of darkness.
The Rav says a Jew today must not be affected by the polluted atmosphere but must affect it, bringing kedushah where there is tumah.

title.en: Vayigdelu at fifteen and a tzaddik's passing

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the brothers parted ways at thirteen, though Avraham died when they were fifteen, and asks how Elisha could receive double Eliyahu's spirit. He answers with the Bnei Yissaschar that at a person's passing all his mitzvos gather, and with the Chasam Sofer's regret at missing his rebbe's passing.

title.en: Every tzaddik has his antagonist

summary.en: The Rav explains that every tzaddik faces an antagonist from the same level in tumah: Avraham had Nimrod, Yitzchak had Yishmael. He notes that the written Torah shows nothing wrong with Nimrod, Yishmael or Esav, and only the Oral Torah reveals who they are.

title.en: When the tzaddik leaves, his opponent leaves

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, who told his talmidim that the debaters of the nations would leave the scene with him, and Rashi on Rivka's words that Esav died on the day Yaakov was buried.

title.en: Esav kills Nimrod; the color red

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that on the day Avraham died Esav killed Nimrod, and that Esav asked for 'the red stuff'. He digresses on the Shach about wearing red, explaining that red is middas hadin and white is chesed, and that everything about Esav is red.

title.en: Two passings, two brothers grow

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: Yaakov stood at Avraham's bedside and absorbed his kedushah, while Esav was present at Nimrod's death and absorbed his evil, so both grew that day. He concludes that atmosphere is a great power.

title.en: The atmosphere of a Jewish home

summary.en: The Rav brings Chana, who davened near Eli, as a source for standing near a tzaddik, then describes the atmosphere of a home with mezuzah, sefarim and Shabbos, and how television and internet contaminate it, just as physical pollution mirrors spiritual pollution.

title.en: Gan Eden with Yaakov, Gehinnom with Esav

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yitzchak sensed Gan Eden when Yaakov entered and Gehinnom when Esav entered. He speaks of the trials of today's polluted surroundings, saying Hashem places each neshamah where it belongs and that the task is to bring kedushah there.

title.en: The waxing moon and Esav's territory

summary.en: The Rav explains that a chuppah is made while the moon waxes, since the moon represents Klal Yisrael, and that the Yamim Tovim fall in the first half of the month. Purim cannot go past the fifteenth, because after it begins the territory of Esav and the sitra achra.

title.en: Chanukah: light into the domain of darkness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah is the exception: at the end of the month, at night and in the reshus harabim, the domain of the sitra achra. Since the Greeks invaded the kedushah, the Chanukah lights carry the Beis Hamikdash into their territory, against their decree to write on every door that Jews have no share in the G-d of Israel.

title.en: Our generation's task and the menorah's empty cups

summary.en: The Rav brings the sefarim that neshamos of earlier generations return for a tikkun, and says there is a reason this generation faces so many trials. Its task is to create an atmosphere of kedushah where there is tumah, like the menorah's empty cups, which are neshamos waiting to be lit until the eighth day, the number of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: התורה מודיע שישמעאל מת (מפלתו). ורש"י מגלה שזה בגלל שיעקב למד תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the Torah reveals Yaakov's years of learning in Beis Ever only through the count of Yishmael's years: the fall of Yishmael depends on Yaakov taking on the yoke of Torah, and the fire Yishmael holds belongs to the children of Yitzchak.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the closing verses of Chayei Sarah, where Yishmael 'fell', and the Baal HaTurim's remark that when Yishmael falls at the end of days Moshiach will sprout from the offspring of Yitzchak. Rashi at the end of Toldos derives from Yishmael's years that Yaakov hid fourteen years in Beis Ever. The Rav asks why the Torah teaches this only through Yishmael, and why Moshiach is tied to Yitzchak. He answers that Yishmael died just when Yaakov went to learn: the fall of Yishmael depends on the Jews accepting the yoke of Torah. Yitzchak is the attribute of fire, the fire of the mizbeach and of 'Bereishis'; today Yishmael controls fire and energy and the place of the mizbeach, and when he falls he must return it to Yitzchak's children. He then explains Yitzchak's tefillah as praise sung before the salvation, the passing of a tzaddik as the day all his days gather, Yaakov's growth at Avraham's passing and Esav's at Nimrod's, and closes on toiling to dig the well within.

en: Rashi learns from the count of Yishmael's years that Yaakov spent fourteen hidden years learning in Beis Ever, and Yishmael died exactly when Yaakov left for Charan.
The Torah ties the two facts together to teach that the fall of Yishmael depends on Yaakov, and his children, accepting the yoke of Torah.
Yitzchak is the attribute of fire and of the mizbeach; the fire Yishmael controls today is not his, and when he falls he must return it to the children of Yitzchak.
Rivkah was barren so that Yitzchak would daven; tefillah is the first cause, and every tefillah of a Jew is accepted and stored.
The tefillah of tzaddikim is song and thanks before the salvation, out of trust that Hashem will help.
On the day of a person's passing all the days of his life gather together, which is why one present at a tzaddik's passing can receive a double portion.
The blessings of the parsha come only to one who works for them, like digging a well to reach living water.
