title.en: Yishmael's fall and Yaakov's hidden years

summary.en: The Rav links the opening of Toldos to the end of Chayei Sarah, where Yishmael 'fell', and brings the Baal HaTurim that Moshiach comes from Yitzchak's offspring when Yishmael falls. He then lays out Rashi's calculation from Yishmael's years that Yaakov spent fourteen years in Beis Ever.

title.en: Two questions, and Yishmael's power today

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah teaches Yaakov's learning only through Yishmael, and why the Baal HaTurim ties Moshiach to Yitzchak rather than to Avraham or Yaakov. He then shows how 'his hand against all and all hands against him' is being fulfilled today, as all nations must come to the Arab lands for oil.

title.en: Torah learning brings Yishmael's fall

summary.en: The Rav explains that the final exile is that of Yishmael, who holds Eretz Yisroel in the merit of milah, and that Torah brings Moshiach. Yishmael died exactly when Yaakov went to learn, a sign for his descendants: when Yishmael is at his height, his fall comes when Yaakov's children accept the yoke of Torah.

title.en: Yitzchak and the fire of the mizbeach

summary.en: Avraham is chesed, water; Yitzchak is gevurah, fire. The Rav finds the mizbeach and its fire in the word 'Bereishis', ties fire to the creation with midas hadin and to the Akeidah on the place of the mizbeach, and says that in Moshiach's days the world will be led with midas hadin.

title.en: Yishmael holds fire that is not his

summary.en: Today the element of fire, energy, is in Yishmael's hands, and so is the place of the mizbeach. The Rav explains that fire belongs to Yitzchak, and when Yishmael falls he will have to return what he took to the children of Yitzchak; this is why Moshiach is tied to 'the offspring of Yitzchak'.

title.en: Barrenness for the sake of tefillah

summary.en: On 'Vaye'tar Yitzchak', the Rav brings Rabbeinu Bachya that tefillah is the first cause: Hashem desires the prayers of tzaddikim, so Rivkah was barren in order that they daven. Every tefillah of a Jew is accepted, and twenty years of their tefillos became a store of prayer for Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Praise before the salvation

summary.en: From an acrostic in the machzor, Yitzchak on one side and Rivkah on the other, the Rav reads 'opposite his wife' and explains that their tefillah was not crying but songs of praise with trust. Tzaddikim thank Hashem in advance, as in the words said before Kiddush and in Modim, and the women at the sea prepared drums before the salvation.

title.en: Thirteen or fifteen, and Elisha's double portion

summary.en: Rashi says 'the lads grew' means age thirteen, yet Avraham died when they were fifteen. The Rav turns to Elisha's request for a double portion and explains that on the day of a person's passing all his days gather together, as with Moshe Rabbeinu, the end of Shabbos and Shemini Atzeres, so at that moment a double portion can be given.

title.en: Every tzaddik and his counterpart

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's regret at missing his rebbe's passing, and the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the heretics, to show that for every tzaddik there is a rasha of equal strength. Avraham's lifelong war was with Nimrod, who was killed the day Avraham died, and Esav likewise died the day of Yaakov's burial.

title.en: The day both lads grew

summary.en: Yaakov, at fifteen, was present at Avraham's passing and received a double portion of holiness, while Esav, who killed Nimrod that day, drew Nimrod's power of tumah onto himself. So 'the lads grew' was fulfilled that day, and this is why Yaakov told Esav to sell the birthright 'as of this day'.

title.en: Blessings come through digging

summary.en: Toldos is a parsha of blessings, given on the night of Pesach according to Targum Yonasan, and this Shabbos brings blessings to every Jew who wants them. Through the dreams of the butler and the baker the Rav shows that one must work for it, and like the Avos digging wells, each person must dig to reach the living water of his soul.

catalogTitle: “בארות אשר חפרו” - מעיינות התפילה; “וסתמם פלישתים” - ע"י ליצנות.

oneLiner.en: Building on the wells Avraham dug and the Plishtim stopped up, the Rav calls on his chevra to renew its avodas hatefillah: to daven with strength, together and on time, with baalei tefillah who lift the tzibbur, undeterred by mockery.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Kol Simcha: the wells Avraham dug were wellsprings of avodas Hashem, which the Plishtim stopped up until the service became rote, and Yitzchak dug them anew. At a melave malka in Kislev, the month of renewal, he applies this to his chevra, founded on tefillah. He reads the Konigsberg Rav's letter to Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz about a long Rosh Hashanah davening that drew ridicule, and Rabbi Yonasan's answer that standing in tefillah is his portion. He explains how tefillah stands beside Torah, how each person reaches dveikus by his level with toil and a raised voice, and, from the Chovos HaLevavos, how one climbs beyond his ability. He then stresses davening together and on time, learning from Bilgah's closed window and a story of the Chiddushei HaRim, demands that baalei tefillah lift the tzibbur, and closes with ahavas Yisrael and a warning against talking during davening and learning.

en: The wells Avraham dug are the wellsprings of avodas Hashem; when the Plishtim stop them up, the service turns into rote habit and must be dug anew, as Yitzchak did.
Each person, by his own level, can reach moments of dveikus and outpouring of the soul in tefillah when he davens with toil, a raised voice and all his strength.
Davening together strengthens each one; therefore the Rav asks everyone to come on time and begin Hodu together.
A baal tefillah must lift the tzibbur, davening loudly, beautifully and with strength, and false humility has no place at the amud.
In Kislev, the month of renewal, each person should re-dig the point of Avraham within him, built on love between Jews and on keeping davening and learning free of talk.

title.en: Re-digging Avraham's wells

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kol Simcha: the wells were sources of avodas Hashem that the Plishtim stopped up until the service became rote, and Yitzchak renewed them. He applies it to the chevra gathered at a melave malka in Kislev, praising its young men who stay together, yet saying one must dig deeper to renew it.

title.en: Rabbi Yonasan's long davening and the mockers

summary.en: The Rav reads a letter of the Konigsberg Rav asking Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz what to do when his long Rosh Hashanah Shacharis drew ridicule, and Rabbi Yonasan's answer that standing before Hashem in tefillah is his portion even if he is mocked. He adds a similar saying from the Brisker Rav's family and Dovid HaMelech's words on those who mocked his tefillah.

title.en: Torah, tefillah and dveikus by one's level

summary.en: Through the Baal HaTanya's Hilchos Talmud Torah and the early chassidim who spent hours on davening, the Rav explains that tefillah has its own place beside Torah as the mitzvah of dveikus. Each person, by his level, can reach outpouring of the soul when he davens with toil and a raised voice; he brings the Beis Aharon on true tzaddikim who rise even in a whisper.

title.en: Climbing beyond one's ability

summary.en: Returning to Kislev and the stopped wells, the Rav reads the Chovos HaLevavos's twenty-first accounting: a person accustoms himself to the avodah he can do, then strives and prays for more, and Hashem opens gates beyond his ability, like a craftsman who comes to invent. He adds R' Mordechai of Chernobyl's teaching that one must daven with all one's limbs and strength.

title.en: Davening together, on time

summary.en: The Rav explains that davening in shul works because one person strengthens the other, citing the Baal HaTanya and the togetherness of the angels' kedushah, and asks everyone to come on time and start Hodu together. He stresses Shacharis as the main tefillah that colors the day, illustrated by a man he saw studying Gemara bareheaded in a public library, and the Beis Aharon's saying that learning and davening need each other.

title.en: Bilgah's closed window

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah about the family of Bilgah, whose window in the Beis HaMikdash was closed; one opinion is that they came late, which Rashi explains as a sign the service was not dear to them. He reads it as the stopped-up wells: each person has a window, a channel of blessing from his soul's root, and when it is blocked he should draw strength from friends until his own opens again.

title.en: Too late: the Chiddushei HaRim and the churban

summary.en: The Rav tells a story from a reliable sefer: on his last erev Shabbos the Chiddushei HaRim was heard telling a soul that he could no longer help it because candles were already lit. He explains that one who comes late to serving Hashem in this world comes late above as well, and that the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed partly because Shlomo HaMelech rose late on the day of its inauguration; so one must not destroy his own Beis HaMikdash by lateness.

title.en: The baal tefillah must lift the tzibbur

summary.en: The Rav addresses the baalei tefillah: the Stoliner Rebbe and the Sanzer Rav each removed a sleepy chazzan mid-davening because a baal tefillah must lift the congregation. He rejects starting Hodu quietly out of humility, citing the need for chutzpah in the time before Moshiach, criticizes those who refuse to go up, and brings a Midrash on a prophet punished for refusing to use his fine voice: a talent is given for one's tikkun.

title.en: Kislev renewal and love among Jews

summary.en: The Rav calls for re-digging the point of Avraham in each person in Kislev, the month of chinuch and renewal, and says the key is love between Jews, as the Arizal began davening by accepting the mitzvah to love one's fellow; hatred is a klipah to uproot, and one should look at one's own faults. He urges everyone to come daven together, since 'the more Jews, the more G-dliness', and calls the shul the place that holds together those no longer in yeshiva.

title.en: No talking in shul; closing blessing

summary.en: The Rav warns against chatting during learning and against learning or talking during davening, bringing R' Mordechai of Chernobyl, and compares one who talks to someone opening a window in freezing weather, chilling everyone; the shul must stay warm. He closes saying he speaks to himself too, and blesses that on Rosh Chodesh Kislev all renew their learning and davening with vitality.

catalogTitle: “מכרה כיום את בכורתך לי” - חילוק בין שיטת הצדיק והרשע

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak sensed the kedushah that the one who prepares food puts into it, and that the sale of the bechorah 'kayom' reflects the opposite views of Yaakov and Esav about what 'today' is for.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Toldos as a parsha of brachos: brachah means increase, shown in the letter beis and in Chanukah's lights that keep adding, against Greece that wanted to add to its own domain. He then asks why Yitzchak needed tasty food in order to bless. Great tzaddikim take no pleasure from food, as stories of the Levushei Srad and the Yismach Moshe show. The answer is the Ramban's rule that the doer's power enters what he makes, illustrated by the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Chozeh of Lublin and Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir's cholent. Rivka secretly prepared Esav's food, so Yitzchak tasted kedushah and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik; Yaakov's food brought Gan Eden. Through the Bach on the fruits of Eretz Yisrael he explains the brachah of dagan and tirosh. Finally, 'michrah kayom' contrasts a Jew's 'today' of mitzvos with Esav's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'.

en: Brachah means increase, and Chanukah's essence of 'mosif veholech' is an increase in kedushah, the opposite of Greece's wish to add to its own domain.
Great tzaddikim take no pleasure in physical food; their pleasure is Torah and mitzvos.
The power of the one who makes a thing enters the thing he makes, so food prepared in kedushah carries kedushah.
Yitzchak ate from Esav because Rivka secretly slaughtered and cooked, and the kedushah he tasted led him to think Esav was a hidden tzaddik.
Food grown in Eretz Yisrael carries kedushah, which is why Yitzchak's brachah of grain and wine is read as Torah.
'Michrah kayom' reflects two views of today: for a Jew today is for doing mitzvos and the reward comes tomorrow; for Esav today is for enjoying this world.

kedushah of the fruits of eretz yisrael
today for mitzvos, tomorrow for reward

title.en: Brachah as increase: Chanukah and Toldos

summary.en: The Rav calls Toldos a parsha of brachos and explains that brachah means increase, shown in the letter beis and in Chanukah's lights that are added each night, against Greece that wanted to enlarge its own domain. He notes that Toldos is the sixth sedra and that every aliyah in it mentions brachah.

title.en: Tzaddikim who did not taste their food

summary.en: Turning to Yitzchak's request for matamim, the Rav stresses that great tzaddikim are detached from this world, and tells how the Levushei Srad drank bottles of brandy unaware while learning, and how the Yismach Moshe ate a pot of dirty water instead of soup without noticing.

title.en: The doer's power enters what he makes

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yitzchak needed food to give a brachah of Torah, and brings the Ramban's rule that the doer's power is in what he makes, with the Ba'al Shem Tov reading a carpenter's thoughts in a table, the Chozeh of Lublin's bed, the Mesilas Yesharim, and Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir's cholent cooked 'lekavod Shabbos kodesh'.

title.en: How Yitzchak ate from Esav and was misled

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yitzchak could eat from Esav's hunt when Esav was a mumar whose shechitah is nevelah, and how he was fooled about him. He answers that Esav excelled in kibud av, and that Rivka, who knew the truth from prophecy, secretly slaughtered and cooked so that Yitzchak tasted kedushah and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik.

title.en: The day of the brachos: Gan Eden and Gehinom

summary.en: On the day of the brachos Rivka prepared food for Yaakov instead, and Yitzchak sensed Gan Eden in it, while Esav's own food brought the taste of Gehinom. The Rav reads 'ki tzayid befiv' to mean that Esav deceived his father by bringing food he had not prepared himself.

title.en: The kedushah of the fruits of Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem Himself oversees Eretz Yisrael so its fruits grow in kedushah, and brings the Bach's explanation of 'to eat from its fruit' in the after-brachah. This is why Yitzchak blessed Yaakov with grain and wine, which the Midrash reads as halachah and aggadah.

title.en: 'Michrah kayom': two views of today

summary.en: The Rav explains Yaakov's words 'sell me as of today your birthright': a Jew's today is for doing mitzvos with the reward tomorrow, while Esav's today is 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'. By Esav's own view he has no need for the bechorah, and Esav agrees.

catalogTitle: אלה תולדות יצחק - על פני כל אחיו נפל - The Fall of ישמעאל in our Time Heralds Moshiach

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows from the Baal HaTurim that the fall of Yishmael, which closes the previous sedra, heralds Moshiach from the children of Yitzchak, and ties this to the fall of Yishmael's leaders in his day, to Kislev as the month of bracha, and to Yaakov and Esav each growing on the day of a petirah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the last words of Chayei Sarah, 'al pnei chol echav nafal', which Rashi reads as Yishmael's fall, and the Baal HaTurim's teaching that it is followed by 'eleh toldos Yitzchak': when Yishmael falls, Moshiach from Yitzchak's children is near. He connects the twelve nesiim of Yishmael to the nesiim read on Chanukah, and sees the recent fall of two of Yishmael's leaders as a sign. He brings the Zohar that Yishmael's empty milah holds Eretz Yisrael only while it is empty, explains why Yitzchak is named (every tzaddik has an adversary), and gives gematrios. He then shows that Kislev and Toldos are bound up with bracha and with the number six. Finally he asks how Rashi's age of thirteen fits the calculation of fifteen, and answers that on the day of Avraham's petirah Yaakov grew in kedushah, while Esav, present when he killed Nimrod, grew in tumah.

en: According to the Baal HaTurim, the juxtaposition of Yishmael's fall with 'eleh toldos Yitzchak' teaches that when Yishmael falls, Moshiach from Yitzchak's children is on his way.
The Rav explains that Yishmael's milah is an empty milah, so per the Zohar he holds Eretz Yisrael only while it is empty, and will be shaken out when Jews return.
Moshiach is linked specifically to Yitzchak because every tzaddik has his adversary, and Yishmael is Yitzchak's.
Kislev is the month of bracha, and Toldos, the Shabbos that blesses Kislev, is a sedra full of bracha, tied to the number six.
One who is present at the petirah of a tzaddik receives a double portion, as Elisha did from Eliyahu.
Vayigdelu hane'arim refers to Yaakov growing in tzidkus at Avraham's petirah and Esav growing in rishus at Nimrod's death, both on the same day.

title.en: Yishmael's fall heralds Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Baal HaTurim that 'al pnei chol echav nafal' followed by 'eleh toldos Yitzchak' means Moshiach comes when Yishmael falls. He links the twelve nesiim of Yishmael to the nesiim read on Chanukah and Kislev, and points to the recent fall of Saddam and Arafat as a sign to act on.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah and the empty land

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Yishmael claims Eretz Yisrael through his milah, and is told his milah is empty, so he holds the land only while it is empty. He notes the great return of Jews to Eretz Yisrael in recent decades as a sign that the time has come.

title.en: Why Yitzchak: every tzaddik's adversary

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshiach is tied to Yitzchak and answers that every tzaddik has an adversary, and Yishmael is Yitzchak's. He brings gematrios linking 'Hashem melech olam va'ed avdu goyim me'artzo' and the name Arafat to 'Yishmael ben Avraham', and uses the rule that with danger two times make a chazakah.

title.en: Kislev, the month of bracha

summary.en: The Rav describes Chanukah as a victory over those who wanted Jews to forget the Torah, and says Toldos blesses Kislev, the month of bracha. He brings the Maharal that the letters of 'barach' (beis, reish, chaf) each show doubling in the ones, tens and hundreds.

title.en: Yosef, the sixth, is bracha

summary.en: The Rav explains that of the seven ushpizin, Yosef, the sixth, embodies bracha: his name means adding and he became two shevatim. He connects this to Chanukah's added candle each night and to Toldos being the sixth sedra, in which every aliyah contains a bracha.

title.en: Sixes of bracha and holding on to it

summary.en: The Rav lists signs of six in the sedra: the sixth aliyah 'Veyiten lecha', the word bracha counted 32 times, Yitzchak aged sixty, the sixtieth day from Rosh Hashanah, the sixth perek of Brachos and the lulav. He says one must be a vessel for bracha with no 'hole in the pocket', tells of a tzaddik who explained why Havdalah on wine had not brought a man sons, and links shalom, wholeness, and the bechorah to bracha.

title.en: Thirteen or fifteen: a difficulty in Rashi

summary.en: The Rav reads Rashi on 'vayigdelu hane'arim', that at thirteen Yaakov went to the batei midrash and Esav to avodah zarah, and that Avraham died five years early so as not to see Esav go bad. He shows the calculation gives fifteen, not thirteen, brings Rabbeinu Bachya, and leaves the difficulty open for now.

title.en: Double portion at a petirah; the day Avraham died

summary.en: The Rav tells how Elisha received a double portion by being present when Eliyahu was taken, and how the Chasam Sofer lamented in his hesped that he was not at his rebbe's petirah. He then describes the day of Avraham's petirah: Yaakov cooked lentils, Rivka's fear of losing both sons in one day and Esav's death at the Me'aras HaMachpelah, and Esav's killing of Nimrod, noting that each tzaddik and his adversary die on the same day.

title.en: Two deathbeds, and this Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav paints two scenes: Avraham's petirah, where the Shechinah, the great tzaddikim and all his mitzvos gathered and Yaakov received a double portion of kedushah, and Nimrod's death in the forest, where all his sins gathered and Esav received a double portion of tumah. This answers Rashi: 'vayigdelu' is growth in tzidkus and rishus. He closes that this Shabbos, as Kislev is blessed and Arafat is buried, Jews can grow greatly, and prays for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: עבודת יעקב ביציאה מסביבה של קדושה לארצת קליפת חכמת החיצוניות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Parshas Vayetzei as the guide for a Jew who must leave a surrounding of kedushah for Charan, the land of worldly wisdom: Yaakov stayed bound to Be'er Sheva, worked for Hashem rather than for Lavan, and redeemed the Jewish souls there.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying the parsha itself cries out its lesson: Vayetzei is the going out from a place of kedushah to Charan. Because Yaakov never broke his bond with his father's house, the whole sedra is written without a single break. Charan was the land of the Bnei Kedem, the center of worldly wisdom and progress, and Lavan was its great sage. A Jew's healthy state is to dwell apart, yet at times Hashem forces him out, as Yaakov was sent. Then he must leave tied by an oath, a rope, to Be'er Sheva, armed with bitachon. The Rav describes Yaakov's fourteen years for Rachel and Leah as service of Hashem, the sheep as Jewish souls he must redeem, and Rachel weeping for her children in exile. He closes with the trials of Beis Lavan, with going there only when compelled and after preparation, and with stories showing that Torah without yiras shamayim is not Torah.

en: Vayetzei teaches how a Jew must conduct himself when he leaves his surrounding of kedushah and lives in Charan, the land of outside wisdom.
The sedra has no break because Yaakov never interrupted his bond with his father's house during his twenty years away.
A Jew's healthy state is to dwell apart, but when Hashem forces him into the world he must remain inwardly separate, tied by an oath to Be'er Sheva like a rope tied above a pit.
Yaakov was not Lavan's employee but Hashem's; his fourteen years of work for Rachel and Leah were service of Hashem, like tefillin and tzitzis.
Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls, and his task in exile is to shepherd and redeem them from under Lavan's rule.
Beis Lavan is full of sudden trials; one may go there only when compelled, after asking a sheilas chacham and after years of preparation in kedushah.

Yaakov Avinu as shepherd of Jewish souls
Rachel and Leah and the Shechinah

title.en: A parsha with no break

summary.en: The Rav says the parsha itself teaches yiras shamayim: Vayetzei is the going out from a surrounding of kedushah to Charan. He brings the Sfas Emes that the sedra has no break because Yaakov never interrupted his bond with his father's house.

title.en: Yaakov's way in exile, then and now

summary.en: The Rav explains the dream as a lower level fitting exile, and Yaakov as the one who instituted prayer in darkness and left his children a way of conduct for Vayetzei. He contrasts the Jews of the past, set apart in their own surroundings, with today, when Jews must go out into the progressive world.

title.en: Charan, the land of the Bnei Kedem

summary.en: The Rav describes Charan as the land of the Bnei Kedem, the center of worldly wisdom and progress, where Avraham sent the sons of the concubines, and Lavan, identified with Bilam, as its greatest sage. Yaakov's healthy state is isolation, as in 'vayishkon Yisrael betach badad' and Yeshaya's counsel to close the doors in exile.

title.en: Forced out, tied to Be'er Sheva

summary.en: The Rav explains that at times Hashem forces Jews to be exposed to the world, as Yaakov was sent to Charan. The counsel is to stay inwardly separate; Be'er Sheva is the oath, a rope tied above, with which Yaakov could descend into Charan, and before going he hid in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever.

title.en: Seven years for Rachel, seven for Leah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rachel and Leah correspond to two aspects of the Shechinah, as in Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah of Tikkun Chatzos, so Yaakov had to prepare and toil for them. His seven years for each are like the counting of seven times seven, and through them he broke the wall between gashmiyus and ruchniyus; Vayetzei is the seventh sedra.

title.en: Arriving with nothing but bitachon

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov offered seven years, and explains that the sheep were Jewish souls he had to raise. Yaakov arrived penniless, and the Rav brings the Midrash on 'esa einai el heharim' that Yaakov placed his trust only in Hashem. He applies it to bochurim who say they need college for parnassah.

title.en: No answer about bread

summary.en: The Rav goes through Yaakov's requests in his vow and shows from the Midrash that Hashem answered each one except the request for bread and clothing. The silence means: rely on Me. Parnassah depends on the decree of Rosh Hashanah, not on going to Beis Lavan, and a person should worry about yiras shamayim while Hashem worries about parnassah.

title.en: Yaakov's task: redeeming the souls

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Yitzchak, whose shidduch was brought to him, with Yaakov, who had to toil, and explains that Yaakov's task was to go into exile and redeem Rachel, Leah and the Jewish souls. He brings the Midrash that Yaakov came home with six hundred thousand sheep, the root souls of Klal Yisrael, and tells of the Apter Rav, who remembered being one of Yaakov's sheep.

title.en: Hashem's employee at the well

summary.en: From Rashi that Yaakov worked the second seven years faithfully as well, the Rav explains that Yaakov was Hashem's employee, not Lavan's, and left every Jew a guidance for exile until he becomes our shepherd. At the well he saw Rachel as the Shechinah in exile, belonging to his mother's root, and saw the sheep as Jewish souls, so he watered them himself.

title.en: Rachel on the way, weeping for her children

summary.en: The Rav brings an explanation he heard of the Midrash on the three flocks at the well: they are Jewish souls who cannot drink under gentile shepherds. With Rashi in Vayechi that Rachel was buried on the way to help her children going into exile, and the passuk of Rachel weeping for her children, he explains Yaakov's weeping. Yaakov used no tricks; the angels brought him the sheep.

title.en: The Arizal, the Alshich and Lavan

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Arizal delighted in a derashah of the Alshich explaining how Lavan deceived Yaakov a hundred times, because Lavan himself came to listen and nodded at each true point. He brings the Kotzker on the wells the Pelishtim stopped up, then warns that Beis Lavan is a great danger: one may go only when compelled, after asking a sheilas chacham and preparing in kedushah.

title.en: The trials of Beis Lavan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Lavan took Yaakov for a fool for working fourteen years for two women, not knowing whom Yaakov served. He speaks of the many trials in Beis Lavan, of talmidim who withstood them, and of Yosef's trial bearing fruit years later, and says one must be bound to Be'er Sheva and ready for sudden trials, or one's Torah is worth little.

title.en: Torah without yiras shamayim is not Torah

summary.en: The Rav tells of a gadol who could tell from a piece of Torah alone, without seeing the author's name, whether a yarei shamayim had written it, and of a child prodigy who could recite only seforim written with yiras shamayim. He ends with the Baal Shem Tov's parable, brought by the Toldos Yaakov Yosef, of a simple worker who kept miscounting his wages.

catalogTitle: גלות יעקב לחרן' מקום חרון אף של מקום; ועבודתו שם לאוקמא שכינתא מעפרא

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Yaakov's descent into galus in Charan, the place of Hashem's anger, and his work there of raising the Shechinah, represented by Rachel, from the dust.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov went out into galus to pave the way for his children. Leaving Eretz Yisrael, he saw the Beis HaMikdash built and destroyed, instituted Maariv, the prayer of darkness, and went to Charan, the place of Hashem's anger. When he kissed Rachel and wept, the people of Charan, proud of their modesty, accused him of breaching the fences of the world; the Rav identifies them with Lavan, who is Bilaam, and notes that the nations display virtue exactly where they are most corrupt. He then explains that Rachel represents the revealed Shechinah that goes into galus with Klal Yisrael: this is why Yaakov wept, why Rachel is not buried in Me'aras HaMachpelah, and why Lavan's switch mattered. Yaakov never broke his bond with Be'er Sheva, and today's galus among 'progressive' people demands separation, Torah, Tehillim and tears.

en: Yaakov went into galus in Charan, the place of Hashem's anger, so that his children would know how to conduct themselves and survive their own galus.
The Shechinah resting on Klal Yisrael is called Rachel in its revealed aspect and Leah in its hidden aspect, and the revealed aspect goes with the Jews into galus.
Every mitzvah is meant to reunite Hashem with the Shechinah, and this is the purpose of all Torah and mitzvos.
Rachel is not buried in Me'aras HaMachpelah because Klal Yisrael had to go into galus, and she weeps for her children.
Yaakov never broke his bond with Be'er Sheva, his source, even in Charan, and every Jew carries a spark of Yaakov.
In today's galus a Jew must keep apart from the nations as far as he can and bind himself to Torah, Tehillim and tears before Hashem.

candidateTopics: Rachel and Leah as aspects of the Shechinah
galus in an age of progress

title.en: Yaakov goes out to pave the way through galus

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov went out into galus so that his children would know how to conduct themselves there, and his deeds gave them strength. Leaving Eretz Yisrael, he sees in his dream the Beis HaMikdash built and destroyed on the night of Tisha B'Av, institutes Maariv, the prayer of darkness, and goes to Charan, the place of Hashem's anger, where the Midrash sees the galuyos in the stone on the well.

title.en: Yaakov's tears and Charan's complaint

summary.en: The Rav addresses a mistaken reading he heard among bochurim about Yaakov kissing Rachel and weeping. He brings the Midrash that the people of Charan, who since the flood had kept away from immorality, whispered that Yaakov was breaching the fences of the world, and Rashi that he wept because he saw she would not be buried with him. He identifies these people as Lavan's circle, and Lavan as Bilaam according to Targum Yonasan.

title.en: Bilaam's advice and the nations' display of virtue

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's question why Hashem gave the nations a prophet, and notes that Bilaam, of the same circle that accused Yaakov, advised corrupting Klal Yisrael through the daughters of Moav and Midyan. He observes that the nations display their fineness exactly where they are most corrupt, and that Yaakov saw how deep a galus he had entered, a galus his children would live in.

title.en: Yaakov's holiness and the meeting with Rachel

summary.en: The Rav describes Yaakov as perhaps the holiest man in the world, completely pure, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar's account that from a young age he saw only holy names. If lesser tzaddikim reached such levels, Yaakov's meeting with Rachel must be a lofty matter beyond our grasp, written for every Jew at his level; he begins to explain it a little through Tikkun Chatzos.

title.en: The Shechinah called Rachel and Leah

summary.en: The Rav explains Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah: the Shechinah resting on Klal Yisrael has many names, its hidden aspect called Leah and its revealed aspect Rachel. In galus the revealed aspect goes with the Jews and appears cut off from Hashem, though in truth it is always bound to Him, and every mitzvah is meant to reunite them. Since the Shechinah in galus is called an orphan and a widow, he says one may not take pride in one's avodah.

title.en: Kiddushin and the reunion of souls

summary.en: The Rav asks why Maseches Kiddushin opens by learning 'kichah kichah' from the field of Efron, a burial purchase, when at a wedding one looks for good signs. He answers that a match reunites two halves of one soul already joined above, a bond that lasts even after death, which is why couples lie together in Me'aras HaMachpelah, the 'double' cave.

title.en: The Ramban: Yaakov's apology to Yosef

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban on Yaakov's words to Yosef about Rachel's burial: Yaakov did not bury her in Me'aras HaMachpelah because he was ashamed before his fathers for having married two sisters. He asks why Yaakov should be ashamed of something he did rightly, and answers that Yaakov had to take both Rachel and Leah for hidden reasons of Torah beyond our grasp even on the level of pshat.

title.en: Yaakov's plan and Lavan's switch

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov wanted to marry Rachel first: seeing she would die young, he could marry Leah after her death and never have two living sisters, and Rachel would lie with him in Me'aras HaMachpelah. Lavan's deception overturned this. Rachel's absence from the cave reflects that Klal Yisrael must go into galus, with the Shechinah cut off from the aspect of Yaakov.

title.en: Rachel weeps for her children

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rachel had to be outside the cave because Jews go into galus and she weeps for her children, as in Yirmeyahu. Lavan, a spark of the Satan, fought Yaakov all his life; had Yaakov married Rachel first there could have been no galus. Yaakov wept on meeting Rachel because he saw the galus of the Shechinah, like the Gemara's voice cooing like a dove, and this is the root of Tikkun Rachel.

title.en: Bound to Be'er Sheva, going down to Bnei Kedem

summary.en: The Rav notes that Parshas Vayetzei has no break in the Torah because Yaakov never interrupted his attachment for a moment. Be'er Sheva hints at the oath every soul takes before birth, and Yaakov carried with him a rope that tied him to the Kisei HaKavod. 'Vayisa Yaakov raglav' hints at the generation of the heels, and Bnei Kedem, the 'forward' people, at a galus of progress and higher education.

title.en: Yeshayahu's counsel for galus: stay apart

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's true strength is being set apart from the nations, as in 'vayishkon Yisrael betach badad', and brings Yeshayahu's counsel 'lech ami bo vachadarecha' as the doctrine of how Jews must conduct themselves in galus. In earlier generations ghetto walls kept Jews apart; today the walls have been broken and Jews rub shoulders with the nations in the street, the subway, business and higher education. Where one is truly forced, he says, there is siyata dishmaya.

title.en: Fourteen years of preparation; Lavan's misreading

summary.en: The Rav explains that before going to Lavan, Yaakov learned fourteen years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever, preparing to turn fourteen years of physical work into spirituality. Lavan, a poor man, could not understand why Yaakov offered seven years of work; Yaakov knew that Rachel is the Shechinah and that one must prepare, as the six workdays prepare for Shabbos. He adds that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls.

title.en: Yaakov's secret: Tehillim and Shir HaMaalos

summary.en: The Rav asks how Yaakov stayed Yaakov in Lavan's house and brings the Midrash that he said Tehillim and the fifteen Shir HaMaalos. He reads Lavan's 'nakvah secharcha' as the offer to a man he took for a fool, compares the Ropshitzer who fooled the Satan until his last day, and says that one who must live in today's galus has to bind himself to Torah, Tehillim and tears.

title.en: A great yetzer hara; angels greet Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav tells of a chassid on his deathbed who recalled the teaching that there is a great yetzer hara. He notes that the sedra ends with angels meeting Yaakov after his years in Lavan's house and rejoicing over him, and closes that every Jew carries a piece of Yaakov and prays to pass through his trials.

catalogTitle: A Lesson for the 'גלות איד' from יעקב

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov Avinu, the greatest of the Avos, grew in Lavan's house by serving Hashem through earthly life, and that a Jew must likewise hallow his business and physical life after his davening.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Lechovitcher, who said no Torah on Vayeitzei: the parsha itself shows how a tzaddik grew in Haran while raising a family and amassing wealth. When Yaakov left, he was astonished by the angels; returning, the angels were astonished by him. The Avos are the Merkava, and Yaakov, the choicest of them, served Hashem with earthly matters, as a Jew may bring shelamim and eat for the sake of Heaven while a goy may not. He kissed Rachel because he saw in her the Shechinah, and wept when the locals mocked him; his seven years of work felt like days because the preparation was itself avodah. Lavan saw only lust. The sheep Yaakov worked to acquire were Jewish neshamos imprisoned by Lavan, which he raised into the 600,000 Jews of Mitzrayim. The lesson: after Shacharis, a Jew's business must be hallowed. In answer to questions, he speaks of becoming a mensch.

en: Yaakov Avinu grew greater in Haran, amid Lavan's impurity and earthly affairs, than he had been in Eretz Yisrael, so that the angels themselves were astonished at him on his return.
The Avos were the Merkava, a dwelling place of Hashem every moment of their lives, and the tzaddik is the ladder through which all creation rises or falls.
Unlike the goy, who gives G-d His due and keeps the rest for himself, a Jew can harness his body, his eating and his wealth to the service of Hashem, and this is Yaakov's distinction.
Rachel and Leah represent aspects of the Shechinah, and Yaakov's love for Rachel and his fourteen years of work were holy longing, which Lavan misread as lust.
Lavan's sheep were Jewish neshamos held captive by him, and Yaakov's mission in Haran was to free them and raise them until they became the 600,000 Jews in Mitzrayim.
Davening with tallis and tefillin is a preparation, like Yaakov's years in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever, so that a Jew's work and business afterward should also be hallowed.

candidateTopics: Rachel and Leah as the Shechinah

title.en: Yaakov grew in Haran; the angels astonished

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Lechovitcher said no Torah on Vayeitzei, since the parsha itself shows how Yaakov stayed a tzaddik and grew in Haran. He brings the Zohar contrasting Yaakov's astonishment at the angels on leaving with the angels' astonishment at him on his return twenty years later.

title.en: The Avos are the Merkava; Yaakov the ladder

summary.en: The Rav explains Chazal's teaching that the Avos are the Merkava, the heavenly chariot Yechezkel saw: every moment of their lives was attachment to Hashem. Yaakov himself is the ladder of his dream, on whom creation rises or falls, and Hashem stands upon him; Yaakov is the choicest of the Avos.

title.en: Serving Hashem with earthly life: olah and shelamim

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Avraham's and Yitzchak's mesiras nefesh with Yaakov, who dealt with family and wealth yet is the greatest. He brings a Midrash on the nations' olos slaughtered in the north and Yisrael's shelamim in the south: a goy separates his pleasures from G-d, while a Jew can eat, marry and prosper for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Kissing and weeping; touching the Avos' deeds

summary.en: The Rav shows Hashem's presence on Yaakov in all he did, and asks why Yaakov both kissed Rachel and wept, two opposite emotions. Before answering he cautions that no one can simply decide to be like Yaakov, but each Jew must aspire that his deeds touch those of the Avos and hallow his physical life.

title.en: Rachel and Leah as the Shechinah

summary.en: The Rav describes Tikkun Chatzos and its two parts, Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah, showing that Rachel and Leah stand for aspects of the Shechinah. Yaakov saw in Rachel the seat of the Shechinah and kissed her as a Jew kisses his tefillin; when the locals jeered at him, he wept out of pity that they could not understand.

title.en: Fourteen years of preparation, seven like days

summary.en: The Rav links Yaakov's fourteen years of work for Rachel and Leah to the fourteen sleepless years he learned in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever, a preparation of his body. Yaakov himself offered seven years, and they seemed like days because the preparation was itself avodas Hashem, like the joy of building a sukkah.

title.en: How Lavan saw Yaakov; Kedosh Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav explains that Lavan, the embodiment of earthliness and temptation, read Yaakov's devotion as lust, hinting with 'nakvah' that he could offer him another woman. In truth Yaakov was wholly holy, which is why Hashem is called Kedosh Yaakov and the third bracha of Shemoneh Esrei, corresponding to Yaakov, speaks of holiness.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep and the tzaddikim who remembered

summary.en: The Rav notes that on the surface Yaakov used devices to acquire Lavan's sheep, but the Arizal's Etz Chaim has a section named akudim, nekudim, berudim. Every Jew was once a sheep of Yaakov; the Midrash speaks of 600,000 flocks. He tells of the Yismach Moshe, who remembered being neutral in Korach's dispute and bore a mark from Yaakov's staff, and of the Apter Rav, who remembered Yaakov's tune.

title.en: Freeing the captive neshamos from Lavan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish neshamos imprisoned by Lavan, who was the Satan and was Bilaam. Yaakov's mission, for which he prepared fourteen years, was to free them and raise them from sheep into the 600,000 Jews in Mitzrayim, and through this he grew more than in the house of Shem and of Yitzchak.

title.en: After Shacharis: hallowing the workday

summary.en: The Rav draws the lesson of the sedra: a Jew does not give Hashem His due in shul and then live as he pleases. Davening with tallis and tefillin is the preparation, like Shem and Ever, so that his business is hallowed; he should learn as much as possible and not overextend in business. Hashem's holiness, Kel HaKadosh, is not confined to the shul and beis medrash.

title.en: Questions: from animal to mensch

summary.en: Answering a question on how the sheep came to Lavan, the Rav says they had been people who lost their human status in a prior life. He explains that a person's life work is to become a mensch rather than an animal in human guise, tells of a tzaddik who saw a visitor as an ox, and identifies the people of Sodom with Korach's congregation.

catalogTitle: עיקר השתלשלות של כלל ישראל הוא דוקא בגלות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows from Yaakov's years in the house of Lavan that the main growth of Klal Yisrael, from Yaakov himself to the twelve tribes and the six hundred thousand, happened specifically in galus and under hard conditions.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yaakov leaving Eretz Yisrael for Charan, the place of the greatest impurity. Yaakov hid fourteen years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever, and the Torah too hides those years inside the count of Yishmael's years. Esav did not chase him to Lavan, because Lavan, who was Bilam, was the root of impurity. Yaakov's stay with Lavan is a sign for his children's galus: at the start of the parsha Yaakov was surprised by the angels, and twenty-two years later the angels were surprised by him. The Rav then shows that three of the four stages in the growth of the Jewish people happened outside Eretz Yisrael, and that Yaakov became the kadosh of the Avos in Lavan's house. He describes the history of Jews in galus, explains that the angels, not tricks, gave Yaakov his flocks, connects the parsha to Chanukah, and ends by urging use of the last moments of galus.

en: Yaakov went specifically to the place of the greatest impurity, Lavan's house, and his stay there is a sign for the galus of his children.
Instead of Yaakov being surprised by the holiness of the angels, after twenty-two years with Lavan the angels were surprised by the holiness of Yaakov.
Three of the four stages in the development of Klal Yisrael (Avraham, the twelve tribes, the six hundred thousand) took place outside Eretz Yisrael and under hard conditions.
Yaakov, the chosen of the Avos and the one called kadosh, became great specifically through suffering in the house of Lavan.
Jews accomplished more in galus than in Eretz Yisrael, and the Torah sheb'al peh of the Talmud Bavli developed there.
Yaakov's wealth came because the angels brought him the sheep, and Lavan himself was blessed only through Yaakov, as later countries were blessed through the Jews.
Avodah in galus, under hard conditions, gives Hashem more nachas ruach than in Eretz Yisrael, so the last moments of galus must be used.

title.en: Yaakov hidden, and why Esav did not chase him

summary.en: The Rav describes Yaakov leaving for Charan, the place of greatest impurity, and hiding fourteen years with Shem and Ever, years the Torah itself hides inside the count of Yishmael's years. He explains that Esav did not chase Yaakov to Lavan because Lavan, identified with Bilam, was the essence of impurity.

title.en: The angels surprised by Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav calls Yaakov's stay with Lavan a sign for his children's galus. He brings Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch's observation that at the start of the parsha Yaakov 'met' the angels, while at its end the angels 'met' him, surprised that a man stayed holy in such a place.

title.en: Four stages in the growth of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav traces the stages of the Jewish people: Avraham alone, the twelve tribes, the seventy souls and the six hundred thousand. Avraham grew in Ur Kasdim, the tribes were born outside the land, and the people formed in Egypt; only the seventy souls were in Eretz Yisrael, because they correspond to the seventy nations.

title.en: Yaakov became the kadosh in Lavan's house

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov, the chosen of the Avos, corresponds to the bracha of kedushah and became holy specifically through suffering in Lavan's house. He adds that the middah of emes, the hardest to acquire, comes from Yaakov, as seen in his dealings with Lavan.

title.en: The history of Klal Yisrael in galus

summary.en: The Rav calls Yaakov the symbol of Jews going into galus and asks how a Jew must conduct himself among the nations. He says Jews accomplished more in galus than in Eretz Yisrael, as the Talmud Bavli shows, compares Eretz Yisrael to Shabbos and galus to the weekdays of preparation, and describes how the nations barred Jews from farming, envied their success in trade and spread blood libels.

title.en: The angels brought Yaakov's sheep

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's sticks were not a trick to gain sheep: as Rashi says, the angels brought him the sheep, and they were the source of the souls of the six hundred thousand. He adds that Lavan was blessed only because of Yaakov, as countries like Spain declined after expelling their Jews.

title.en: Chanukah, and using the last moments of galus

summary.en: The Rav concludes that preparation for Moshiach comes specifically in galus, and ties this to Chanukah, a weekday Yom Tov whose menorah stands on the left side in the dark nights. He says that in the days of Moshiach there is no bechirah, that avodah in galus gives more nachas ruach, and calls for learning, davening, tzedakah and work on middos now.

catalogTitle: דרך הישרה להתנהג בגלות -הכנעה (כמו שיעקב אע"ה התנהג לעשו)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why, before the time of tikkun, the right way for Jews in exile is Yaakov's way of submission, prayer and gifts toward Esav, and how to recognize Esav even when he appears as a talmid chacham.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a contradiction: the Midrash criticizes Yaakov for submitting to Esav, while the Ramban says Chazal learned from him how to deal with Esav. The Chiddushei HaRim answers that the Midrash speaks by drash and the Zohar by sod; before the tikkun, since Adam's sin, the layers of Torah can seem to clash. Following Rabbeinu Bachya, in exile the way is prayer and gifts, not war. The Rav applies this to the dispute over Soviet Jewry, Mordechai and Haman, and the Maharal on Rachel's plea. He warns that before Moshiach the erev rav, Esav disguised as a talmid chacham, will seem vindicated by signs, and that the test is following the earlier generations, as the Chasam Sofer taught. He closes with the gift to Esav, Esav's descendants, the alufim of Esav, and when war is warranted.

en: The Midrash's criticism of Yaakov and the Ramban's lesson from him are both true: one speaks by drash, the other by sod.
Since the sin of Adam HaRishon, before the world of tikkun, the parts of Torah can seem to contradict each other; with Moshiach the contradictions will be smoothed out.
In the time of exile the way toward the nations is prayer and gifts, not war, because of the oath not to rebel against them.
Before Moshiach the erev rav will appear as talmidei chachamim and even show signs, and a Jew must hold fast to emunah regardless.
The test of who is genuine is whether he follows the ways of the earlier generations, as the Chasam Sofer taught that anything new is forbidden by the Torah.
War is warranted only when Yiddishkeit itself is at stake, as the Chashmonaim fought the Hellenizers, not when it concerns the nations.

title.en: Midrash and Zohar on Yaakov's submission

summary.en: The Rav presents the contradiction between the Midrash, which criticizes Yaakov for submitting to Esav, and the lesson Chazal drew from him, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim's answer: the Midrash speaks by drash, the Zohar by sod, and before the tikkun the layers of Torah can clash.

title.en: Prayer and gifts, not war, in exile

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov saw the layers of Torah and chose submission, since the kings of Edom had to reign first; the Tannaim followed him before Rome. He brings the Ramban that Yaakov prepared gifts, prayer and war, and Rabbeinu Bachya that in exile only gifts and prayer remain, because of the oath in the Gemara.

title.en: A test of emunas chachamim: Russia and Mordechai

summary.en: The Rav describes the recent dispute over Soviet Jewry: the gedolim favored shtadlanus and Tehillim, the militants favored confrontation, and the militants seemed to succeed. He compares it to Mordechai, whose refusal to bow brought Haman's decree, and says that before the tikkun such contradictions leave room to criticize the gedolim, a test of the time before Moshiach.

title.en: The Maharal on Rachel's plea

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal in Netzach Yisrael on the Midrash of Rachel's plea: she was not jealous of Leah and gave her the signs, so why is Hashem jealous of the idols? The Maharal explains that Rachel understood it was not yet the time of tikkun, that contradictions must be smoothed out through exile, and that Jews' sins come from the state of the world, not their essence.

title.en: Causing sin is worse than killing

summary.en: The Rav says one must think carefully and go in the straight path: Russia lets Jews out, but many have left Yiddishkeit, and causing someone to sin is worse than killing him. He tells how the Baal HaTanya prayed for Russia's victory over Napoleon, preferring hardship for Jews over spiritual decline, and says Heaven measures by other standards.

title.en: False prophets with true signs

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the battle in Eretz Yisrael led by erev rav leaders, and of a tradition that before Moshiach the fire will descend on the altar of Baal, reversing Eliyahu at Carmel. With the Chiddushei HaRim on the passuk of the prophet who gives a sign, he says false ideas will seem confirmed from Heaven, and a Jew must cover his eyes, say Shema and hold to emunah.

title.en: Esav's angel disguised as a talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav explains that the man who wrestled with Yaakov appeared to him as a talmid chacham, and that Esav's angel can disguise himself as one. The worst exile will be that of the erev rav, and the Midrash says that when Esav sits among the tzaddikim in a tallis, only Hashem Himself will cast him down.

title.en: The exile of the erev rav today

summary.en: The Rav says the erev rav will join Gog and Magog against Moshiach, and points to events in Jerusalem against the Jews of Meah Shearim. The exile of the erev rav is harder because they are our brothers; Yaakov prayed to be saved from his brother, the talmid chacham Esav, and the question is how to tell who is who.

title.en: Follow the earlier shepherds; the sense of smell

summary.en: The Rav brings Shir HaShirim as Chazal read it: in the confusion of exile, follow the tracks of the flock, the ways of earlier generations. The test is whether one introduces nothing new; he brings the Chasam Sofer's battle against Mendelssohn's innovations, R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's opposition to the new Chief Rabbinate, and explains that the tzaddikim had a sense of smell like the one Havdalah needs.

title.en: Where the Torah shows who Esav is

summary.en: The Rav notes that a reader of the plain pesukim could think Esav was not so bad; a cheder boy knows he was a rasha only from his rebbe. But at the end of this parsha, as Rashi brings from Chazal, the Torah shows openly the mamzerus among Esav's descendants, and there one can recognize who Esav is.

title.en: Yaakov's gift and the captured souls

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov was pained at sending a gift to Esav, since his animals had Jewish souls; before the tikkun many Jewish souls are captured by Esav. He compares Eliyahu's bull at Carmel, and brings the Midrash of an am ha'aretz who read 'minchah yashivu' as the return of Yaakov's gifts, explaining that his soul's root was among those gifts.

title.en: Shechem: milah without becoming a Jew

summary.en: The Rav turns to the episode of Shechem: a milah that is not done to become a Jew is no milah. From the Mishnah in Nedarim he explains that orlah is only an outer klipah on a Jew, while a non-Jew remains an arel even after cutting; a ger means becoming a proper Jew.

title.en: The alufim of Esav and when to fight

summary.en: The Rav explains that saying the names of the alufim of Esav returns Esav to his root, where he has no existence, which is a preparation for Chanukah. He sets the rule that one fights only when Yiddishkeit is at stake, as the Chashmonaim did, and closes by urging his listeners to hold on to the parsha, connect to the tzaddikim, and stand firm in emunah against the erev rav.

catalogTitle: ביאור במעשה שכם והמלחמה עליהם' ושייכות זה לחנוכה. ועוד כמה עניני חנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav reads the episode of Dina and Shechem as a war over the tznius and holiness of Klal Yisroel, the same war Yehudis fought at Chanukah, and ends by calling on each listener to check whether he thinks like Yaakov or like Lavan.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ran's view that women were central to the Chanukah miracle through Yehudis, and the Chasam Sofer's question why women then do not light as mehadrin. He answers that the mitzvah's segulah of sons who are talmidei chachamim comes from tznius, which women keep by staying home. Turning to the parsha, he explains how Shimon could marry Dina, why Shechem belongs to Yosef and the guarding of the bris, and how Shimon and Levi truly 'circumcised' the city by removing its people. From Shechem's five expressions of love he learns how much more a Jew must yearn for Hashem, adds the Rambam's warnings about arayos, and contrasts Yaakov's spiritual war with Esav to the war against Shechem. He ends with the Yismach Moshe on Yaakov and Esav, Lavan's crooked logic, and a call for a cheshbon hanefesh before Chanukah.

en: Women were central to the Chanukah miracle, and the mitzvah's segulah of sons who are talmidei chachamim flows from the tznius Yehudis gave her life for.
Shechem is the place tied to Yosef and the guarding of the bris, and therefore it was first covered by the coarsest 'orlah', Shechem son of Chamor.
A non-Jew is orlah through and through, so cutting does not help him; Shimon and Levi did the true 'milah' by removing the people of Shechem so that the holy place remained.
If Shechem gave up so much for a passing worldly pleasure, a Jew must be ready to give far more for his love of Hashem.
Shimon and Levi were right to fight Shechem, but they should have asked Yaakov first; acting on their own let the trait of cruelty settle in them.
Every Jew rubs shoulders with Esav and Lavan, and must ask whether his way of thinking comes from the house of Shem and Ever or from the house of Lavan.

candidateTopics: love of Hashem learned from worldly desire
Yaakov and Lavan's way of thinking

title.en: Why women don't light as mehadrin

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ran and Tosafos that the main Chanukah miracle came through women, through Yehudis, and the Chasam Sofer's question why women are then not among the mehadrin. He finds the Chasam Sofer's answer, that lighting used to be outside, still difficult.

title.en: Chanukah lights and tznius

summary.en: From the Gemara that Chanukah lights bring sons who are talmidei chachamim, and the Midrash that this comes from the tznius of women, the Rav explains that women lose nothing by staying home, since tznius is the point of the mitzvah. He ties this to Dina going out and to preparing for Chanukah with tznius.

title.en: How Shimon could marry Dina

summary.en: The Rav asks how Shimon could marry his sister Dina. He answers with the Targum Yonasan that Dina was conceived by Rachel and moved to Leah, the Rambam that a ben Noach is liable for killing a fetus, and the Parashas Derachim that Shimon and Levi held the sons of Yaakov had the status of bnei Noach, so Dina counted as Rachel's daughter.

title.en: Shechem, Yosef and the bris

summary.en: The Rav explains why Yaakov gave Shechem to Yosef: Yosef's level is guarding the bris, and Shechem is the place in Eretz Yisroel tied to it. Since the shell precedes the fruit and the orlah covers the bris, the place was first held by Shechem son of Chamor the Chivi, names he reads as coarse physicality and the snake, while Shechem itself stands for Shem Kevod Malchuso.

title.en: 'Like us' versus 'as they are circumcised'

summary.en: The Rav describes the people of Shechem as sunk in coarseness and drawn to sensation, and notes that the brothers demanded 'become like us' while Chamor told his people 'as they are circumcised'. With the Mishnah in Nedarim and the passuk that all the nations are uncircumcised, he explains that a Jew becomes whole when the orlah is removed, but a non-Jew is orlah through and through.

title.en: The true milah of Shechem

summary.en: With a parable of printers who imitated the Slavita print only in appearance, the Rav explains that the circumcision of Shechem's people did not fulfil the condition, and Shimon and Levi fulfilled it by removing them so that holy Shechem remained. He contrasts 'all who go out of the gate of his city' here with 'all who come into the gate' at the purchase of Me'aras Hamachpelah.

title.en: Learning Hashem's love from the rasha

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Hashem's love for Klal Yisroel is expressed in the same terms used of Shechem, and that we learn them from the parsha of this rasha. He explains that worldly pleasures exist as a mashal: if Shechem gave so much for a fleeting pleasure, how much must a Jew give for the eternal pleasure of closeness to Hashem.

title.en: The sweetness of Torah and numbed senses

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Skverer Rebbe, who wondered that one also gets reward for learning Mesechta Mikvaos when the learning itself is so sweet. Only those who laugh at worldly pleasures feel this, as the Lechovitcher read the Gemara of the two jesters; one who feels no taste in a blatt Gemara has senses numbed by sin, like an anesthetic.

title.en: Eishes chayil and the Rambam on arayos

summary.en: The Rav explains that eishes chayil hints at the Torah, the true object of a Jew's love, of which worldly desire is only the refuse. He reads the Rambam that nothing is harder to separate from than arayos, that every community has people who are lax in it, and that the best counsel is to turn one's mind to Torah, adding the Kotzker's reading of the Targum on 'do not come near a woman' that one cannot stand on both sides.

title.en: Two wars: Esav and Shechem

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Purim, a physical rescue celebrated with feasting, with Chanukah, a war over Jewish holiness celebrated with Hallel and lights, and notes the Chofetz Chaim's word on fighting the Yevsektsia. In the same way Yaakov's struggle with Esav was won mainly by tefillah, while the war against Shechem, who sought to kill the soul and the tznius of Klal Yisroel, was like Yehudis' war; Rav Hirsch's reading of 'nevalah' shows Shechem wanted Jews to fall from their level.

title.en: Why Yaakov rebuked Shimon and Levi

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov was angry if Shimon and Levi were right, and answers from the Midrash that they acted on their own instead of asking Yaakov. With the Ohr HaChaim on the ir hanidachas, he explains that one who carries out harsh deeds without a command can develop cruelty, and this is how Shimon and Levi later came to plot against Yosef.

title.en: Edom, redness and David HaMelech

summary.en: The parsha ends with Esav, father of Edom, and the Rav traces Esav's redness through the pesukim and the custom not to wear red. With the Midrash contrasting Esav and David, both 'admoni', he explains that David shed blood only with the sanction of beis din, and applies the power of Edom to the 'red' power of his day, which David's holy din will avenge; Chanukah, he says, removes the redness that clings from Esav.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's dream

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe's dream: Yaakov and Esav shared one womb so that something of each rubbed off on the other, and Yaakov is rewarded for not being swayed by Esav's evil while Esav is punished for not using Yaakov's good. This, he says, is Yaakov's hint in 'im Lavan garti': nothing of Lavan clung to me.

title.en: The logic of Lavan's house

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew in exile rubs against Esav and Lavan through reading, media, the street or work, and that the very way a Jew thinks comes from Sinai. He shows it from Yaakov's argument with Lavan at the end of Vayeitzei: after Yaakov's sound reasoning Lavan still answers 'the daughters are my daughters', because Lavan's logic was formed in his house, not in the house of Shem and Ever.

title.en: A cheshbon hanefesh before Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav calls on each person to ask where his thinking comes from, tells of a father who complained that his son lacked yiras shamayim and his answer that the yeshivah is not the only influence on the boy, and asks whether one thinks like Yaakov or like Lavan. He ends by tying this to preparing for Chanukah and to uprooting Esav at the end of the parsha.

catalogTitle: Anti Semitism: It's Necessity, Its Irrationality, and It Is Inevitable

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the hatred of the nations for the Jews is a natural, irrational decree from Har Sinai that preserves Klal Yisrael from assimilation, and shows it already in Lavan's sons accusing Yaakov of living off their father.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that hatred came down to the nations at Har Sinai and Rashi's 'it is a halacha that Esav hates Yaakov'. This hatred is natural, like an animal's, and serves as a preservative against assimilation. He turns to the era of Ikvesa d'Meshicha, when much of Klal Yisrael left emunah altogether, and to Herzl's plan to end antisemitism with a Jewish state, which instead became its main cause. A fable of animals blaming a sheep for a plague illustrates how Jews are always the culprits. In the parsha, Lavan's sons call Yaakov a parasite although Lavan prospered through him. The Rav explains Kabbalistically that Lavan's sheep held lofty souls Yaakov came to redeem, that his peeled rods were his tefillin, and tells of the Arizal smiling at the Alshich's drasha. He ends that no human solution removes the hatred, and that Hashem is guiding events in Eretz Yisrael toward the geulah.

en: Hatred of the nations for Klal Yisrael came down at Har Sinai; it is natural and instinctive, like the hatred between animals, and needs no reason.
The hatred has a purpose: it is a preservative that keeps Jews in golus from assimilating, and where Jews have freedom, assimilation spreads.
Herzl's plan to end antisemitism through a Jewish state failed; the State itself has become a main cause of hatred, and no solution of those who left the Torah has helped.
Lavan's sons calling Yaakov a parasite, although Lavan was blessed through him, is the pattern of Jews in every golus: they bring prosperity and are accused of robbing it.
Yaakov did not cheat Lavan: the sheep were brought by malachim, his peeled rods were his way of fulfilling tefillin, and his task was to redeem the holy souls held in Lavan's flocks.
What Hashem is doing in Eretz Yisrael now cannot be understood, like black splashes in an unfinished painting, but when the picture is complete every step will be understood.
