title.en: Hatred from Sinai, a natural preservative

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that hatred came down to the nations at Har Sinai and Rashi's 'halacha' that Esav hates Yaakov. He calls it a natural, instinctive hatred that preserves Jews from assimilation, brings the Zohar that it stems from jealousy, and the Yismach Moshe that Hashem puts hatred between tzaddik and rasha so nothing rubs off.

title.en: Ikvesa d'Meshicha and the departure from emunah

summary.en: The Rav says that before the geulah there will be reshaim who leave Hashem entirely, as Malachi and the end of Daniel describe, and that the Chofetz Chaim saw the signs of Ikvesa d'Meshicha already in his time. Unlike the ancient pull of avodah zarah, today's trial is atheism, which began with the Haskalah in Germany; he brings the Meshech Chochmah that the punishment would also come from Germany.

title.en: Herzl's solution and its reverse

summary.en: The Rav describes Herzl's plan that a Jewish state would end antisemitism, and says the State of Israel has instead become its cause, citing a European poll naming Israel as the world's main troublemaker. He points to the hypocrisy of condemning Jews for defending themselves while America does the same in Iraq.

title.en: The animals' trial and the Black Plague

summary.en: The Rav tells a fable: during a plague in the jungle the beasts excuse the leopard and the wolf for their killings but convict a sheep that ate straw from a shepherd's shoe. So too the Jews are blamed for every trouble, as in the Black Plague, which Jews were spared through their cleanliness and were then accused of causing.

title.en: Lavan's sons: Yaakov the parasite

summary.en: The Rav brings the end of the parsha where Lavan's sons say Yaakov took everything from their father, though they themselves were born through Yaakov's blessing, as Rashi and Lavan's own words show. Without the Oral Torah Yaakov looks like a cheater; the nations always paint Jews so, as in Shakespeare's Shylock, because Jews prosper wherever they go and are then libeled out of jealousy.

title.en: The holy souls in Lavan's sheep

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that malachim brought Yaakov sheep from Lavan's flocks, then opens a deeper matter: according to the Arizal, based on the Zohar, the great souls of the Dor HaMabul, the Dor Haflagah and Sedom came down again in Lavan's sheep. Yaakov's task was to redeem these 600,000 souls from the sitra achra and bring them to their tikkun.

title.en: Lavan's power and Yaakov's switches

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar's question why Esav did not pursue Yaakov at Lavan's house: Lavan was the merkava of the Samech-Mem, and Esav relied on him, but Hashem protected Yaakov. Before Matan Torah the tzaddikim could fulfill mitzvos in their own way; mitzvos are like switches that light up the upper worlds, and Yaakov's peeled rods were his tefillin. The redeemed sheep went down to Mitzrayim and became Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The Arizal smiles at the Alshich's drasha

summary.en: The Rav praises the Alshich HaKadosh and tells how the Arizal attended his Shabbos drasha on Parshas Vayeitzei and smiled throughout. Asked why, the Arizal said that Lavan's soul had come to listen, and nodded at each of the hundred tricks the Alshich found in the pesukim, admitting he had tried it on Yaakov and it had failed.

title.en: The pattern of golus: blamed for prosperity

summary.en: The Rav returns to Lavan's sons, jealous of Yaakov although Lavan prospered through him, like the Jewish finance ministers of Europe accused of disloyalty. He explains that Jews turned to lending with interest only because the nations barred them from land and confined them to ghettos, and that the nations prospered from it, as Yaakov told Lavan. No solution, neither Herzl's nor communism, removes the hatred.

title.en: Hatred, freedom, and the wandering of Torah

summary.en: The Rav says hatred in golus is a decree that keeps Jews from assimilating, and now that there is freedom, assimilation in America and elsewhere is enormous. Yaakov at Lavan is a mirror of all of golus. He then speaks of the Torah's stations through the exile, bringing the Gra that America would be the last golus of Torah, and describes the flowering of Torah in Williamsburg after the war.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael: an unfinished painting

summary.en: The Rav says Torah has now moved to Eretz Yisrael and keeps growing despite a leadership that fights it. What is happening there is beyond understanding, like black splashes in a painting not yet finished; Hashem has a master plan, and when it is complete every step will be understood.

catalogTitle: בדיבורים של יעקב לעשו ובפרשה של “ואלה המלכים” נטמן עומק נצחון של יעקב

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Yaakov's humble words to Esav and the parsha of the kings of Edom hide Yaakov's true victory: the Jewish souls he raised in Lavan's flocks, the path of 'diminution that leads to increase', and the light of Chanukah that comes down to those who cannot rise.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Yaakov's eight bowings to Esav correspond to the eight kings of Edom, and explains that a tzaddik speaking to a rasha is really speaking to Hashem, as David did with Naval. He asks why the Midrash reads 'shifchah' in 'vayehi li shor vachamor' as Avigail. To answer, he explains that Lavan's sheep were fallen Jewish souls that Yaakov went to Charan to raise, so Yaakov's message to Esav described spiritual wealth, not cattle. Avigail, who stopped David from killing Naval (Lavan reborn), is why Yaakov did not fight Lavan. He then explains the kings of Edom through sheviras hakeilim: tzaddikim go from diminution to increase, reshaim from increase to collapse; the eighth king is the tikkun. He ends with Chanukah, when Yaakov's light descends into the longest night to give back the tzelem Elokim.

en: When Yaakov called Esav 'my master', he was speaking to the Ribono shel Olam, and Esav understood the double meaning.
Yaakov's twenty years in Charan were spent raising Jewish souls that had sunk so low they were born as Lavan's sheep.
'Vayehi li shor vachamor tzon ve'eved veshifchah' told Esav of Moshiach ben Yosef, Yissachar, Klal Yisrael, David and Avigail, not of animals.
The kings of Edom allude to sheviras hakeilim: the seven who died are the broken vessels, and the eighth, Hadar, is the tikkun.
Tzaddikim are led by diminution after diminution that ends in increase, while reshaim receive increase after increase that ends in collapse.
Chanukah is the light of Yaakov coming down in the darkest time to give the tzelem Elokim to souls that cannot rise by themselves.

title.en: Yaakov's words to Esav were spoken to Hashem

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov's eight 'adoni' to Esav correspond to the eight kings of Edom, and explains that tzaddikim speaking to a rasha really speak to the Ribono shel Olam. Esav, raised in the home of Avraham and Yitzchak, understood this; the Zohar explains David's greeting to Naval the same way.

title.en: Shor, chamor, eved, shifchah: why Avigail?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash Rabbah that the shor is Yosef, the chamor Yissachar, the tzon the Jewish people, the eved David and the shifchah Avigail, and asks why Avigail of all people. He retells the episode of David, Naval and Avigail, notes other midrashim that read shifchah as Ruth or Esther, and mentions Rashi's comment that Yitzchak's blessing had not been fulfilled.

title.en: The angels who fell in Sodom escort Yaakov

summary.en: Going back to last week's parsha, the Rav brings the Targum Yonasan that the angels on Yaakov's ladder were those expelled for revealing the secret of Sodom's destruction. A place of impurity can harm even angels; by escorting Yaakov, which binds souls together, they were repaired, since Yaakov only grew greater in Charan. These are the angels he then sent to Esav.

title.en: Lavan's sheep were fallen Jewish souls

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov had to spend twenty years in a place like Charan. He brings the sefarim that Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls, traces their fall through the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion, and explains that Lavan was the great rasha of his generation opposite the tzaddik Yaakov, so these souls fell under him and were born as animals.

title.en: Yaakov sees Rachel and waters the flock

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov saw in Rachel the Shechinah and in Lavan's flock his own future children who had lost their tzelem Elokim. Out of mercy he took them from Lavan's influence, because the one who feeds has power over the one fed, and watered them. He tells of the Yismach Moshe and the Ohev Yisrael, who remembered being lambs with Yaakov.

title.en: Raising the souls: 600,000 rams

summary.en: Yaakov's shepherding, feeding and singing raised the souls step by step until the shevatim were born. The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov had 600,000 rams, which, following the Arizal, are the 600,000 root souls, and reads 'my brothers, where are you from?' as Yaakov asking the souls about their root. Rashi's reading of 'vayatzel' as rescue shows he was redeeming captives.

title.en: Yaakov's message: my wealth is souls

summary.en: The Rav explains that with 'vayehi li shor vachamor' Yaakov told Esav his animals were Jewish souls: Moshiach ben Yosef, Yissachar, Klal Yisrael, David. Following Rashi, Yaakov said Yitzchak's blessing of heaven and earth was not fulfilled in him; the Rav explains that his true wealth comes from a place higher than heaven and earth, and that this frightened Esav.

title.en: The chen in Esav's eyes; the touch on Yaakov's thigh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Esav's head was buried in the Cave of Machpelah and that descendants of Haman learned Torah in Bnei Brak: the 'eyes' of Esav are the righteous converts who come from him, and Yaakov's 'to find chen in your eyes' hints at them. He then explains the angel's touch on Yaakov's thigh, which the Midrash reads as the generation of persecution, as no loss but the cause of Esav's downfall.

title.en: Why Yaakov did not fight Lavan: Avigail

summary.en: If Yaakov was so powerful, Esav could ask, why did he let Lavan cheat him for twenty years? The Rav brings the Arizal that Lavan was reborn as Naval and David carried Yaakov's soul, so David guarding Naval's sheep and wanting to kill him repeated Yaakov and Lavan. Avigail stopped him, saying Hashem will do it; Yaakov's 'shifchah' tells Esav that Avigail's soul was with him.

title.en: The awesome parsha of the kings of Edom

summary.en: The Rav turns to 've'eleh hamelachim' at the end of the parsha. Rabbeinu Bachya calls it an awesome parsha hinting at the creation of the world and the force of evil, the Midrash speaks of worlds built and destroyed, and the Derech Hashem says it shows the greatness of the Torah. He notes that seven kings are said to die but not the eighth, Hadar, whose wife is named, and compares our grasp of this to a child who knows a few letters of a page of Gemara.

title.en: Sheviras hakeilim and two ways Hashem leads

summary.en: The Rav explains sheviras hakeilim simply: the light was too great for the small vessels, they broke, and our avodah is to repair the fallen sparks; the seven kings who died are that world, and the eighth is the tikkun. From a sefer he brings that the world is run by the Torah's rules, so tzaddikim receive diminution after diminution that leads to increase, while reshaim receive so much shefa that their vessels burst.

title.en: Why the kings of Edom are in Vayishlach

summary.en: The Rav concludes that the eight kings follow Yaakov's eight bowings not as a punishment but as the path of diminution that leads to increase; the Zohar says that had Esav grasped Yaakov's wisdom he would have killed himself. He identifies the first king, Bela ben Be'or, with Bilaam and so with Lavan, and explains Avigail as the way of letting Lavan's increase bring his own fall, until the tikkun.

title.en: Chanukah in the longest nights

summary.en: The Rav ties this to the long nights of Teves, when the klipos are strongest, and to Chanukah, the soul of Yaakov coming down to clothe Jews in a tzelem Elokim. He tells of a tzaddik who saw no human form in a well-dressed communal leader, brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah comes from the days of Moshiach, links the eight days to the eighth king, and contrasts Shabbos, to which one must rise, with Chanukah, which comes down.

title.en: The Mikdash comes to Yaakov

summary.en: Yaakov wanted to go up to the Mikdash, but Hashem showed that since he now carried souls who could not rise there, the Mikdash would come to him. The Rav brings the dispute of Rashi and the Ramban on the kefitzas haderech and explains that the Shechinah came to Yaakov as he lay down to sleep, the level of Chanukah, when Hashem comes down to His children even in their lowest state.

title.en: Chanukah completes Rosh Hashanah; the oil on the stone

summary.en: The Rav brings from sefarim that Chanukah is the final time for those who did not finish their teshuvah, since it is the time of the eighth king. Rosh Hashanah recalls 'let us make man', and one who still lacks a human form receives the tzelem Elokim on Chanukah from Yaakov. He brings the Midrash, cited in Ner Mitzvah, that the oil Yaakov poured on the stone was the cruse later found by the Chashmonaim.

title.en: A little oil holds much: rejoicing on Chanukah

summary.en: The stone is the human form and the oil the light of Chanukah; like the Mikdash's place, where a little holds much, the small spark in every Jew can flare up. The Rav says one must rejoice on Chanukah, against the Greeks' claim that Jews have no portion in the G-d of Israel, mentions the custom to gather and sing praises, thanks the gabbaim, and closes with a wish that the light of Chanukah bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: הנסיונות הגדולות של יעקב בפרשה זו - כנגד הנסיונות הגדולות של סוף הגלות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how Yaakov, having stayed pure in the house of Lavan, could repair the angels who had fallen in Sodom and face Esav, and draws from this the great trials of emunah at the end of the exile.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Yismach Moshe: Yaakov met two camps of angels, those created by his mitzvos and those Hashem sent in his honor, and sent the second to Esav. He then brings the Targum Yonasan that the angels of Sodom were expelled from their place for saying 'we are destroying', and asks how angels could forget their Sender. Following the Arizal on Egypt, he answers that Sodom's impurity damaged even Gavriel and Rafael, and only a tzaddik free of that flaw could repair them. Yaakov, prepared in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever and unharmed by Lavan, did so, and sent those angels to Esav as witnesses. Since the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the end of the exile brings the same trials, above all in emunah. He explains the two Kabbalas Shabbos psalms as a redemption of din or of chesed, ties Moshiach on a donkey to toil in prayer, and ends with the angel who must concede Yaakov's blessings.

en: Yaakov met two camps of angels, those created by his own mitzvos and those Hashem sent in his honor; he sent the second camp to Esav, not wanting to use his mitzvos in this world.
The angels of Sodom were harmed by its impure atmosphere, just as the Arizal says Hashem did not send an angel into Egypt lest it be harmed there.
Only a tzaddik who is himself free of a flaw can repair it, so the fallen angels had to wait for Yaakov, who stayed untouched in the house of Lavan.
Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, Yaakov's return from Lavan and his struggle with Esav foreshadow the last trials before the redemption.
The main trial of the end of the exile is emunah, and the Rav says one must guard it, including in speech, since with emunah alone the Jews will leave the exile.
A small generation that has lived through many disappointments can be asked only for emunah, and so the redemption must come in the way of Nissan, of chesed, and not of Tishrei, of din.
The completeness of the redemption is that even the side of evil must concede the blessings, as the bad angel must answer amen on a Friday night prepared by a week of avodah.

title.en: Two camps of angels

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe: angels are created by a person's mitzvos, and Yaakov met a second camp sent by Hashem in his honor. He sent that camp, not the angels of his mitzvos, to Esav.

title.en: The angels expelled after Sodom

summary.en: The Rav brings the Targum Yonasan that the angels Yaakov saw at the ladder had been expelled from their place for saying in Sodom 'we are destroying', and now went back up. He asks how angels could err, why they were forgiven now, and how they forgot their Sender.

title.en: Why the angels were harmed in Sodom

summary.en: From the Arizal on 'I and not an angel' in the Haggadah, that Egypt was so impure that an angel would have been harmed there, the Rav explains that Sodom was the same, so even Gavriel and Rafael were damaged. He speaks of the power of bad company and says the damaged angels could not return until repaired.

title.en: Only one free of the flaw can repair it

summary.en: The Rav tells how souls came to tzaddikim such as the Arizal, the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Kozhnitzer Maggid for a tikkun, and explains that one can repair a flaw only if one is free of it. Yaakov first spent fourteen years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever, filling himself with kedushah, so he could enter Lavan's house unharmed and repair the angels, which Avraham and Yitzchak could not.

title.en: Lavan's impurity and the reversed 'vayifge'u'

summary.en: The Rav describes Lavan as the greatest impurity, identified with Bilam, and Yaakov as the one who could stay with him and grow in kedushah. From the Zohar on 'vayifga' he explains that going to Charan Yaakov was surprised by the angels, while coming back the angels were the ones who had the joy of meeting him.

title.en: The repaired angels sent to Esav

summary.en: With a story of the Chernobyler, the Rav explains that a tzaddik is bound to help one who serves him, so Yaakov repaired the angels sent to escort him. He then sent them to Esav, since they, who had fallen in an impure place, could testify firsthand that he lived with Lavan and kept the mitzvos, and he did not fear the four hundred men.

title.en: Yaakov's return as a sign for the ingathering

summary.en: Using the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Rav explains that Yaakov's joyous return to Eretz Yisrael with all the future Jewish souls is a sign of the return from exile. To know what the last struggle with Esav and Lavan will look like, he says, one must study the end of last week's parsha and the beginning of this one.

title.en: The trial of emunah before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the end of Daniel, the last chapter of Malachi and the Gemara that before Moshiach the wicked will succeed and one who turns from evil will be mocked. From the Arizal and the Ohr HaChaim he explains that at the end Jews will fall even into the fiftieth gate, heresy, and says that today even observance is often mere tradition; we are now in the house of Lavan and facing Esav.

title.en: Guarding emunah, and Chavakuk's one principle

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew must make a cheshbon hanefesh whether he could say 'I lived with Lavan and kept the mitzvos'. He teaches that emunah depends on guarding the bris, which includes guarding speech from lashon hara and mockery, and brings the Gemara that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on one: 'the tzaddik lives by his emunah'.

title.en: Two psalms: redemption in Nissan or Tishrei

summary.en: Explaining Chavakuk's name as embracing emunah, the Rav turns to two Kabbalas Shabbos psalms that end almost alike, one with 'ki va' twice and 'be'emunaso', the other with 'ki va' once and 'bemeisharim'. He prefaces the Gemara's dispute whether the redemption comes in Nissan or Tishrei, which the Satmar Rav read as a redemption of chesed or of din.

title.en: A generation of disappointments that still believes

summary.en: The Rav describes how Jews waited for the redemption through many promised dates and disappointments, and how from such small generations nothing can be expected but emunah. With 'shomrim laboker' and 'hinei Elokeinu zeh kivinu lo' he explains that after each disappointment they hope again.

title.en: The psalms explained, and Esav's kiss

summary.en: The Rav explains that the psalm with one 'ki va' and 'bemeisharim' describes a redemption of din, preceded by the shofar of Tishrei, while the psalm with 'ki va, ki va' and 'be'emunaso', preceded by the joy of Nissan, describes a redemption earned by renewed hope and emunah. So it was when Yaakov met Esav: Esav had no power to bite and his bite became a kiss.

title.en: 'Shor vachamor': the sparks Yaakov drew out

summary.en: On 'vayehi li shor vachamor' the Rav brings the Midrash that these allude to the two Moshiachs, and asks why Yaakov tells Esav this. He explains with the Midrash that Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls held by the forces of evil, which Yaakov repaired and drew out; so he warns Esav that he too will be made to give up the holy sparks in him, such as the souls of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Meir.

title.en: Moshiach rides on the toil of prayer

summary.en: The Rav says that in the final war of good and evil a Jew must cry to Hashem 'save me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esav'. He explains that the greater one's spark of Moshiach, the harder his davening, and Moshiach 'riding on a donkey' means he comes through the groaning prayers of simple, physical Jews and through toil like Yissachar's.

title.en: The angel must concede the blessings

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov needed the angel of Esav to concede his blessings, and answers with the Gemara of the two angels who accompany a Jew home on Friday night: when the house is ready the bad angel must answer amen, and that is the completeness of the redemption. Each Jew must prepare by a week of avodah, so that when the great Shabbos comes the angels meet him as they met Yaakov.

catalogTitle: “וישלח יעקב מלאכים” - עדות לגדלותו' שנשאר צדיק בסביבת רשעים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov sent Eisav the very angels he had restored to heaven, as living witnesses that he remained a tzaddik even in Lavan's place of tumah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Targum Yonasan: the angels who escorted Yaakov to Charan were the angels of Sedom, banished from heaven for saying 'ki mashchisim anachnu', and they returned only now. Why now, and why send such angels to escort Yaakov? Using the Arizal on why Hashem Himself went down to Mitzrayim, he explains that Sedom was a place of tumah that blemished the angels. Following the Derech Hashem, those who are not perfect tzaddikim are repaired by attaching themselves to a tzaddik; the angels needed a tzaddik who could live amid tumah unharmed. Yaakov, trained by Shem and Ever, kept his level at Lavan, so escorting him restored them, and he later sent them to Eisav as witnesses. The Rav then turns to Dinah, Leah's tears that freed her from being Eisav's zivug, Lavan's plan in switching the sisters, and the power of tears.

en: The angels who escorted Yaakov to Charan were the angels of Sedom, who had been kept out of heaven after saying 'ki mashchisim anachnu'.
A place of great tumah, like Mitzrayim or Sedom, blemishes even a holy angel who enters it.
Following the Derech Hashem, those who are not complete tzaddikim gain their tikkun by attaching themselves to a tzaddik and serving and supporting him.
Yaakov remained a tzaddik in Charan, the stronghold of tumah, and he prepared for this by learning at the yeshiva of Shem and Ever how to serve Hashem among goyim.
Yaakov sent these same restored angels to Eisav as witnesses that he had lived with Lavan without being harmed.
Leah was destined as Eisav's zivug, but her tears uprooted her from his mazal and brought her into Yaakov's.
Because Leah had belonged in potential to Eisav, Yaakov owed him, and this is why he was faulted for hiding Dinah from Eisav.

candidateTopics: tikkun through attachment to a tzaddik

title.en: The banished angels of Sedom

summary.en: The Rav brings Targum Yonasan that the angels escorting Yaakov were the angels of Sedom, kept out of heaven for saying 'ki mashchisim anachnu'. He asks why they were readmitted now, why such angels were sent to escort Yaakov, and how angels could sin at all.

title.en: Tumah of Mitzrayim and Sedom blemishes angels

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that Hashem Himself went down to Mitzrayim for makas bechoros because its tumah would have blemished an angel. He applies this to Sedom, which Lot saw was 'like the land of Mitzrayim', and concludes that the angels were blemished by entering it and so could not return to heaven.

title.en: Tikkun through attaching to a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav brings the Derech Hashem that the world was created for complete tzaddikim, and others gain a tikkun by attaching to a tzaddik, serving and supporting him. The angels likewise needed a tzaddik who had been in a place of tumah and remained unharmed, and they waited until Yaakov came.

title.en: Yaakov in Charan and the yeshiva of Shem and Ever

summary.en: The Rav describes Charan and the land of Kedem as the center of avodah zarah, kishuf and tumah, where Yaakov nevertheless remained a tzaddik and even grew. In the name of Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky he explains that Yaakov first learned fourteen years at the yeshiva of Shem and Ever, which taught how to serve Hashem among goyim, something he could not gain in Yitzchak's house.

title.en: The restored angels as witnesses to Eisav

summary.en: Heaven sent the angels to escort Yaakov; by serving a tzaddik who could stand in a place of tumah unharmed, they were repaired and readmitted to heaven. When Yaakov returned, the same angels met him, and he sent them to Eisav as trustworthy witnesses that he had lived with Lavan and kept the mitzvos.

title.en: Dinah in the box and Leah's tears

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yaakov hid Dinah in a box from Eisav and was punished for withholding chesed from his brother, and asks why a Jew should have to give his daughter to a rasha. He answers with 'kol hamon k'kol Shakai': people said Lavan's older daughter would marry Yitzchak's older son, Leah cried because it was so in her mazal, and a zivug is truly part of a person.

title.en: A zivug, tefillah, and Lavan's trick

summary.en: The Rav explains that a zivug is decreed before birth, yet through tefillah one can take another's zivug, which will not last; so he says one should daven for a good shidduch, not for a specific person. Lavan, who wanted to destroy Yaakov, switched Leah for Rachel, reckoning that Yaakov would not divorce her and would have to die so that Leah could reach her true zivug.

title.en: The power of tears and Yaakov's debt to Eisav

summary.en: Lavan did not know the power of tears: the Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that Eisav's crying opened the gates of heaven and earned him a new brachah, and Leah's tears likewise changed her root from Eisav to Yaakov. Since she had been bound to Eisav, Yaakov owed him Dinah, which is why he was faulted; the Rav ends without time to explain the good that came of it.

catalogTitle: יעקב's Tremendous Accomplishment in Taking the Sheep of לבן

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's taking of Lavan's sheep was not trickery but the redemption and cleansing of great souls, a forerunner of Yetzias Mitzrayim and of the Jewish people's history in golus.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with bechirah: each person is measured by Hashem according to his own nature, and the hardest test is to act against one's own character. Each of the Avos had his midah, and the Akeidah tested Avraham and Yitzchak against theirs; Yaakov's midah was emes, so his test was to say sheker at Rivka's prophetic command. He then explains why Hashem wanted Yitzchak to bless Yaakov thinking he was Esav. Turning to the sheep, he traces the great souls of the Dor HaMabul through the Dor HaHaflagah, a stage as Lavan's sheep, and Mitzrayim, explaining along the way why Noach was meant to be Moshe. Yaakov extricated these souls from Lavan; his sticks, says the Zohar, were the mitzvah of tefillin, done in secret against the Satan. Vayeitzei is the parsha of golus: Yaakov brought blessing to Lavan, who still claimed everything was his, as Jews have brought blessing to every land of their exile.

en: Bechirah is measured individually: Hashem judges each person by what is expected of his nature, and the hardest test is one that goes against a person's own character.
Yaakov's midah was emes, so his great test was to say sheker because Rivka told him so through prophecy.
The great souls of the Dor HaMabul returned in the Dor HaHaflagah, then as Lavan's sheep, and then as the Jews of Mitzrayim, being cleansed at each stage.
Yaakov extricated these souls from Lavan and brought them toward Eretz Yisrael and Mitzrayim, a redemption like Yetzias Mitzrayim.
According to the Zohar, Yaakov's carved sticks were the mitzvah of tefillin, and he did not trick Lavan at all.
Vayeitzei is the parsha of golus: Yaakov brought blessing to Lavan's house, yet Lavan claimed everything was his, as the nations say of the Jews who enriched them.

Jews bringing blessing to the nations

title.en: Bechirah is measured by each person's nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah gives every person bechirah, but Hashem measures each one by what is expected of his own nature: not killing earns nothing for one who cannot kill, and a natural masmid is asked why he did not learn even more.

title.en: The midos of the Avos and the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav describes Avraham's midah of chesed and Yitzchak's midah of din, and explains that the Akeidah tested each of them against his own midah. Yaakov's midah was emes, so pure that he would rather have died than say sheker.

title.en: Why Yaakov had to say sheker

summary.en: The Rav explains that every creation, even sheker, has a purpose, with a mashal of an artist offended by criticism of his painting. Rivka commanded Yaakov through prophecy to deceive Yitzchak; like Eliyahu at Har HaCarmel, a navi may command a one-time aveirah, and breaking his midah of emes was Yaakov's greatest avodah. He then explains why Hashem wanted Yitzchak to bless Yaakov while thinking he was Esav, and introduces the sheep of this week's parsha.

title.en: The Dor HaMabul and Noach who should have been Moshe

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Dor HaMabul were choice neshamos whom Hashem wanted to give the Torah; since Torah is like water and they refused it, the water came instead, forty days like the forty days of Matan Torah. Through the Zohar he explains the Gemara that finds Moshe in the Torah in the words 'beshagam hu basar': Noach was meant to be Moshe, failed to daven for his generation, and was replanted as Moshe Rabbeinu.

title.en: Mei Noach, the Haflagah and Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Navi calls the flood 'the waters of Noach' and how Moshe's 'mecheini na' repaired Noach's failure. The same souls returned in the Dor HaHaflagah, were scattered instead of destroyed thanks to their unity, and came back again as the Jews in Mitzrayim, where they were purified.

title.en: The souls as Lavan's sheep; the benefit of golus

summary.en: The Rav adds the stage he left out: between the Haflagah and Mitzrayim these souls were Lavan's sheep, which Yaakov domesticated, and the Midrash hints that he had 600,000 sheep, like the 600,000 who left Mitzrayim. Vayeitzei is a parsha of golus, and the Rav explains that Klal Yisrael accomplishes more in golus, as Torah reached its completion in Bavel.

title.en: Gedolim from golus and the sheep remembered

summary.en: The Rav lists Rabbanim of Yerushalayim and the Beis Yosef as products of golus, then returns to Yaakov extricating the sheep and bringing them to Eretz Yisrael and Mitzrayim. He describes the great souls sent down in the time of the Ba'al Shem Tov and tells of the Yismach Moshe, who remembered being Yaakov's sheep, and of a Rebbe who sang the niggun Yaakov played for his sheep.

title.en: Yaakov's sticks were tefillin

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that angels brought the sheep to Yaakov, and the Zohar's different account of the sticks. With the mashal of breakfast that works without our understanding it, he explains that mitzvos work even when we do not know how. The Avos made the same tikkunim before Matan Torah, and the Zohar says Yaakov's sticks were the mitzvah of tefillin, which recall Yetzias Mitzrayim, since he was redeeming these souls from Lavan.

title.en: A hidden battle with the Satan

summary.en: The Rav stresses that Yaakov did not trick Lavan; it was a battle of kedushah against tumah, as the Zohar shows in explaining why Esav never pursued Yaakov to Charan. Such a battle must be fought in secret so the Satan does not catch on, which is why the Torah presents it as a trick. He then calls Vayeitzei a parsha of deep golus and gives Lavan's complaint that Yaakov takes everything.

title.en: Yaakov's blessing to Lavan and the story of golus

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov took only what was his, yet Lavan claimed everything belonged to him, although Yaakov brought blessing to his house, as Lavan himself admitted. This, he says, is the story of golus: Jews brought prosperity to every land, as seen in Spain's decline after the expulsion and in America, while the nations accuse them of sucking their blood, as in Shakespeare's Shylock. He ends that Yaakov does leave Lavan and the world will yet acknowledge the truth.

catalogTitle: “הבוא נבוא אני ואמך ואחיך להשתחות לך ארצה”? - השכינה יורדת למטה מעשרה טפחים? (שייכות לחנוכה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Yosef as the all-inclusive tzaddik whose imprisonment and release foreshadow the galus and the geulah, and reads Yaakov's cry at the dream of the sun and moon bowing as a cry over the Shechinah's descent in a long galus, which Chanukah's lights below ten tefachim answer.

abstract.en: The Rav raises a series of questions on the parsha: why the ksones passim stirred such jealousy, why the Midrash credits Rachel's silence rather than her giving the signs to Leah, how Yaakov failed to know that 'your mother' meant Bilhah, why Potiphar's wife did not give Yosef her daughter, how the Midrash can both praise and fault Yosef's bitachon, and why Yaakov's rebuke is a sign for shouting at prophets. He builds the answers on 'maaseh avos siman labanim': Yosef is the all-inclusive soul and tzaddik, earned through guarding the bris, so his prison and release mirror galus and geulah. The Asnas Midrash and the hidden law that one who raises an orphan is like a parent answer the Bilhah and Potiphar questions. A parable of tzimmes that improves as it cooks explains Yosef's refusal of the cupbearer's favor and Yaakov's outcry. He closes with Chanukah's light below ten tefachim.

en: The Rav explains that the ksones passim showed Yosef to be the tzaddik and mashpia for whom the sea would split, and this is what alarmed the brothers.
Following 'maaseh avos siman labanim', Yosef is the all-inclusive soul of his generation, so his descent to prison and rise to kingship are a sign of Klal Yisrael's galus and geulah.
Yosef earned the level of tzaddik and provider through guarding the bris, and Rachel's silence under the chupah was the same guarding in the form of guarding speech.
The law that one who raises an orphan is considered its parent was hidden from Yaakov and from Potiphar's wife so that Yosef would have his test, and after it was revealed through Yosef.
The longer the galus 'cooks', the greater the geulah; therefore Yosef chose two more years in prison over being freed through the cupbearer's favor.
Yaakov's outcry at Yosef's dream was not criticism but a cry from the heart over a galus so long that the Shechinah descends to the very ground.
Chanukah lights are placed below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah otherwise does not descend, because on Chanukah it comes down to lift Knesses Yisrael.

title.en: Chanukah as the final sealing

summary.en: The Rav opens with a Chazal about the Greeks' decrees against Jewish purity, which Hashem overcame through a miracle, and brings from the seforim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples that Chanukah is the final sealing after Yom Kippur. He says he will return to this later.

title.en: The ksones passim and Rachel's silence

summary.en: The Rav calls the parsha difficult and asks why Yaakov's gift of the ksones passim stirred such jealousy, noting that 'passim' hints at the splitting of the sea for Yosef. He then brings the Midrash that Yosef's sheaf stood up in the merit of his mother Rachel's silence when Lavan switched her, and asks why the Midrash does not name the greater merit of giving the signs to Leah, for which Hashem promised the return of her children.

title.en: 'Shall I and your mother come?'

summary.en: The Rav explains that the brothers took Yosef for a false prophet, and that Yaakov rebuked him because a prophetic dream cannot contain something impossible, Rachel being no longer alive. He asks how Yaakov, who knew the whole Torah, did not know, as Rashi says, that 'your mother' meant Bilhah who raised Yosef. He then asks, on Rashi's comparison of Potiphar's wife to Tamar, why she did not simply give Yosef her daughter, through whom the destined line would come.

title.en: Yosef's bitachon and 'ki im zechartani'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that applies 'ashrei hagever asher sam Hashem mivtacho' to Yosef and then faults him for asking the cupbearer to remember him, for which he stayed two more years in prison, and calls the Midrash self-contradictory, since the Chovos Halevavos holds that effort is no lack of bitachon. He also asks what the unusual words 'ki im' in Yosef's request come to exclude.

title.en: Yaakov's rebuke as a sign for the prophets

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov's rebuke of Yosef was a sign that Jews would one day shout at their prophets, and asks why the Midrash chose this mild rebuke when far worse was done to prophets. Turning to next week's parsha, read on Chanukah, he brings the Midrash 'ketz sam lachoshech': there is a set end to darkness, and a set time for Yosef to leave prison.

title.en: The all-inclusive soul and Yosef the provider

summary.en: The Rav lays down the principle of 'maaseh avos siman labanim': the Avos' souls included all of Klal Yisrael, and in every generation there is an all-inclusive soul, the tzaddik of the generation. He explains that Yosef earned this through guarding the bris in his great test, and so became the channel of blessing and the provider for the world, the middah of yesod. He brings the Sfas Emes that Yosef rose to the level of the Avos because his own sons became tribes.

title.en: Yosef's prison as a sign of the galus

summary.en: The Rav brings Targum Yonasan and Rashi on 'even Yisrael' to show Yosef as both father and son, the all-inclusive soul, so that what happened to him is a sign for Klal Yisrael: his going down to Egypt, his rise from prison to kingship as the end of galus, and the harsher last stretch in prison as the harder end of galus. He speaks of the fixed end that no one knows, and of a hint from the Arizal on 'mikeitz shnasayim yamim' that he says he has already cautioned about.

title.en: Hidden chiddushim and the Midrash of Asnas

summary.en: The Rav brings from seforim that certain chiddushim cannot be revealed before their time, such as 'Moavi v'lo Moavis', which became clear only in the time of Boaz and Ruth. He then tells a Midrash brought by Rabbeinu Bachya: the daughter of Dinah and Shechem was hidden by Yaakov with an amulet, carried to Egypt by the angel Michael, raised by Potiphar's wife, and recognized by Yosef through the amulet she threw to him.

title.en: The hidden law of raising an orphan

summary.en: The Rav answers that Potiphar's wife, like Yaakov, did not know that one who raises an orphan is considered its parent; the law stayed hidden so that Yosef would have his test, and once he passed it, it was revealed from a passuk about Yosef, and he earned the name tzaddik. He connects the bris of the eyes and of speech with the bris milah, and reads Yosef's signs to his brothers in Mikeitz, circumcision and lashon hakodesh, in this light.

title.en: Rachel's silence as guarding the bris

summary.en: Returning to Rachel, the Rav distinguishes two merits: giving the signs to Leah, which earned the return of her children, and her silence under the chupah, so as not to shame her sister, which is guarding speech and thus guarding the bris. In that merit Yosef's sheaf stood and he became the provider and king. He adds that Yosef is the power of Klal Yisrael's geulah, and brings the Maharal that the sea split in the merit of Yosef, who split his own physicality.

title.en: Why the brothers feared the ksones passim

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: by making the ksones passim, Yaakov showed that Yosef was the tzaddik and provider for whom the sea would split. The brothers objected, since in their eyes Yosef spoke lashon hara, a flaw in the bris of speech, though he meant it for their good, and they feared being pushed aside; so they first stripped him of the garment and what it symbolized.

title.en: The villager and the tzimmes

summary.en: The Rav tells of a simple villager in shul on Rosh Hashanah who thought the people were crying from hunger, consoled himself that the tzimmes at home gets better the longer it cooks, and then despaired when they cried again at the shofar. He applies it to the galus: it is a preparation for the geulah, and the longer it 'cooks' the greater the geulah; Mitzrayim, Bavel and the present long galus show this, and though it is hard to wait, it is worth it.

title.en: The fallen queen and the cupbearer's dream

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar on 'nafla lo tosif kum' that there is a time when Moshiach must come, and the Chesed L'Avraham that the Shechinah falls further with the galus until a lowest point. He tells the Zohar's parable of a queen who, cast down a third time, refuses to rise until the king himself lifts her. He then explains that the cupbearer's dream, with its four mentions of 'kos', was a dream of geulah, and the baker's a dream of galus.

title.en: A geulah owed to no one

summary.en: The Rav explains that at the destined end the geulah will come from Hashem alone, not from the nations' favor or votes about Eretz Yisrael. Yosef, knowing his release foreshadowed Klal Yisrael's, could have left after ten years through the cupbearer, but preferred two more years in prison over owing him; he brings the Chasam Sofer in this spirit. So he reads 'ki im zechartani' and 'va'asisa na imadi chesed' as Yosef asking not to be remembered, unless the cupbearer would need him, as the Midrash shows happened.

title.en: Yaakov's cry over the long galus

summary.en: The Rav resolves the Midrash on Yosef's bitachon: he waited for a better geulah. He explains the Midrash on prophets through Yirmiyahu's letter to the exiles that the galus would last seventy years and they should build houses, for which Shemayah the Nechelami complained. Yaakov's shout at the dream of sun, moon and stars bowing to the ground, the Shechinah descending to the earth, was not criticism but Klal Yisrael's cry over so long a galus.

title.en: Chanukah: the Shechinah below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah light below ten tefachim shows the Shechinah descending lower than at any other time, revealing the light of Moshiach ben Yosef. In the longest nights of Teves, when the galus is long, the Shechinah comes down to lift Knesses Yisrael, and each Jew's lighting kindles the point of hope in his heart. He closes that Yosef's parsha is read on Chanukah as the dawn of the geulah, Chanukah is the final sealing, and blesses that Hashem Himself bring the geulah.

catalogTitle: החילוק בין כיבוד אב של יעקב וכיבוד אב של עשו

oneLiner.en: The Rav contrasts Esav's outward, formal kibud av with Yaakov's loving kibud av, explaining that true honoring of a father means honoring one's root, which ties it to Eretz Yisroel, to the month of Av, to Yosef and to Chanukah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Vayeshev Yaakov: Yaakov had feared Esav's merits of kibud av and of living in Eretz Yisroel, and Hashem comforted him with Yosef, who grew great precisely far from his father and outside the land. He then brings Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's praise of Esav's kibud av, Dama ben Nesina and Avimi, and explains that each mitzvah is a button that lights a world above: kibud av awakens the attribute of Av, the merciful Father, which is why Avimi understood the churban as mercy. Esav's kibud av gives him a hold on the month of Av, yet it is external: formal speech, fine garments, and hatred in the heart. The Maharal and the Philistines of Ashkelon show the emptiness of gentile kibud av. True kibud av, like yishuv Eretz Yisroel, means honoring one's root. Yosef in Egypt, helped by his father's image, leads to Chanukah, a light in the deepest darkness.

en: Yaakov feared Esav because of Esav's merits of kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel, and Hashem answered him with Yosef, who became great away from his father and outside the land.
Every mitzvah is like a button on a switchboard that lights up a world above; kibud av lights up the attribute of Av, the merciful Father, and brings down mercy.
Esav's kibud av is real enough to give him a hold on the month of Av, but it is only external: formality, fine garments and hatred in his heart.
Yaakov's kibud av is loving and direct, the way a child speaks to a father he loves, not the formal third-person speech of Esav.
Kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel are one mitzvah: honoring the root one comes from, which is why they share one reward.
Chanukah, in the darkest time of the year, is like Yosef in Egypt: a light that reaches into the deepest exile.

Chanukah in the darkness of exile

title.en: Yaakov's fear of Esav's two merits

summary.en: The Rav opens with Vayeshev Yaakov and the Midrash that Yaakov feared Esav's merits of kibud av and of living in Eretz Yisroel. He brings the parable of the straw and the wheat and Rashi's parable of the flax, and says Hashem comforted Yaakov with Yosef.

title.en: Yosef grew great away from his father

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yosef became the tzaddik precisely when torn from his father and outside Eretz Yisroel. The juxtaposition of Yehuda and Tamar with Yosef shows that one can be with the father in the land and stumble, or far away and reach perfection.

title.en: Esav's kibud av and Dama ben Nesina

summary.en: The Rav brings Yaakov's words to Esav, that he kept the taryag mitzvos with Lavan except kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel, and a puzzling Midrash on them. He brings Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement that he never reached Esav's kibud av, asks why, and tells the Gemara's story of Dama ben Nesina, asking why kibud av must be learned from a gentile.

title.en: Avimi and the song of Asaf

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara's story of Avimi, who stood bent over his sleeping father with water in hand, and then understood why Asaf sang a 'mizmor' over the churban: Hashem poured His wrath on wood and stones and spared the Jews. He explains that Hashem treats us as a merciful father, which is why the month of the churban is called Av.

title.en: Mitzvos as buttons on a switchboard

summary.en: The Rav compares a person to a switchboard full of buttons: each mitzvah lights up a particular world above, like the shofar arousing the world of teshuvah. Kibud av lights up the attribute of Av and brings down mercy; Avimi, who kept kibud av like no one else, therefore merited to see the churban as an act of mercy.

title.en: Hidden chesed and Esav's hold on Av

summary.en: The Rav says each person has a mission, and Avimi's name hints that the days of Av are hidden chesed. A gentile's good deeds are a switchboard not plugged in, yet the Gemara says taking tzedakah from gentiles delays the redemption. After a story of a child who answered that the same Satan sends the gentiles to school and keeps him in bed, the Rav explains that the same force pushes Esav to kibud av, giving him a hold on the month of Av, the month of the churbanos.

title.en: Esav's honor is only on the outside

summary.en: The Rav explains Esav's kibud av as the pig showing its split hooves: Esav married at forty like his father, a show of honor. Outwardly he honored Yitzchak more than Yaakov did, but in his heart he waited for his father's death. With the Chasam Sofer he contrasts Esav's formal third-person speech with Yaakov's loving 'kum na'.

title.en: True kibud av is love

summary.en: The Rav explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's words: Esav's honor lay in the garments, while a son who truly honors is at home with his father. He recalls how as a child learning Kiddushin he felt something was wrong with Dama ben Nesina's choice, since any father would want his son to earn the fortune, and explains that 'av' means love, so honor without love is a false kibud av.

title.en: The Maharal: intellect, body and soul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal, who reads Dama ben Nesina's name as the obligation that understanding gives, and explains that a gentile, whose whole world is this world, owes his father more gratitude than a Jew whose essence is the soul. He then brings a pshat that a Jew's kibud av is like parah adumah, beyond reason, and explains that every mitzvah is honoring the Father in Heaven.

title.en: Ashkelon, the Philistines and Amalek

summary.en: The Rav notes that both of Chazal's stories of gentile kibud av come from Ashkelon, a Philistine city, and explains that the Philistines descend from mamzerus and so have no root, which shows the emptiness of their kibud av. Yaakov therefore did not truly fear Esav's kibud av but Amalek, born of Elifaz and Timna.

title.en: Honoring fatherhood; Elifaz's kibud av

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, who reads 'honor your father' as honoring fatherhood itself, and explains that Esav and Elifaz defiled it. He tells of Elifaz, sent by Esav to kill Yaakov, asking what to do with his father's command, and contrasts this with a Jew who knows that kibud av cannot override a mitzvah. Such empty honor, he says, was still enough to destroy the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Honoring the root; Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav says Yaakov fulfilled kibud av even far away, through the way he lived, and resolves the puzzling Midrash: as Dama ben Nesina's claim was answered by the Jews' parah adumah, so Yaakov's. Kibud av means honoring one's root, the Father in Heaven, and Eretz Yisroel is the root of the Jewish people, from whose soil Adam was formed.

title.en: One mitzvah, one reward; back to Yosef

summary.en: The Rav explains that Esav honored a false root, which is why Eretz Yisroel was given in exile only to the Yishmaelim, who have no connection to fatherhood. Kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel are one mitzvah with one reward. He returns to Vayeshev: Yaakov's fear was answered by Yosef, the inner essence of Yaakov, who reached his height away from his father and the land yet remained bound to both.

title.en: Yosef's trials and his father's image

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yosef, who acknowledged his land, was buried there, unlike Moshe. He describes Yosef's daily trials in Egypt, how he struggled with all his strength, and how only when he could no more did heavenly help come through his father's image. The Rav says a person must toil himself, and then he is helped from above.

title.en: Chanukah: Yosef in the darkness

summary.en: The Rav connects Yosef in Egypt to the Jews in the darkest part of exile and to Chanukah, which falls in the longest nights. He notes that Vayishlach ends with the kings of Edom and that Vayeshev is read in the darkest week, and explains that the Chanukah light, placed below ten tefachim, is the Father bending down to the child.

title.en: From Chanukah light to Shabbos light

summary.en: The Rav explains Chanukah as a weekday festival of the deep exile, where the Shechinah comes down into our weekday state, and says the aim is for the Chanukah light to become the Shabbos light. Each Jew must kindle himself, all his limbs with love and fear of Hashem. He closes with Tamar's 'haker na' and Yehuda's staff, calling Chanukah the final sealing after Yom Kippur, and wishes a bright Chanukah.

catalogTitle: פרשה זו קשה להבין אבל בו נטמן אורו של מלך המשיח

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Parshas Vayeshev, a parsha full of troubling questions on the Shevatim and on Hashem's ways, is exactly where the hidden light of Moshiach is concealed, as in the Chanukah lights that shine in the darkest time of the year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling Vayeshev a hard parsha that hides the light of Moshiach, always read before Chanukah, when the final sealing of judgment ends. Having finished the Avos, the Torah turns to their children, and the plain reading raises hard questions: Yosef's talebearing, the brothers' hatred and sale, Yehuda and Tamar, and Yosef imprisoned after withstanding his test. A Jew with emunah knows the Shevatim were awesome tzaddikim; questions on tzaddikim lead to questions on Hashem, so the parsha is a drill in emunah. Bringing the Maharal, he explains that Torah mirrors the state of Klal Yisrael: this is the parsha of galus and hester panim, falling in Teves, and therefore the greatest light is hidden in it. Yosef reached his perfection in Mitzrayim, on Nittel, the darkest day. The Rav then shows that Zos Chanukah completes the Days of Awe, alluded to in the 122nd passuk from Nitzavim, and closes with preparing for Chanukah.

en: Vayeshev, always read before Chanukah, is a hard parsha to explain, yet in it the hidden light of Moshiach is concealed.
Read plainly without emunah, the parsha raises questions on the holy Shevatim, and questions on tzaddikim lead to questions on Hashem Himself; the parsha is a test of emunah.
Following the Maharal, what happens to Klal Yisrael is reflected in the Torah, so Vayeshev, where galus begins and in the month of Teves, is a parsha of hester panim.
Where the impurity is greatest the holiness is strongest, so the greatest light, the light of Moshiach from Yehuda and Yosef, is hidden in this parsha, like the Chanukah lights lit outside and low.
Yosef reached his perfection not at his father's table but in Mitzrayim, on Nittel, the darkest day, by fighting his test with all his strength.
Zos Chanukah is the end of the gmar chasimah, alluded to in the 122nd passuk counted from Nitzavim, which speaks of seeing the land from afar.

title.en: A hard parsha that hides Moshiach's light

summary.en: The Rav calls Vayeshev a hard parsha that hides the light of Moshiach and prepares for Chanukah, when the gmar chasimah ends. He brings a teaching that 'about three months' after Rosh Hashanah Tamar, Knesses Yisrael, is judged and shows her signs, and describes Teves as the darkest month, whose head Chanukah crushes.

title.en: From the Avos to the troubling story of their children

summary.en: After the Avos, the Torah begins the toldos of Yaakov, and one expects to learn how worthy the children were. Instead the plain reading shows Yosef at seventeen fixing his hair and speaking lashon hara, the brothers' hatred and plot, and the story of Yehuda, which would shock a simple reader.

title.en: How great the Shevatim truly were

summary.en: The Rav tells, as heard from the Ruzhiner, how the Maggid of Mezritch trembled after touching the Ba'al Shem Tov's kittel, to show how much greater the holiness of the Shevatim was. He brings the Torah's refusal to break the passuk after Reuven's deed and the Ramban on Yaakov's strength coming from yiras shamayim, and admits that no smooth explanation of the Shevatim's deeds is found.

title.en: Yosef's test and the question on Hashem

summary.en: Questions on tzaddikim lead to questions on Hashem, and the parsha turns there: Yosef, who constantly whispered his trust in Hashem, withstood the daily test of Potiphar's wife for a year, and was then thrown into prison. The Rav concludes that the whole parsha is a drill in emunah.

title.en: Torah mirrors Klal Yisrael: a parsha of galus

summary.en: Bringing the Maharal on the Gemara that halachos would be scattered, the Rav explains that the Torah, the soul of Klal Yisrael, goes into galus with them, and today's collections of seforim mirror the beginning of the ingathering. Vayeshev falls in Teves, the time of the sitra achra, and begins galus Mitzrayim, so it is a parsha of hester panim, when tzaddikim are not seen.

title.en: The hidden light of Moshiach and Chanukah

summary.en: Where impurity is greatest, holiness is strongest, so the ohr haganuz is hidden in Vayeshev like a diamond in a garbage can. The Rav brings the Midrash that while the Shevatim, Reuven, Yaakov and Yehuda were each occupied, Hashem was creating the light of Moshiach, and ties it to the Chanukah lights lit outside, below ten tefachim, as a weekday yom tov of galus.

title.en: Yosef's perfection on the darkest day

summary.en: Yosef is the mashpia of Klal Yisrael: seventeen years his father supported him and seventeen years he supported his father. The Rav explains that Mitzrayim is the lowest place and that the calendar also has a lowest day, Nittel, and following Rashi on 'vayehi kehayom hazeh' he says Yosef won his test and became Yosef hatzaddik on exactly that day.

title.en: Every Jew's part in Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew in hard trials should consider that perhaps now he can bring Moshiach, as Yosef became Moshiach ben Yosef only through his trials. In this sedra one must believe the ohr haganuz is hidden in the parsha and in oneself; one spark of the soul can overcome all darkness, and Chanukah's eight days shine into the darkness of the nations' season.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: renewal above time

summary.en: Zos Chanukah is the end of the gmar chasimah, a tradition from the Ba'al Shem Tov's students with no source in the written Torah. The Rav explains Chanukah as renewal, like the chanukas hamizbe'ach and Yehuda's marriage after the sale, and shows that unlike Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh its date is fixed by 'eight', above time, so it can still complete Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: From Elul to Zos Chanukah: 122 pesukim

summary.en: The Rav describes the stages of judgment: forty days to Yom Kippur, then Sukkos and Ha'azinu for those who build on emunah, and Zos Chanukah for those with only a little emunah. Counting the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Ha'azinu against the days to Zos Chanukah, he finds that day's passuk speaks of seeing the land from afar, like the Chanukah lights that may only be looked at.

title.en: Asking Hashem for Chanukah gelt

summary.en: Zos Chanukah is a time of teshuvah and of praying for Moshiach. Chanukah is from the word chen, a free gift, so as children ask for Chanukah gelt a Jew should ask Hashem for Torah, yiras shamayim and emunah, and learn Torah as G-dliness, not as wisdom. Standing between the mezuzah and the Chanukah lights leaves its mark for the whole year.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh for Torah, not fighting in galus

summary.en: The Chashmonaim fought with mesiras nefesh, and a Jew should likewise give himself for Torah, but the Rav brings the Chofetz Chaim and Rabbeinu Bachya that in galus one does not fight the nations unless they interfere with avodas Hashem, and questions a recent demonstration. No land of galus is safe, and he notes the hidden miracles of every day, citing Targum Yonasan on Esav's return to Seir.

title.en: The mezuzah story and preparing for Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav tells a story he heard in Yerushalayim of a man who reads people's situation from their mezuzos, to show that the mezuzah at the door shapes the whole year, and Chanukah is a partner in this. He closes by urging real preparation for Chanukah through its halachos, chassidus and mussar seforim and teshuvah, to uncover the hidden light in one's heart, with a brachah for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: A Deeper Understanding of יעקב's Present to עשו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the 580 animals Yaakov sent Esav are Jewish souls handed to Esav's rule, and that this gift, like Dina who was taken by Shechem, must return to Yaakov's flock.

abstract.en: He opens with the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person's belongings hold sparks of his soul, which is why Yaakov risked his life for small jars. Counting the gift to Esav with the Ohr HaChaim, he finds 580, the value of Seir and of the names of the two chiefs of evil, so the gift resembles the Yom Kippur goat: a bone thrown to Esav. The animals were Jewish souls who volunteered, surpassing Eliyahu's ox. Through the Midrash of Rabbi Hoshaya and the unlearned man who explained 'they will return a gift', he shows that these are the Jews ruled by the yetzer hara, that this man's letter in the Torah lay in these verses, and that his wish to be quoted was his soul seeking redemption. He closes with Dina, owed to Esav in place of Leah, who returned via Osnas, Shechem and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon.

en: According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, every belonging of a person holds sparks of his soul, and he must use it to elevate them; this is why Yaakov went back for small jars.
The gift of 580 animals equals Seir and the combined names of the chief of evil and his mate, so it was an appeasement thrown to Esav like the Yom Kippur goat.
The animals sent to Esav stand for the unlearned and the wicked among Jews, whose judge is the yetzer hara.
When Moshiach comes, Esav must return Yaakov's gift, meaning that every Jew who strayed will return to Yaakov's flock.
Every Jew has a letter in the Sefer Torah from which he draws his life, and so every Jew says a chiddush in Torah at least once.
Yaakov was faulted for hiding Dina because, having married Leah who was destined for Esav, he owed Esav a wife; Dina was taken by Shechem and later returned through her descendants.

title.en: Sparks of the soul in one's belongings

summary.en: The Rav recalls that Yaakov's animals are Jewish souls and that Yaakov endangered himself on a dangerous night for small jars. He explains with the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person's belongings hold sparks of his soul, and that every creature is guided by individual providence.

title.en: The birds, the donkey and the small jars

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who saw that no bird is caught without a heavenly decree, and the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair that would not eat untithed oats because it held sparks of its master's soul. From here he explains why Yaakov crossed back for the jars.

title.en: 580 animals: a bone thrown to Esav

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim, who counts the gift as 580, the value of Seir, and shows that the names of the chief of evil and his mate also total 580. The gift is like the Yom Kippur goat, as the Zohar connects it, and he asks why Yaakov would give away animals that were Jewish souls.

title.en: Eliyahu's ox and Yaakov's volunteers

summary.en: The Rav tells how the ox chosen for the Baal at Eliyahu's contest refused to move until Eliyahu told it that it too would sanctify Hashem's name. Yaakov's animals stood higher: they volunteered to go to Esav, exactly 580 of them.

title.en: Rabbi Hoshaya and the unlearned man's chiddush

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash of an unlearned man who asked Rabbi Hoshaya to repeat his chiddush in his name: the verse in Tehillim says the kings 'will return' a gift to Moshiach because Esav must give back Yaakov's gift. Rabbi Hoshaya agreed, and the chiddush entered the Midrash.

title.en: Every Jew's letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew has his own letter in the Sefer Torah, his channel of blessing, and brings the teaching that one who sees his letter at hagbah is lit up by it. He then notes that the animals sent to Esav are now managed by Esav.

title.en: Who judges the tzaddik, the beinoni and the rasha

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the angel of Esav is the Satan, the yetzer hara and the angel of death, and describes his three roles. With the Gemara on three judges in the heart, he explains that the yetzer hara is the judge of the wicked, and these are the animals that went to Esav.

title.en: Why Esav had to receive something

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov pacified Esav, who complained about the brachos, because Hashem runs the world with a balanced scale and Esav's complaint would otherwise have prevailed. He digresses about the house of David coming through Rus in a hidden way, then returns: this is why some Jews are under Esav's dictates.

title.en: The unlearned man's letter among Esav's animals

summary.en: The Rav explains that without Torah, the only antidote to the yetzer hara, the unlearned man must often have fallen, so his letter is likely among the animals sent to Esav. Since every letter is alive and gives light, every Jew says a chiddush at least once, even without realizing its depth.

title.en: The returned gift is returning souls

summary.en: The Rav asks what 580 animals could mean to Moshiach, king of the whole world, and answers that they are Jewish souls, each a world, so their return means that all who strayed will return. He then asks why the unlearned man wanted his chiddush repeated, rejecting that it was for honor.

title.en: The soul's request for redemption

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Ba'al Shem Tov and his disciples heard the soul's plea behind a person's physical request. The unlearned man's wish was his soul's: since repeating Torah in the speaker's name brings redemption, he sought redemption from Esav's rule, and his declaration that he will return speeds his return.

title.en: Why Yaakov was faulted for hiding Dina

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yaakov hid Dina in a box from Esav and was punished, since she might have brought Esav back to his roots; Dina was then taken by Shechem. He asks why Yaakov is faulted, when no tzaddik ever sought a rasha for his daughter.

title.en: Leah's tears and the debt to Esav

summary.en: The Rav explains that Leah was destined for Esav and escaped through her weeping and tefillah, so Yaakov took what was Esav's and owed it back. Dina, the extension of Leah, should have been the 581st gift; withheld, she went to Esav anyway through Shechem.

title.en: Osnas, Shechem and the gift's return

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Dina's daughter Osnas was saved by Yaakov, brought to Mitzrayim and married Yosef, who was given Shechem and buried there. With the Ohr HaChaim he shows that Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon descended from this episode, and closes that the whole gift, every Jewish soul, will return, as the present drizzle of teshuvah shows.

catalogTitle: ביאור עמוק ונפלא בשנאת אחים ונסיון של יוסף (שייכות לחנוכה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yosef was the tzaddik of his generation, crowned through shmiras habris, and that the halacha which would have spared him his trial was hidden until after it, tying this to Osnas and to the light of Chanukah against the darkness of Yavan.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the kesones passim and Yosef's words 'my sheaf rose', which the Midrash reads as his mother's silence. Why credit Rachel's silence and not her greater, active deed of giving Leah the signs? He then asks why Yaakov did not know that the moon in the dream meant Bilhah, though the Gemara teaches that one who raises an orphan is like a parent, and why Potiphar's wife, acting for Heaven's sake, did not simply offer her daughter. After laying foundations on the tzaddik hador, Yosef's trials, and halachos revealed only in their time, he brings the Midrash that Osnas was Dinah's daughter, adopted by Potiphar. The halacha was hidden so that Yosef would face his test. He explains the three brisos, Rachel's silence as shmiras habris, the kesones passim, and finally Chanukah: Yavan broke down the separations, and Yosef, like the Chanukah light, brings light into darkness.

en: Yosef was the tzaddik hador, the channel of all blessing in his generation, and he reached that level through shmiras habris and the trials of Egypt.
Some halachos are revealed only when their time comes; the rule that raising an orphan makes one a parent was hidden from Yaakov and from Potiphar's wife so that Yosef would face his trial.
According to the Midrash, Osnas was the daughter of Dinah, sent to Egypt and adopted by Potiphar, and Yosef recognized her by the amulet Yaakov had hung on her.
Yosef's kingship came from his mother's silence, her guarding of the bris of the mouth, not from her active deed, and the kesones passim hinted at his shmiras habris.
Yavan fought against chodesh, Shabbos and milah because each is a havdalah, and Chanukah, lit in the darkest time of year, answers it measure for measure by bringing light into darkness.
Every person holds a hidden light within, and at Chanukah one must find it and kindle oneself together with the Chanukah lights.

title.en: The kesones passim and Rachel's silence

summary.en: The Rav opens with the kesones passim, which the Midrash ties to the splitting of the sea, and with Yosef's words 'my sheaf rose', read as his mother's silence. He brings the Midrash of Rachel's plea and asks why Yosef credited her silence rather than her greater, active deed of giving the signs to Leah.

title.en: Why Yaakov did not know the moon meant Bilhah

summary.en: On Yosef's dream of the sun and moon, Rashi explains that Yaakov did not know the moon meant Bilhah, who raised Yosef. The Rav asks how Yaakov could not know the simple Gemara that one who raises an orphan is as if he bore him, learned from 'the sons of Yaakov and Yosef'.

title.en: Potiphar's wife meant it for Heaven's sake

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Potiphar's wife, like Tamar, acted for Heaven's sake, having seen in her astrology that she would have children from Yosef, and links it to Moshiach ben Yosef and ben David. Yosef refused to sin even to bring Moshiach. The Rav then asks why she did not simply offer her daughter.

title.en: Yosef the tzaddik hador and his trials

summary.en: As a first foundation, the Rav explains that every generation has a tzaddik hador through whom all blessing flows, and in the time of the shevatim this was Yosef, perfected in shmiras habris. To earn it he was sent to Egypt, the most corrupt place, and tested daily by Potiphar's wife; so he rose to the midah of yesod and the level of the Avos. He adds that, as Yosef's exile ended in kingship, the hardest time of the Jewish exile comes right before the dawn.

title.en: Halachos revealed only in their time

summary.en: As a second foundation, the Rav explains that some halachos are revealed only at a set time, like 'a Moabite man and not a Moabite woman', unknown when Machlon and Kilyon married. Since the Satan fears Moshiach, Hashem hides the line of David in unlikely places, like Lot's daughters, so the Satan suspects nothing.

title.en: The Midrash of Osnas, daughter of Dinah

summary.en: The Rav relates the Midrash brought by Rabbeinu Bachya: Dinah's daughter from Shechem was sent away by Yaakov with an amulet, brought by the angel Michael to Egypt and adopted by the childless Potiphar. When the girls threw jewels at Yosef from the wall, Osnas threw her amulet, and Yosef, recognizing his family, asked to marry her.

title.en: Why the halacha was hidden until after the trial

summary.en: With these foundations the Rav answers: Potiphar's wife did not know that an adopted daughter counts as her own, just as Yaakov did not know it. The halacha was hidden so that Yosef would face his great trial and be raised to the level of the Avos; it was revealed retroactively once the dream came true. He compares it to the Gemara on recording the size of a kezayis, and finds the halacha's root in Yosef's dream.

title.en: The three brisos and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that becoming a tzaddik and mashpia requires guarding three brisos: of the eyes, the tongue and the flesh. Yosef guarded all three and so merited Shabbos, as Chazal learn from 'and prepare'. He reads 'your eyes see that it is my mouth speaking' as Yosef showing his brothers his shmiras habris, and adds that a clean mouth is a sign of shmiras habris.

title.en: Rachel's silence and the meaning of the kesones passim

summary.en: Returning to the opening, the Rav explains that Yosef's kingship came not from Rachel's active deed but from her silence, her shmiras habris of the mouth. The kesones passim was a garment hinting at shmiras habris, with the power to split the sea; the brothers asked how one who spoke lashon hara could be the guardian of the bris. He shows how the letters of Yosef's name and of 'passim' hint at this, and why the brothers stripped him of the kesones.

title.en: Chanukah against Yavan's darkness

summary.en: The Rav asks why no one speaks of Osnas's righteousness and why she bears that name, then turns to Chanukah: Yavan broke the walls, and Chanukah, following Beis Hillel, keeps adding light. Yavan is darkness; it breached the soreg separating Jew from gentile and fought chodesh, Shabbos and milah because each is a separation.

title.en: Korach, the havdalos of creation, and day against night

summary.en: The Rav brings Korach, who also fought the separations, and Rashi's answer from 'boker', since creation itself consists of havdalos. Light and darkness parallel Israel and the nations; most mitzvos are done by day. Yavan wanted night to enter the realm of day, so measure for measure Hashem gave Chanukah, lit in the darkest nights of the year.

title.en: Yosef as the light of Chanukah, and Osnas

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yosef, whose name means adding, is the tzaddik of 'or zarua latzaddik', the hidden light that goes down into the darkness of Egypt, like the Shechinah in the thornbush. Osnas, alone in Egypt, saw how Yosef held to kedushah and drew from his example; Yosef preserved her, and the credit is his.

title.en: Kindling the hidden light within

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Chanukah teaches that every person, a small world, holds a hidden light like a pilot light, and one must find it and kindle oneself. He explains the shamash as a high light coming down to illuminate Jewish souls, and closes with a wish to break the walls that separate one from Hashem.

catalogTitle: (רש"י) “אלה ישוביהם וגלגוליהם עד שבאו לכלל ישוב” - כל אריכות הגלות מתגלגל סביב משיח; חנוכה - דרוש לתרץ קושית ב"י

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that all the turns of the exile, which begin with the sale of Yosef, revolve around Moshiach, and that on Chanukah the light of Moshiach was revealed, which is how he answers the Beis Yosef's famous question.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children. Having lived through all the signs of the exiles, Yaakov hoped to taste the World to Come in this world, but this world cannot hold it, and instead the real exile of Egypt began with the sale of Yosef. Rashi's 'eleh yishvoseihem vegilguleihem' teaches that every turn of history is a planned revolution of Hashem's decree; one who judges it from one dark spot is like a fly on a great painting. Chanukah, at the darkest point of the exile, reveals the hidden light of Moshiach, and the dreidel, whose letters equal Moshiach, shows that everything turns around him. The kings of Edom hide the whole of Divine providence. Finally the Rav answers the Beis Yosef: at Chanukah the light of Moshiach came down and time itself slowed, so the oil burned naturally for eight days and the mitzvah was fulfilled.

en: Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Rav explains that all of Yaakov's experiences foreshadowed the later exiles and redemptions.
Yaakov wanted to dwell in tranquility, to experience the World to Come in this world, but this world cannot contain even a trace of it, so the exile of Egypt began instead.
Rashi's 'eleh yishvoseihem vegilguleihem' teaches that all the revolutions of history are planned turns that lead to the final purpose, the coming of Moshiach.
On Chanukah, at the darkest point of the exile, the hidden light, the light of Moshiach, is revealed when a Jew lights the Chanukah candles.
The Rav answers the Beis Yosef's question by explaining that at Chanukah the light of Moshiach came down and time slowed, so that one day lasted eight days and the oil burned naturally.
The Chashmona'im merited the light of Moshiach through mesiras nefesh in their wars, and every Jew is called on at Chanukah to reveal his own hidden light through mesiras nefesh.
