title.en: Yaakov's wish to dwell in tranquility

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are signs for their children and traces how Yaakov's life foreshadowed the exiles. Yaakov hoped to taste the World to Come in this world, but this world cannot hold it, so the exile of Egypt began instead.

title.en: Sitting down among the dogs

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash's parable of a traveler who meets a pack of dogs and sits down among them, and the Chiddushei HaRim's reading that one should not flee troubles but know that Hashem is there. He then asks why the Midrash ties Vayeshev to the verse of the kings of Edom.

title.en: Rashi: their settlings and their turns

summary.en: The Rav reads Rashi's 'eleh yishvoseihem vegilguleihem ad shebau lichlal yishuv' as the start of a long, planned story, and brings the Ramban that the decree is true and cleverness is false. All the turns, from the sale of Yosef through the desert, led to settling in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The fly on the painting and the turning sun

summary.en: The Rav compares a person who asks questions on Hashem's ways to a fly that lands on a black spot of a great painting. Through the verses of Koheles on the generations and the sun that sets and returns, he explains that everything turns with a reckoning toward the purpose of creation, the coming of Moshiach.

title.en: The long 'jest' of Egypt

summary.en: The Rav explains 'asher hisalalti beMitzrayim' as a jest that lasted over two hundred years: all the wealth Egypt gathered through Yosef and Yaakov was in the end taken out by the Jews. So too, when Moshiach comes, the laughter of 'az yimalei sechok pinu' will show that the exile was for the Jews.

title.en: Chanukah light and the dreidel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah falls at the longest night, the height of the exile, and that the hidden light of Moshiach is then revealed through the Chanukah candles, as the Bnei Yissaschar brings. The dreidel's letters equal Moshiach, showing that all the turns of history revolve around him.

title.en: The secret of the kings of Edom

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramchal and the Zohar that the short parsha of the kings of Edom hides the whole of Hashem's guidance of the world, and that the eighth king, Hadar, with no mention of death, alludes to Chanukah and Moshiach. With this he answers the Midrash: seeing this parsha, Yaakov sat down among the 'dogs', knowing Hashem is there.

title.en: Every home a Mikdash; the nusach of the Chanukah piyut

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that lighting Chanukah candles makes every Jewish home a Mikdash: the Greeks broke into the Mikdash, and on Chanukah the Mikdash's lights go out into the weekday and the public domain. He then raises the nusach 'mitzvas shemonas yemei Chanukah' and the unusual wording of the Gemara and the Shulchan Aruch.

title.en: The Beis Yosef's question and Reb Chaim

summary.en: The Rav presents the Beis Yosef's famous question on the eight days and Reb Chaim's point that new oil created by a miracle could not serve for the mitzvah, so the miracle was in the quality of the oil. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that even a birth by a miracle of quality does not fulfill a mitzvah, since a mitzvah needs the natural way.

title.en: Rabbi Chanina's menorah and the Megaleh Amukos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash Tanchuma in which Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim saw the menorah burn for a whole year without oil, and asks why the eight days of Chanukah are celebrated so greatly. He then brings the Megaleh Amukos that in the days of Moshiach time will stretch, so that a day will last as long as a year today.

title.en: The miracle: one long day of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah miracle was that Hashem sent down the light of Moshiach, under which nature slows, so that in the Mikdash the twenty-fifth of Kislev lasted eight days and the oil burned naturally. This explains the custom of saying 'Vihi Noam' and the Gemara's wording 'on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, the days of Chanukah are eight'.

title.en: A mitzvah below, and mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Rabbi Chanina's miracle, where Hashem lit the upper menorah and its light came down without any mitzvah, with Chanukah, where Hashem wanted the Jews to have a real mitzvah and so sent the light of Moshiach. The Chashmona'im merited this through mesiras nefesh in their wars, which the Rambam lists as a sign of Moshiach.

title.en: Revealing each Jew's hidden light

summary.en: The Rav concludes that when a Jew prepares his menorah he should know that his home and his body become a Mikdash, and that at Chanukah each Jew must reveal his hidden light through mesiras nefesh, above all in the war against the yetzer hara. He ends with a tefilah that all merit the light of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Two Approaches of Being מקרב People to Hashem

oneLiner.en: From the Midrash that Yitzchak too brought people close to Hashem, the Rav explains two ways of kiruv, Avraham's open outreach and Yitzchak's hidden influence through his own holiness, and shows that Chanukah is the hidden reaching-out of the Shechinah to souls who cannot rise to Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah of loving the ger, which covers anyone distant who must be brought near. The Midrash says Avraham and Yaakov made converts, and learns from 'megurei aviv' that Yitzchak did too. The Rav reads 'megurei' three ways: making converts, dwelling, and fear. Yitzchak's way was fear and withdrawal, like Shammai, who pushed converts away while Hillel drew them close. Yet by learning and davening in seclusion, Yitzchak drew down kedusha that stirred thoughts of teshuvah in his city, hidden kiruv that the Torah too tells only by hint. Through the candle as a picture of the soul, he contrasts Shabbos, the day of the soul, with Chanukah, lit outside, at the left of the door, below ten tefachim, in the longest nights: there the Shechinah descends to extinguished souls. Yosef going down to Mitzrayim and his dream are read the same way.

en: A ger is anyone who is distant and must be brought near, and there is a mitzvah to love him and make him feel at home; all the more so one whose soul is distant.
Avraham served Hashem with chesed and outreach, Yitzchak with fear and withdrawal, and Hillel and Shammai received their Torah through these same two channels.
Yitzchak brought people to teshuvah without going out to them: the kedusha he drew down in seclusion spread through his city and stirred thoughts of teshuvah in people who never knew its source.
Both ways bring people close to Hashem; the one who learns alone is not selfish, he only works in Yitzchak's way rather than Avraham's.
The candle is the picture of the soul: Shabbos, the day of the soul, lights up souls that are prepared, while Chanukah reaches souls that cannot take the Shabbos light.
Chanukah is lit in the dark, in the public domain, at the left of the door and below ten tefachim, because there the Shechinah comes down to the distant; Chanukah is itself bringing in the distant.

title.en: Who is a ger; the Avos made converts

summary.en: The Rav explains that a ger is anyone distant who must be brought near, and describes the mitzvah to love him and not to hurt him. He then brings the Midrash that Avraham and Yaakov made converts, and that the passuk 'megurei aviv' teaches the same of Yitzchak.

title.en: Three meanings of 'megurei'; Avraham's love, Yitzchak's fear

summary.en: The Rav asks how the Midrash knows 'megurei' means making converts, when it could mean dwelling or fear. He explains Avraham's service of love and outpouring against Yitzchak's fear of Hashem's greatness, Pachad Yitzchak, and shows the two in Pesach and Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Hillel and Shammai with the converts

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara's account of the converts whom Shammai drove away and Hillel drew close. He explains that Hillel's Torah came through Avraham's channel of chesed and Shammai's through Yitzchak's channel of din, like the same water in a white glass and a red one.

title.en: Yitzchak's kiruv from within his room

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak never went out to make converts, yet by learning and davening in seclusion he drew down kedusha that spread through his city, as Rashi says a tzaddik's leaving a place leaves a mark. People there got thoughts of teshuvah without knowing from where, so there are two ways to bring people back.

title.en: Open kiruv and hidden kiruv

summary.en: The Rav puts the three meanings of 'megurei' together: by dwelling there Yitzchak made converts, and he did it that way because his midah was fear. He says neither way is selfish, contrasts Avraham's public preaching with the hidden thought of teshuvah Yitzchak stirred in a man in the market, and explains that the Torah tells the hidden kiruv only by hint.

title.en: The candle as a picture of the soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that physical things are a mashal for spiritual ones, and brings 'Ner Hashem nishmas adam'. A flame rises toward its source like the soul, and is held down by the vessel, the oil and the wick, ner, pesilah and shemen, whose initials spell nefesh; he adds that body and soul feed each other, as the Rema explains in the brachah of Asher Yatzar.

title.en: Shabbos candles, Chanukah, and the darkness of Yavan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos is the day of the soul, ushered in by the candle that beckons the soul to rise, but souls unprepared by their week cannot bear it. For them there is Chanukah; he brings the Midrash that the four words of darkness at creation are the four exiles, Yavan being 'choshech', whose letters spell forgetting.

title.en: Wicks not lit on Shabbos; Yaakov and Esav

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that wicks and oils not lit on Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, which the seforim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim read as souls that cannot take the Shabbos light, extinguished souls on the outside. He then contrasts Yaakov, singular, who belongs to Shabbos and the private domain, with Esav, plural, the public domain, and right with left.

title.en: Chanukah lit in Esav's territory

summary.en: The Rav shows that the Chanukah light is lit in the darkest nights, in the public domain, at the left of the door and below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah otherwise never descends. Like visiting the sick, the Shechinah comes down to souls who cannot rise to Shabbos and lights them, so Chanukah is bringing in the distant.

title.en: Vayeshev, Yosef and the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav ties the parsha to Chanukah: Yitzchak, the left side, makes converts for those on the left, and Yosef, whose name means adding, goes down to Mitzrayim to light the Chanukah light there. He reads Yosef's dream of the sun, moon and stars bowing as the stooping to light below ten tefachim, and says a Jew lighting his candle is like Yitzchak in his hidden room, like a man who presses a switch and lights a whole tower.

title.en: Moshiach in the Chanukah light; a question

summary.en: The Rav closes with wishes for Shabbos Chanukah and says that both Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid appear in this parsha in their descent, Yehuda going down and Yosef brought down. Answering a listener's question about the soul's nullification in its source, he says such things are understood by those who practice Judaism, not by philosophizing.

catalogTitle: יוסף צדיק נסתר' בבחינת אור הגנוז שמאיר בחושך מצרים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the law that raising a child counts as bearing it stayed hidden from Yaakov, Yosef and Potiphar's wife, so that Yosef would pass his trials in Egypt and become the hidden tzaddik, the concealed light (or haganuz) that shines in the darkness of exile like the Chanukah lights.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yosef's dream and the merit of Rachel's silence, then Yaakov's objection that Yosef's mother had died, answered by Rashi: Bilhah raised him, and one who raises an orphan is as if he bore him. He asks why Yaakov, who learned all of Torah, did not know this, and why Potiphar's wife tried to sin rather than wait for her daughter Asenath. He lays three foundations: the tzaddik yesod olam earns his place through trials in guarding the bris; chiddushim in Torah are revealed in their time; and the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer account of Asenath. The law stayed hidden so that Yosef would face his trials and earn kingship. The Rav then ties Yosef, first of the hidden tzaddikim, to the hidden light of Chanukah, and closes with the Lubliner story and Chanukah as a final sealing.

en: Rashi answers Yaakov's question about Yosef's dead mother: Bilhah raised Yosef, and one who raises an orphan in his home is regarded as having given birth to him.
Not every chiddush in Torah is revealed in every generation; some are concealed until their time, as with the law permitting a Moabite woman, revealed only in Boaz's day.

The law that a raised child counts as one's own stayed hidden from Yaakov, Yosef and Potiphar's wife so that Yosef would have to face his trials in Egypt and so become the tzaddik yesod olam and king.
Kingship is earned through guarding the bris, and guarding the mouth is its parallel; this is why Yosef invoked his mother's silence rather than her act of giving the signs.
The Chanukah lights reveal the or haganuz, the hidden light that is the light of Moshiach, which today is found concealed in the Torah.
Yosef was the first of the thirty-six hidden tzaddikim, a hidden light set in Egypt, the most impure place, and a sign for Jews kindling Chanukah lights in exile.
Chanukah is the final sealing of judgment, because at Chanukah even weak people receive strength beyond their own, as 'many in the hands of the few'.

candidateTopics: or haganuz and the Chanukah lights
raising an orphan as giving birth
chiddushei Torah revealed in their time
trials of youth in a corrupt world

title.en: Yosef's sheaf and Rachel's silence

summary.en: The Rav reads Yosef's dream of his sheaf standing up as an allusion to the merit of his mother's silence, and asks why silence is cited when Rachel actively gave Leah the signs. He brings the Midrash that Rachel's plea for the Jewish people was accepted because she was not jealous of her sister.

title.en: Bilhah as Yosef's mother

summary.en: Yaakov asks how Yosef's mother could bow when she had died, and Rashi answers that it means Bilhah, who raised him. The Rav brings the Gemara that raising an orphan counts as bearing him, and asks how Yaakov, who learned all of Torah, did not know this. He then brings Rashi on the juxtaposition of Tamar and Potiphar's wife.

title.en: Two Moshiachs and Potiphar's wife's intent

summary.en: The Rav explains that every parsha holds Moshiach, and that the parshiyos of Yehuda and Yosef correspond to Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef; both Tamar and Potiphar's wife acted for the sake of Heaven. He asks why Potiphar's wife sought to sin instead of waiting for Yosef to marry her daughter.

title.en: First foundation: the tzaddik yesod olam

summary.en: The Rav lays the first of three foundations: in every generation there is a tzaddik yesod olam, sometimes revealed and sometimes hidden, who sustains the world and reaches his level through trials in guarding the bris. Yosef is the tzaddik of this kind, and this merit leads to kingship.

title.en: Second foundation: chiddushim revealed in their time

summary.en: The Rav explains that new insights in Torah bring renewal into creation, and that rulings can change between generations, illustrated by measurements for a future korban. Some chiddushim are concealed until their time, like the law permitting a Moabite woman, revealed in Boaz's day and hidden earlier so that the Satan would not interfere with the line of Moshiach.

title.en: Third foundation: the story of Asenath

summary.en: The Rav brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer: Asenath, Dinah's daughter from Shechem, was sent away by Yaakov with an amulet, carried to Egypt and adopted by Potiphar's childless wife; she threw the amulet to Yosef, who recognized his father's writing and married her. Rabbeinu Bachya explains that she is called Potiphera's daughter because she was raised there.

title.en: Why the law stayed hidden: Yosef's trials

summary.en: The Rav answers the questions: Potiphar's wife did not know that a raised daughter counts as her own, and Yaakov did not know it either, because the chiddush had to stay hidden. Yosef had to become king through trials in guarding the bris, alone and young in Egypt; had Yaakov known, he would have taught Yosef, who could have simply offered to marry her daughter. The law was revealed only when Yosef became king.

title.en: The bris of the tongue and Yosef's kingship

summary.en: The Rav brings Sefer Yetzirah and the Toldos Yaakov Yosef that the bris of the tongue parallels the bris of the flesh, and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'ein yisron l'baal halashon'. The brothers argued that one who speaks lashon hara cannot be king; Yosef answered with the merit of his mother's silence, which earns kingship. The Rav stresses that Yosef did not speak lashon hara and that the dispute is beyond us.

title.en: Asenath's name and the hidden light of Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Asenath was hidden in a thornbush and named after it, and turns to Chanukah: Vayeshev and Mikeitz are the Chanukah parshiyos, and the Chanukah lights reveal the or haganuz, the light of Moshiach that will show the world in a new light. That light is hidden in the Torah, and one who toils in Torah sees it according to his level.

title.en: Inferior oils: souls Shabbos cannot kindle

summary.en: The Rav brings the tzaddikim's reading of the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah: 'pesoles' hints at souls, since a soul is a candle. There are souls that even Shabbos cannot kindle, but the Chanukah light can.

title.en: Chanukah light in the public domain

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos means staying in the reshus hayachid, the domain of the One, while reshus harabim is the domain of the other side. The Chanukah light is placed facing the public domain, on the left, below ten handbreadths, on weekdays and in the longest nights, like an oasis in the desert.

title.en: Thirty-six lights, thirty-six hidden tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the thirty-six Chanukah lights correspond to the thirty-six hours Adam enjoyed the hidden light, and links them to the thirty-six hidden tzaddikim. The first of them is Yosef, a tzaddik nistar whom his brothers did not recognize, who kept the Torah in secret in Egypt and is a sign for Jews in exile.

title.en: The One who dwells in the thornbush

summary.en: The Rav brings the blessing to Yosef of 'the One who dwells in the thornbush' and the reason Hashem appeared in a thornbush: He is with the Jewish people in their distress. Yosef stayed holy in Egypt, the most impure land, and Asenath, carried there as a baby with only an amulet, also kept herself noble there, so she bears the name of the thornbush.

title.en: Asenath learned from Yosef; Yosef in today's Egypt

summary.en: The Rav suggests Asenath kept her holiness by watching Yosef in the same house. He then says today's bochurim are in an Egypt worse than before, recalling how much more modest the street once was, and brings the Ohr HaChaim that before Moshiach one can fall into the fiftieth gate of impurity but the Torah protects. He calls on them to be like Yosef and refuse the yetzer hara.

title.en: Chanukah as final sealing; the Lubliner's story

summary.en: The Rav notes that the idea of Chanukah as the final sealing of judgment was revealed only by the disciples of the Ba'al Shem Tov, a further chance for weaker generations. He tells how the Lubliner Rebbe saw an informer shining in all worlds as he lit Chanukah candles, explains that every Jew is good inside, and urges holding on to that light after Chanukah, when Hashem gives strength beyond one's own.

catalogTitle: יוסף משיג סדר טהרות ע"י שורש נשמתו - קדושת יסוד

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that while Yaakov passed on to Yosef the Torah he received from Shem and Ever, Seder Taharos was Yosef's own portion of Torah, which he attained himself through the root of his soul, the holiness of yesod.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk that Yaakov loved Yosef because he was a ben zekunim, which Onkelos renders as a wise son, and with the teaching that Yaakov gave Yosef what he had received from Shem and Ever. He asks why Yaakov needed to receive anything, when Avraham attained the whole Torah on his own. He answers that some parts of Torah belong to particular souls and are given to one person in a generation, illustrating this with the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Or HaChaim, and with Eli and Shmuel. Each of the seven shepherds has his own inyan, and Yosef alone is called tzaddik. Following the Arizal, the six orders of Mishnah match the six days, and Taharos, the sixth, is Yosef's: this he did not need from Yaakov. The Rav ties Yosef to the Chanukah flame, tells a story of the Chozeh of Lublin, and closes by calling to strengthen a kollel that learns Torah with yiras Shamayim.

en: Yaakov passed on to Yosef the Torah he had received from Shem and Ever, which is why Yosef was called ben zekunim.
Some parts of Torah are particular to certain souls and are handed over to only one person in a generation, so even a great soul must receive them from his predecessor.
Each of the seven shepherds has his own inyan, and Yosef is the one called tzaddik, a quality he gained through his trials and not from Yaakov.
Seder Taharos, the sixth order, corresponding to the sixth day, was Yosef's own portion of Torah, which he attained himself.
Chanukah is bound up with Yosef: the parshiyos read around Chanukah speak of him, and the Chanukah flame is the level of Yosef the tzaddik.
A kollel that learns Torah with yiras Shamayim has lasting existence, and the Rav calls on those present to support such a kollel.

the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Or HaChaim

title.en: Why did Yaakov need Shem and Ever?

summary.en: The Rav opens with Yosef as ben zekunim, rendered by Onkelos as a wise son, and the teaching that Yaakov gave Yosef what he received from Shem and Ever. He asks why Yaakov, the chosen of the Avos, needed to receive Torah at all, when Avraham attained the whole Torah by himself.

title.en: Portions of Torah belonging to particular souls

summary.en: The Rav answers that certain parts of Torah are given to only one person in a generation, as when the Ba'al Shem Tov received a level after the Or HaChaim passed away, and as Eli passed the tradition to Shmuel, who began something new. He then explains that each of the seven shepherds has his own inyan and that Yosef alone is called tzaddik, through his trials.

title.en: Seder Taharos, Yosef's own portion

summary.en: Following the Arizal, the six orders of Mishnah correspond to the six days, and Taharos, learned on Friday, is Yosef's; Yosef attained it himself through his trials and holiness, as Avraham attained the whole Torah. The Rav then speaks of Yaakov's bond with the sheep and of how Yaakov sensed holiness in the produce that came from Egypt through Yosef.

title.en: Chanukah is Yosef

summary.en: The Rav brings from the sefarim that Chanukah is Yosef: Vayeshev, Mikeitz and Vayigash, the parshiyos about Yosef, fall around Chanukah, and the Chanukah flame is Yosef's level, as in 'Beis Yosef lehavah'. He then tells a story the Imrei Emes brings from his father about the Chozeh of Lublin, much of which the recording does not preserve.

title.en: Torah with yiras Shamayim endures

summary.en: The Rav says the Chanukah light must be made lasting, and that one kollel is not like another: a kollel learning Torah with yiras Shamayim and a mussar approach has a kiyum. He compares it to Yosef's produce that lasted when Egypt's stores rotted, calls on those gathered to support the kollel, and closes with a brachah of the light of Chanukah and Torah.

catalogTitle: בפרשה זו נטמן משיח בן יוסף ומשיח בן דוד. שייכות לחנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Parshas Vayeshev holds the roots of both Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef, and that the light of Moshiach, which descends to the lowest places, is revealed through the Chanukah lights.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that the weekly parsha is bound up with the events of its week, and tells how the Belzer Rav linked a frozen river to children learning a winter parsha. Vayeshev and Miketz are tied to Chanukah: wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, which hints at souls that only Chanukah's light can kindle, and the Chanukah lamp stands below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah descends to the fallen. He asks why the story of Yehuda and Tamar interrupts the story of Yosef, brings Rashi that Potiphar's wife also meant it for Heaven, and the Kad HaKemach that the light of Moshiach is revealed in the Chanukah lights. His answer: one parsha brings the birth of Peretz, root of Moshiach ben David, the other leads to Asenath and Ephraim, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, two ways Hashem steers history. He ends with Yosef's test on the idolaters' festival, the tekufah, and Chanukah's light on the darkest night.

en: The weekly parsha is connected to the matters of its week, and Vayeshev and Miketz carry themes connected to Chanukah.
The light of Chanukah, brought down through the mesirus nefesh of the Chashmonaim, can kindle even souls that Shabbos cannot kindle.
Citing the Kad HaKemach, the Rav says that while the Chanukah lights burn, the hidden light, the light of Moshiach, is revealed in them.

The parsha of Yehuda and Tamar holds the birth of Moshiach ben David through Peretz, and the parsha of Yosef and Potiphar's wife leads to Moshiach ben Yosef through Asenath and Ephraim, so both Mashiachs are found in this sidra.
Hashem steers history in two ways: sometimes salvation comes through the good deeds of tzaddikim, and sometimes through the acts of the wicked, who are unknowing tools of His plan.
Yosef refused Potiphar's wife even though she argued that Moshiach would come from them, holding that one may not bring Moshiach through an aveirah.
Chanukah usually falls near the tekufah, the longest night, and on that darkest night the Jews kindle the light of Moshiach.

title.en: The weekly parsha and the Belzer Rav's frozen river

summary.en: The Rav says the weekly parsha is tied to what happens that week, and tells of timber merchants who came to Rabbi Sholom of Belz when the river stayed frozen at Nissan time; he told them the children were learning a winter parsha and should learn the parsha of the week.

title.en: Wicks unfit for Shabbos and souls lit on Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah and explains, with the sefarim, that they stand for souls: Shabbos cannot kindle some souls, but Chanukah's light can. He adds that the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten tefachim because on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to those who cannot raise themselves.

title.en: Why Yehuda and Tamar interrupt Yosef's story

summary.en: The Rav asks why the parsha of Yehuda and Tamar is placed in the middle of the story of Yosef's sale, and brings Rashi that just as Tamar meant it for Heaven, Potiphar's wife also did, having seen through astrology that she would have children from Yosef. He then introduces the Kad HaKemach of Rabbeinu Bachya, also discussed in the Bnei Yissaschar.

title.en: The light of Moshiach in the Chanukah lights

summary.en: Following the Kad HaKemach, the Rav explains that the hidden light of the six days of creation, the light of Moshiach, is revealed while the Chanukah lights burn, and eyes made pure through Torah and mitzvos can see it. He says all the signs show this is the generation of Moshiach, who comes down to a very low generation, and that the signs are given so people will do teshuvah.

title.en: Two parshiyos, two Mashiachs

summary.en: The Rav answers the question: in the parsha of Yehuda, Peretz is born, the ancestor of David and root of Moshiach ben David, while Rashi's comment that Potiphar's wife saw children that would come from her daughter Asenath leads to Ephraim and Moshiach ben Yosef. Both parshiyos begin with a descent, hinting that the light of Chanukah and of both Mashiachs comes down to the lowest generation, the heel.

title.en: History as Hashem's plan: through tzaddikim and through the wicked

summary.en: The Rav says the two parshiyos show two ways Hashem leads the world. All of Jewish history, from Avraham through Mitzrayim, the exiles and the unbroken mesorah of Torah, is a wondrous plan; sometimes salvation comes through tzaddikim's deeds, and sometimes the wicked, without knowing it, become the cause of a yeshuah, as with the sale of Yosef.

title.en: Yehuda's desire, Yosef's refusal, and Asenath

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the two births: Yehuda was overpowered by an angel of desire, as the Midrash says, yet Peretz came from it; Potiphar's wife argued that Moshiach ben Yosef would come from her, but Yosef refused to bring Moshiach through an aveirah. Unlike Tamar, who would not shame Yehuda, she had Yosef thrown into prison, which led him to Pharaoh's throne and to marry Asenath, Dinah's daughter raised in Potiphar's house.

title.en: Yosef's test on the idolaters' festival

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rashi tells that the day Yosef came home was the Egyptians' festival, and answers with the Rambam that impure thoughts come only to a mind empty of Torah: that day was the tekufah, a day on which Jews have the custom not to learn Torah. He brings the Gemara in Avodah Zarah that the festival at the tekufah began with Adam HaRishon and was turned by the nations into a day of idolatry.

title.en: Chanukah's light on the darkest night

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yosef came to do his accounts because on that day he could not learn Torah, and connects the day to Chanukah, which falls near the tekufah. The sitra achra imitates kedushah, he says, darkening the night of the 25th with its own lights against the light of Chanukah, and even imitating the eighth day of Chanukah; but on the darkest night the Jews kindle the light of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: The נצחון of the קדושה of יוסף in the Deep טומאה of מצרים. Explanation of the words אלמתי קמה and יוסף's נסיון in מצרים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the halacha that one who raises a child is considered its parent was hidden even from Yaakov Avinu: only so could Yosef face the tests of Eshes Potiphar and become Yosef HaTzaddik, whose holiness protected Klal Yisrael and stands behind Chanukah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yosef's dream of the sheaves and Rashi's reading that Yaakov's words 'your mother' meant Bilhah, who raised Yosef, and asks why Yaakov did not know that whoever raises a child counts as its parent. He then asks why Eshes Potiphar, who meant to bring Moshiach ben Yosef and did not know whether it would come through her or her daughter, did not simply have Yosef marry her daughter. He lays three foundations: Yosef alone earned the title tzaddik by guarding the bris through tests; certain halachos are revealed only in their time; and Asnas was Dinah's daughter, adopted by Potiphar's wife. A long digression applies Torah to the Arab struggle over Eretz Yisrael. The answer: the halacha of adoption stayed hidden so that Yosef would be tested, become a tzaddik, and keep Klal Yisrael pure in Mitzrayim. He closes by linking Chanukah to the holiness of Yosef.

en: Following Rashi, Yaakov's 'your mother' referred to Bilhah who raised Yosef, which raises the question why Yaakov did not know that one who raises a child counts as the parent.
The title tzaddik belongs specifically to Yosef, because he guarded the holiness of the bris through a year of daily tests in Potiphar's house.
Certain halachos given at Sinai remain hidden until their proper time, such as Moavi velo Moavis, revealed only through Boaz.
Asnas was not Eshes Potiphar's natural daughter but Dinah's daughter whom she adopted, so she did not know that Asnas counted as her own.
The whole matter of Chanukah is the victory of the holiness of Yosef, which is why his parshiyos are read in the week of Chanukah.

title.en: Alumasi and Yaakov's 'your mother'

summary.en: The Rav brings the reading that 'alumasi' in Yosef's dream alludes to Rachel keeping quiet, and asks why only her silence is mentioned. He then brings Rashi that Yaakov's 'your mother' meant Bilhah who raised Yosef, and asks why Yaakov did not know that one who raises a child counts as the parent.

title.en: Tamar, Eshes Potiphar and the kasha

summary.en: The Rav explains why the parsha of Yehuda and Tamar is placed next to Yosef and Eshes Potiphar: both meant it for the sake of Heaven, one for Moshiach ben David and one for Moshiach ben Yosef. He then asks why Eshes Potiphar, not knowing whether the offspring would come from her or her daughter, did not have Yosef marry her unmarried daughter instead of taking the risk herself.

title.en: Why Yosef alone is called HaTzaddik

summary.en: In the first of three foundations, the Rav explains that each of the seven shepherds has his own distinction, and Yosef's is tzaddik, the one who guards the holiness of the bris. He describes the seventeen-year-old Yosef's daily tests and threats from Eshes Potiphar, and explains that a title is earned only through tests, which is why the brothers, though holy, are not called tzaddik.

title.en: The Torah as the blueprint of the world

summary.en: Opening the second foundation, the Rav explains that Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, like an architect with a blueprint, and brings the Kotzker that the world is the text and the Torah its commentary. He tells of a woman who asked him for his view of world events, and says he looks into the Torah to understand the world.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah and Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav brings that the angel of Yishmael claimed Eretz Yisrael because Yishmael also has milah, and Hashem answered that their milah is empty, not a bris, so they would hold the land only while it is empty. Now that a third of Klal Yisrael has returned, the Arabs sense their end and fight like a candle flaring before it goes out.

title.en: Halachos revealed in their time

summary.en: Returning to his point, the Rav says the Avos could read the Torah out of the world, yet some matters of Torah are revealed only at their time, like the halacha of Moavi velo Moavis revealed through Boaz, Purim and Chanukah, and the prophecy of Yeshayahu. He then introduces the third foundation from Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer and Targum Yonasan.

title.en: Asnas, daughter of Dinah

summary.en: The Rav tells how Yaakov saved Dinah's daughter from the angry brothers, hung a charm with his name around her neck, and how the angel Gavriel brought her to the childless house of Potiphar, who adopted her. When the girls threw jewelry at Yosef, Asnas threw her charm; Yosef recognized his father's writing and asked for her.

title.en: The answer: a halacha hidden for Yosef's tests

summary.en: The Rav answers: Asnas was only adopted, and Eshes Potiphar did not know that an adopted daughter counts as her own. Yosef did not tell her because he did not know, and he did not know because Yaakov did not know; the halacha was hidden so that Yosef would have his tests and become the tzaddik whose merit kept Klal Yisrael pure in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Chanukah and the holiness of Yosef

summary.en: Briefly, the Rav says that Chanukah is the victory of the holiness of Yosef: Melech Yavan equals Yosef in gematria, and Yehudis annulled the decree against Jewish brides, which is why women are obligated in Chanukah lights and why dairy is eaten. The parshiyos of Yosef are read in Chanukah week, and he says a Jew should strengthen his own boundaries to connect with Kedushas Yosef.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Hashem runs the world by two seemingly opposite ways, the way of Yosef, who keeps the Torah literally whatever the outcome, and the way of Yehuda, through whom Hashem's plan, and Moshiach himself, comes about even through an aveirah, and shows both in Yehuda and Tamar, Yosef and Potiphar's wife, and Pinchas and the sin of Shittim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the haftarah's two sticks of Yehuda and Yosef that Hashem will make into one, bound by a covenant of peace. He compares history to a train running between creation and the perfected world on two tracks that seem to go opposite ways, knowledge and free choice, a question that remains a question. After a digression on the fasts of Teves, he names the two ways: Yosef's, of keeping the Torah literally without calculating results, and Yehuda's, in which Hashem brings about His plan even through an aveirah. The Midrash pairing Tamar with Potiphar's wife, both acting for Heaven's sake, shows Moshiach ben Dovid born through Yehuda while Yosef refuses to bring Moshiach ben Yosef. Moshiach comes hidden, through breaches like Peretz. He then reads the sin of Shittim the same way: the tribes sought Moshiach through Moav, Baal Peor was the idol of rationalization, Bilaam disguised Midianite women, and Pinchas, the ehrliche Yid, ruined the plan.

en: Hashem leads the world on two tracks that seem to contradict each other, like knowledge and free choice, and the contradiction is beyond human understanding, yet the train of humanity keeps moving toward the perfected world.
From the side of man, the way of Yosef: a Jew must keep the Torah to the letter and not weigh what good might come of an aveirah.
From Hashem's side, the way of Yehuda: Hashem sometimes carries out His plan precisely through an aveirah, as with Yehuda and Tamar, from whom Moshiach descends.
Potiphar's wife wanted to bring Moshiach ben Yosef, and Yosef refused, saying in effect that he is not obligated to bring Moshiach but to be an ehrliche Yid who keeps the Torah.
Moshiach comes through hidden and unexpected roots, like Lot and Moav and Peretz, because malchus breaks through barriers.
The sin of Shittim began with an intention to bring Moshiach through Bnos Moav, and one aveirah led to another, to Baal Peor, the idol that justifies disgusting deeds by a good intention.
Pinchas, who acted as an ehrliche Yid by the Shulchan Aruch, overturned Bilaam's scheme, and the Rav says one should be like Pinchas and not try to be over-wise.

title.en: Two sticks made one; the train on two tracks

summary.en: The Rav opens with the haftarah of Vayigash, where the sticks of Yehuda and of Yosef become one and Hashem makes a covenant of peace between them. He then compares history to a train running from creation to the perfected world on two tracks that seem to go opposite ways, knowledge and free choice, citing the Rambam and the Raavad and concluding that the question remains while the train runs on.

title.en: The darkness of the fasts of Teves

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the dark there are moments of light that show the Conductor, and turns to the three fasts of Teves in Megillas Taanis: the Torah's translation into Greek, which brought cultural contact with the nations, the unexplained ninth of Teves, which the Selichos tie to Ezra's passing, and the siege of Yerushalayim on the tenth. Vayigash, he says, is always read in that week and must be connected to these days.

title.en: The way of Yosef and the way of Yehuda

summary.en: The Rav defines the two ways: a tzaddik must act in the way of Yosef, keeping the Torah literally without weighing results, as Yeshaya told Chizkiyahu not to meddle in Hashem's secrets. Hashem, however, sometimes brings about His plan through an aveirah and even hires transgressors as His agents, and this is the way of Yehuda.

title.en: Tamar and Potiphar's wife, both for Heaven's sake

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that asks why the story of Yehuda and Tamar interrupts the story of Yosef, and answers that just as Tamar acted for Heaven's sake, so did Potiphar's wife, who saw in the stars that she would be bound to Yosef. He explains that even before Egypt began, the line of Dovid and Moshiach was being formed through Yehuda and Tamar, and brings the Midrash that the angel over desire turned Yehuda from his way against his will.

title.en: Yehuda's holy desire and 'from Me'

summary.en: The Rav stresses the greatness of the Shevatim: Yehuda had no desire for this world, only a holy desire for Moshiach, and like the great tzaddikim of whom Rebbe Nachman of Breslov speaks, his yetzer was a holy angel that compelled him. The heavenly voice of 'from Me' testifies that it came from Hashem, so Yehuda's aveirah brought Moshiach; the next parsha, of Yosef, belongs to Moshiach ben Yosef.

title.en: Yosef refuses to bring Moshiach ben Yosef

summary.en: The Rav explains that Potiphar's wife wanted to bring Moshiach ben Yosef, as Yehuda had done for Moshiach ben Dovid, and argued it was a great mitzvah. Yosef, as Rashi explains, refused; he held to his own way, that he is not obligated to bring Moshiach but to be an ehrliche Yid, and the Rav says this is the way from man's side, while Hashem uses the way of Yehuda, especially in bringing Moshiach.

title.en: Moshiach hidden from the Satan

summary.en: The Rav shows that Moshiach comes from Lot through Moav and Rus, and brings from the early sources that the Satan blocks Moshiach, so Hashem hides him where no one would look, like a diamond hidden in garbage. Everything, even the stormy wind, serves Hashem's will; such things happen to the great ones of Yehuda because Yehuda, as king, is fully nullified to Hashem and through him Malchus Shamayim is revealed.

title.en: Peretz, the breach of malchus, and the sale of Yosef

summary.en: The Rav explains that a king breaks through barriers, so Peretz, ancestor of Moshiach, was born by breaking through ahead of Zerach. He then brings the Midrash that once Yosef was sold all the strife of the brothers vanished, because Yehuda's plan had accomplished Hashem's plan, as the passuk in Yeshayahu suggests that Hashem put hatred in their hearts. He warns that one who reads these Midrashim and seeks to do great things through an aveirah falls, as many have.

title.en: Pinchas and the tribes' intention at Shittim

summary.en: The Rav turns to Pinchas: his covenant of peace, which the Targum Yonasan explains as his becoming Eliyahu, the herald of the redemption, and the tribes' mockery of him despite his ten miracles. He asks why Midian, not Moav, was punished, links Bilaam with Lavan and Amalek, and explains that the generation of knowledge, Zimri among them, knew that Moshiach would come from Moav and sought contact with Bnos Moav purely for Heaven's sake, with mesirus nefesh, citing the Lubliner; but one aveirah led to the idol of Baal Peor.

title.en: Baal Peor, the idol of rationalization

summary.en: The Rav asks why the sin led specifically to Baal Peor. From the Rambam on the generation of Enosh he shows that idolatry began with a lofty-seeming intention, and he defines idolatry as rationalization, the natural refusal to admit one's own weakness, as in the Gemara that Jews served idols only to permit forbidden relations. Baal Peor, a disgusting service, was the idol that justifies a disgusting deed by a good intention, fitting those who began with Bnos Moav to bring Moshiach; its gematria equals 'the king Moshiach'.

title.en: Bilaam's disguise and Pinchas's zeal

summary.en: The Rav notes the change in the pesukim from Bnos Moav to Bnos Midian: Bilaam, fearing that Moshiach would come, had Midianite women appear dressed as Moavite women, so Kozbi was in truth of Midian. Pinchas, an ehrliche Yid, killed her and ruined the whole plan, and the tribes mocked him, holding he lacked their lofty grasp; the Rav brings a Tosafos on Miriam and Moshe, and concludes that Pinchas, rooted in the holiness of Aharon, knew one must act by the Shulchan Aruch and not be over-wise, and could not let Moshiach be stained.

catalogTitle: ויגש נוט' - וויי געשריגן! הכנת הגאולה לפני התחלת הגלות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Vayigash, the parsha in which the galus of Mitzrayim begins and which is read before Asarah b'Teves, is a cry of 'woe' that already holds the hidden preparation of the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yehudah, who accepted slavery for all the brothers as the decree of galus but fought over Binyamin alone, and who, by taking the suffering upon himself and seeing everything as from Hashem, brought about Yosef's revelation. He reads the Midrash 'Woe to us from the day of judgment' and a teaching that Vayigash spells 'vey geshrien', a cry of woe: the brothers were shaken by Yosef's hidden holiness, as all will be when Hashem says 'Ani Hashem'. The whole parsha is such a cry, since the galus begins in it, yet the geulah is prepared there. Through the wagons Yosef sent, recalling Yaakov's escort and the eglah arufah, the Rav shows that Yaakov feared for Yosef's spiritual survival and was revived by the sign. He ends with Ezra, who died on the ninth of Teves, and with connecting to his kedushah.

en: Yehudah's feeling that everything happening to him came from the Ribono shel Olam aroused Yosef's revelation, and in the same way, when Hashem reveals Himself, it will be seen that there never was a galus.
Vayigash is a cry of woe because the galus of Mitzrayim begins in it and it is read on the Shabbos before Asarah b'Teves, yet the geulah is already prepared in the same parsha.
The wagons Yosef sent were a sign of the escort Yaakov gave him when they parted, when they were learning the parsha of eglah arufah.
Yaakov never believed Yosef was physically dead; he feared for Yosef's spiritual survival in Mitzrayim, since Yosef carries the sixth middah, the holiness of the bris.
Ezra, who died on the ninth of Teves, fought assimilation and brought Jews close, and the Rav calls for connecting with his kedushah, through his takanah of tevilah, as a help toward the geulah.

title.en: Yehudah takes the suffering upon himself

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yehudah, who had agreed that all the brothers would be slaves, now goes to war over Binyamin. He explains that Yehudah saw slavery for all as the decree of galus, and brings the Pri Tzaddik: Yehudah concluded that Yosef, who had suffered for all, must be dead, took that role upon himself, and then Yosef revealed himself.

title.en: 'Woe to us from the day of judgment'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash 'Woe to us from the day of judgment' on the brothers' fright, and a teaching that Vayigash is an acronym for 'vey geshrien', a cry of woe. With the Sfas Emes he explains that the brothers were shaken by Yosef's hidden holiness, the inner point of the bris covered by the orlah, and that the shame of the future will be seeing that inner point in everything.

title.en: From 'Ani Yosef' to 'Ani Hashem'

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yehudah's 'bi adoni' expressed his feeling that everything befalling him came from the Ribono shel Olam, and this aroused Yosef's revelation. So too, when Hashem says 'Ani Hashem', it will be seen that the galus was never a galus; he brings the Zohar on Yosef being appeased when taken from the pit and the passuk 'bivchi yavo'u' as a weeping of joy.

title.en: Why the whole parsha is a cry

summary.en: The Rav asks why the whole parsha is called Vayigash, and answers that in it Yaakov and the Shechinah go down into the galus of Mitzrayim, and it is read on the Shabbos before Asarah b'Teves, when the churban began. Yet the geulah is already hidden in the parsha, and Shabbos, a time above the galus, lets one see it; one should fill oneself with emunah from it and carry it into Asarah b'Teves.

title.en: The wagons and Yaakov's escort

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash and Rashi that the wagons hinted to the eglah arufah Yaakov and Yosef learned when they parted. With the Da'as Zekeinim he explains why: Yaakov escorted Yosef, since escort protects the one who goes, and when Yosef urged him back, Yaakov cited the elders of the eglah arufah who say they did not send the slain man off without escort.

title.en: Wagons of galus, wagons of geulah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Da'as Zekeinim's difficulty that agalos means wagons, not a calf, and its alternative that they learned the parsha of the six wagons of the Nesi'im, along with the Midrash, the Matnos Kehunah and the Ramban on eglah arufah. Then he brings the passuk that the nations will bring the Jews back 'with tzabim', and concludes that the same wagons that carry into galus hint to the return, for the geulah is hinted where the galus is.

title.en: Yaakov's fear for Yosef's spirit

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov never believed Yosef was dead: on 'chayah ra'ah achalas'hu' Rashi sees a hint to Potiphar's wife and Targum Yonasan says it openly, so Yaakov feared for Yosef's spiritual life. His refusal to be consoled shows he knew Yosef was alive, and his fear came because Yosef carries the sixth middah, the tzaddik and the holiness of the bris, in Mitzrayim, the place of immorality.

title.en: Bereishis: the sixth middah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov, the tikkun of Adam HaRishon after Adam and Noach failed, feared that this attempt too had failed, since the world was created for the sixth middah, Yosef's middah of guarding kedushah, and a lone youth could hardly keep it in Mitzrayim. Yosef surprised him: he brings the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov and Rashi on 'bigdei shesh' and the Zohar's reading of Bereishis as 'bris esh', fighting the fire of the yetzer hara with fire.

title.en: Yosef's middah and the redemption

summary.en: The Rav brings that the sea saw Yosef's coffin and fled, and a Midrash that the names of the tribes hint to the redemption, explaining that the Jews were redeemed through holding fast to Yosef's middah. Yaakov therefore feared the whole plan of the geulah had failed: he believed his physical escort protected Yosef, but not that his spiritual power could guard him in Mitzrayim.

title.en: The father's image and the turning wheel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's power did accompany Yosef: his father's image appeared to him and saved him, because Yosef bound himself to his father's kedushah. Yosef sent wagons because a wheel turns around one fixed point, and so everything revolves around the inner point of Yesod; with them he told his father that the escort helped him in spirit even more than in body.

title.en: Not ashamed of six

summary.en: The Rav brings a rule of human nature: a person avoids mentioning the thing in which he failed, as the nations fear the number thirteen, which holds the kedushah of Yisrael, the thirteen covenants of milah. Yosef, unashamed of six, sent six wagons, as he wore 'bigdei shesh', a sign that he had not fallen, and so 'the spirit of Yaakov revived'.

title.en: Shabbos Vayigash escorts into Asarah b'Teves

summary.en: The Rav returns to the sea that saw Yosef's coffin, then explains that Shabbos is Yaakov's portion, and its departure on the Shabbos before Asarah b'Teves is like Yaakov escorting Yosef, as Hashem told Yaakov 'I will go down with you'. So Vayigash is a cry, but a cry of geulah and of 'Ani Yosef', not of galus.

title.en: Ezra and the ninth of Teves

summary.en: The Rav brings Megillas Ta'anis on the eighth of Teves, when the Torah was translated into Greek, and the Magen Avraham that Ezra HaSofer died on the ninth. Ezra stopped the intermarriage of his time, which the Rav likens to the assimilation of the days before Moshiach, and brought Jews close; Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, the tenth generation from Ezra, continued this, and of Ezra's ten takanos the tevilah of a ba'al keri expresses his essence.

title.en: Connecting with the kedushah of Ezra

summary.en: The Rav teaches, in the name of the Ba'al Shem Tov, that a person is where his thoughts are, so one can bind himself to kedushah even from afar. He says that one whose heart aches over the churban and wants to help the geulah should connect with Ezra's kedushah, also through his tevilah, and ties it back to Asarah b'Teves, when the siege covered Yerushalayim like the orlah over the bris, and to the parsha, which holds the root of the geulah.

catalogTitle: שלא להתערב במחלוקת של צדיקים; ואודות ח' ט' וי' טבת

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches from Parshas Vayigash that in galus Jews must hold together, must not mix into the disputes of tzaddikim, and must regain the fine sensitivity of yiras shamayim whose loss the fasts of the eighth, ninth and tenth of Teves mourn.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Vayigash as the parsha of going down into galus, and finds its first advice in love between Jews: Yehuda approaches Yosef to awaken love, and Yosef rose through his care for others. Through the Be'er Mayim Chaim he explains why Yosef hid from his father: all twelve shevatim had to come to Egypt in secret to plant kedushah there. Since tzaddikim are above us, he says, we cannot judge them; from the Midrash on the shevatim watching Yehuda and Yosef, and stories of Ropshitz, Lentshna, Reb Baruch'l and the Kedushas Levi, he warns not to mix into their disputes. He then turns to Teves: the Greek translation of the Torah brought darkness, and Klal Yisrael lost its sensitivity. A shochet must have yiras shamayim to feel a fine nick, and a recent blow to that limb calls for a reckoning. He ends with discussions of damages, tikkun and gilgulim.

en: The Rav says the first advice for galus, given at the start of Vayigash, is love and unity among Jews, as Yehuda sought to awaken love in Yosef.
Following the Be'er Mayim Chaim, Yosef hid himself from Yaakov because the twelve shevatim had to gather in Egypt in secret to plant kedushah there, and a yichud must be hidden to succeed.
The Rav teaches that one may not mix into disputes between tzaddikim, since we cannot understand them, as the shevatim said of Yehuda and Yosef that it was not their concern.
The fasts of Teves mourn the darkness that came with the Greek translation of the Torah, which had the body of the Torah without its soul.
The Rav explains that yiras shamayim gives a fine sensitivity: the Mechaber requires a shochet to be God-fearing so that he can feel even a tiny nick in the knife.
A Jew is measured by small things, and an erliche Yid feels a flaw even where halachah permits, as the talmid of Lechovitch sensed in meat from a shochet who had not gone to the mikveh.
The Rav says that when Klal Yisrael is struck in its limb of yiras shamayim, each person must make a reckoning whether he still senses the hidden darkness.

title.en: Vayigash: love between Jews as the strength for galus

summary.en: The Rav calls Vayigash the parsha of descent into galus and says its advice for chizuk is love among Jews: Yaakov's call to gather, Yehuda awakening love in Yosef, and Yosef's own care for the butler and baker. He adds a story of the Yesod HaAvodah about the value of a good friend for chizuk.

title.en: Why Yosef hid from his father

summary.en: The Rav brings the Be'er Mayim Chaim's question why Yosef pained his father and brothers, and its answer: Egypt is a limb of the world steeped in impurity, and to plant kedushah there all twelve shevatim had to come together in secret. He compares this to the silent Shemoneh Esrei, which must be hidden before the loud repetition.

title.en: We cannot judge what tzaddikim do

summary.en: The Rav finishes the Be'er Mayim Chaim: only once Binyamin came and all twelve were together could Yosef reveal himself. Without this, one could complain about Yosef; so too we have no grasp of what tzaddikim do, as the Ba'al Shem Tov explains that to understand someone one must stand above him, and as the Chasam Sofer says a talmid chacham feels what others do not.

title.en: The shevatim stay out of the kings' dispute

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yehuda and Yosef argued with sharp words, hinted in 'let your anger not flare', and that the trembling shevatim said: kings are disputing with each other, what is it to us. He reads this with the Chasam Sofer's words as a lasting lesson not to mix into disputes between the gedolim.

title.en: Ropshitz and Lentshna: a persecution that protects

summary.en: After noting that Vayeishev is a dispute between tzaddikim, unlike earlier battles of good against evil, the Rav tells of the bitter dispute between Reb Naftali of Ropshitz and Reb Shlomo Leib of Lentshna. The Lentshner's wife brought a kvittel to a great tzaddik, who told her the Ropshitzer's persecution was the greatest favor, freeing her husband from far harsher heavenly judgment.

title.en: Those who joined in paid the price

summary.en: The Rav tells of a great talmid of the Ropshitzer who, at a bris where the Lentshner came late, did the milah himself, then fled to Ropshitz and later ended up broken for life. He concludes that we are not to put our heads between great men, and adds the story of Reb Baruch'l, who knocked the Kedushas Levi so that heaven would still see the need for Moshiach.

title.en: Yehuda's strength: the spark that never despairs

summary.en: Returning to Vayigash, the Rav explains that the name Yehuda carries Hashem's name and the Shechinah goes with every Jew into galus. Yehuda, guilty over Yosef and now over Binyamin, did not despair, because he knew he had a spark of kedushah; with that same spark Jews in Egypt kept their identity.

title.en: The fasts of Teves and Klal Yisrael as one body

summary.en: The Rav brings Megillas Taanis on the eighth of Teves, when the Torah was translated into Greek, the body of the Torah without its soul, and darkness fell for three days; on the ninth something happened that is unknown, and on the tenth Yerushalayim was besieged. He then explains that Klal Yisrael is one complete body in which every Jew is a limb serving Hashem in his own way.

title.en: The shochtim: the limb of emunah and yiras shamayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the shochtim are the limb on which the purity of the heart and emunah depend, since forbidden food dulls the heart. From the Mechaber in Hilchos Shechitah he shows that a shochet needs yiras shamayim, not just sensitive fingers, to feel a fine nick in the knife.

title.en: A blow to the community: what is asked of us

summary.en: Turning to a tragedy that befell one of those who supply kosher food to much of the city, the Rav distinguishes the private side, which is not our business since Hashem's judgments fit together on every side, from the communal side: we must ask why we were struck in the limb of yiras shamayim and sensitivity.

title.en: Small things and the talmid of Lechovitch

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew is measured not by the big mitzvos but by a hundred small things, like the size of a yarmulke or negel vasser by the bed. He tells of a talmid of Lechovitch who would not eat meat that was kosher by halachah, sensing that the shochet had not gone to the mikveh as Ezra's takanah requires.

title.en: Glatt kosher with coarseness

summary.en: From the Gemara at the end of Sotah that when tahara ceased the fragrance ceased, the Rav explains that one must feel the pegam even where halachah permits. He criticizes bringing gentile foods into a Jewish mouth under a glatt kosher label, brings the Midrash that Esav's food was red too, and tells how the Vaitzener Rav, who sensed such flaws, banged on the table at a gathering of rabbanim.

title.en: Jewish food, and sensing the hidden darkness

summary.en: The Rav tells how a Lubavitcher Rebbe in Germany refused chocolate he had not seen by his fathers, holding that a Jew must eat Jewish food as he keeps Jewish dress, language and names, and laments that in America the sensitivity is lost. He explains that Chanukah comes before Vayigash: just as one senses the hidden light, one must sense the hidden darkness.

title.en: The eighth and ninth of Teves: Ezra dies a second time

summary.en: The Rav calls for a reckoning and explains that on the eighth of Teves Jews did not feel the darkness of the 'cultural exchange' with the Greeks. On why the ninth of Teves is unexplained while a piyut says Ezra died then, he brings the Gemara that Rav Ada bar Ahava tore kriah again for Rav: Ezra 'died again' when Klal Yisrael lost the sensitivity of his takanah. He closes with the coming vengeance on Edom.

title.en: Adam hamazik: a person can repair

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person who damages is called 'adam' because he can make a tikkun: the Rambam writes that paying is not enough and he must ask forgiveness, which an animal cannot do. He adds that in heaven a sin is not mentioned outright, only the tikkun the person needs.

title.en: Why an owner pays for his animal

summary.en: Building on the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person's possessions are an extension of his soul, shown by Reb Pinchas ben Yair's donkey and the kohen's slave eating terumah, the Rav explains that an owner pays for his ox's damage because a flaw in his own soul spread into it. When an owner feels the damage came from heaven, he should turn broken-hearted to Hashem for help against the yetzer hara.

title.en: Noach's tefillah, the flood and gilgulim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Noach turned to Hashem admitting he could not overcome the yetzer hara alone, and after the flood Hashem said He would bring no more floods because the heart of man is evil from youth. He brings the Yismach Moshe that the flood generations were reincarnated even into animals, plants and earth and kept sinning, while tzaddikim are reincarnated into fish, which is why eating fish on Shabbos is a tikkun.
